To this it can be said that he knew Him with an intellectual knowledge, knowing that He was God and man, the Saviour of the world, born of the Virgin, and soon to come forth in public, to preach and baptize, and to die for all; but he did not know Him by knowledge of His face, that is, knowing from the outward look of His features which person He was, since he did not hold in his memory, in the imaginative power, a definite image or likeness [*phantasma*: the image of a thing held in the imagination] of the shape of Christ's face and body.

paras.t: Sed huic obviare videtur, quod infra ait Joannes: Et ego nesciebam eum; sed qui me misit baptizare in aqua, ille mihi dixit: Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem, hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto. Ex quo certissime constat, quod descensus columbæ in Christum fuit Joanni datus pro signo cognoscendi Christum. Ideo namque adjecit: Ego vidi, et testimonium perhibui, quia hic est Filius Dei. Si ergo loqueretur Joannes de notitia faciali, Christus fuisset ei hoc modo ignotus usque post baptismum, quia secundum tres Evangelistas, Christo ascendente de aqua, aperti sunt cæli, et descendit super eum Spiritus Sanctus. Unde in Luca legitur: Factum est autem, Jesu baptizato et orante, apertum est cælum, etc. Sed hoc dici non licet. Nam Christo ad Joannem accedente, dixit Joannes: Ego a te debeo baptizari, et tu venis ad me? Ergo tunc novit eum secundum faciem.
paras.en: But against this seems to stand what John says further on: [[1:33|And I knew him not: but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me: He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending|Et ego nesciebam eum; sed qui me misit baptizare in aqua, ille mihi dixit: Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem]], [[1:33|he it is that baptizeth with the Holy Ghost|hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto]]. From this it is quite certain that the descent of the dove upon Christ was given to John as a sign by which to know Christ. That is why he added: [[1:34|I saw: and I gave testimony that this is the Son of God|Ego vidi, et testimonium perhibui, quia hic est Filius Dei]]. If, then, John were speaking of knowledge by the face, Christ would in this way have been unknown to him until after the baptism; for according to the three Evangelists, as Christ came up out of the water the heavens were opened and the Holy Ghost descended upon Him[[Matt 3:16||]][[Mark 1:10||]]. Hence we read in Luke: [[Luke 3:21|Now it came to pass, when all the people were baptized, that Jesus also being baptized and praying, heaven was opened|Factum est autem, Jesu baptizato et orante, apertum est cælum]], etc.[[Luke 3:22||]] But this may not be said. For when Christ came to John, John said: [[Matt 3:14|I ought to be baptized by thee, and comest thou to me?|Ego a te debeo baptizari, et tu venis ad me?]] So at that time he knew Him by His face.

paras.t: Ad hanc difficultatem est triplex responsio: Una Chrysostomi, quæ facta est nunc, scilicet, quod non novit eum facialiter usque ad horam baptismi. Hanc responsionem sequitur Thomas, adjiciens, quod Joannes tempore pueritiæ suæ novit Christum puerum; postmodum vero diu in solitudine conversatus, oblitus fuit dispositionis vultus Christi: et forte, quamvis non fuisset oblitus qualiter erat in pueritia dispositus, tamen ob hoc non novisset eum, quum jam crevit in staturam virilem. Ad instantiam vero nunc factam, sequentes hanc viam respondent, quod Deus revelavit Joanni dupliciter Jesum: Primo, in ipso accessu Domini Jesu ad Joannem, antequam baptizaretur. Secundo, post baptismum, per descensum columbæ: et de hoc signo facit mentionem Joannes, quia solennius fuit, et primo sibi promissum seu intimatum. Unde, secundum Chrysostomum, Joannes dicit se Jesum nescisse, non quia penitus eum non novit, sed ut ostenderet testimonium suum de Christo non debere esse suspectum eo quod esset consanguineus ejus. Ideo dicit, Nesciebam eum, quia non novit eum tunc, nisi ex revelatione divina. Ex quo innotescit, quod testimonium Joannis de Christo non fuit humanæ amicitiæ, sed ordinationis divinæ.
paras.en: To this difficulty there is a threefold answer. One is Chrysostom's, the one just given: that he did not know Him by His face until the hour of the baptism. Thomas follows this answer, adding that John in his boyhood knew Christ as a boy, but afterwards, having lived a long time in the wilderness, forgot the look of Christ's face; and perhaps, even had he not forgotten how He looked as a boy, he would not for that reason have known Him, now that He had grown to a man's stature. To the objection just raised [*instantia*: an objection brought against an answer already given], those who take this way reply that God revealed Jesus to John in two ways: first, at the very coming of the Lord Jesus to John, before He was baptized; second, after the baptism, by the descent of the dove; and John makes mention of this sign because it was the more solemn, and was the one first promised or made known to him. Hence, according to Chrysostom, John says that he did not know Jesus, not because he did not know Him at all, but to show that his testimony about Christ ought not to be suspect on the ground that he was His kinsman. So he says, [[1:31|I knew him not|nesciebam eum]], because at that time he knew Him only by divine revelation. From this it becomes plain that John's testimony to Christ came not from human friendship but from God's ordinance.

paras.t: Alia est responsio Bedæ, quod ideo dicit se Joannes Christum nescisse, quia non novit eum tam profunde ac plene ante descensum Spiritus Sancti, ut postea. Alia est responsio Augustini, quod Joannes ideo dicit se Christum nescisse, sed per columbam didicisse, quia non scivit ante descensum columbæ, quod Christus sibi soli servaret, et nulli ministrorum suorum communicaret, potestatem baptizandi, hoc est potestatem excellentiæ in Baptismo: quæ secundum Thomam et alios consistit in quatuor. Primum est, quod solus Christus Baptismum instituit; secundum, quod effectum Baptismi sine Baptismo conferre potest; tertium est, quod Baptismus a merito passionis Christi efficaciam habet; quartum, quod Baptismus interdum in nomine Christi datus est. Hæc itaque didicit Joannes esse futura, descendente super Christum columba. Porro potestas baptizandi et excellentia ejus auctoritative non convenit nisi Deo Trinitati.
paras.en: Another answer is Bede's: that John says he did not know Christ because before the descent of the Holy Ghost he did not know Him as deeply and fully as afterwards. Another is Augustine's: that John says he did not know Christ, but learned of Him through the dove, because before the descent of the dove he did not know that Christ would keep to Himself alone, and share with none of His ministers, the power of baptizing, that is, the power of excellence in Baptism [*potestas excellentiæ*: the power, proper to Christ as man, which He did not give to His ministers]. According to Thomas and others this consists in four things: first, that Christ alone instituted Baptism; second, that He can confer the effect of Baptism without Baptism; third, that Baptism has its efficacy from the merit of Christ's Passion; fourth, that Baptism was at times given in the name of Christ. These things, then, John learned would come to be, when the dove descended upon Christ. Further, the power of baptizing and its excellence belong by authority [that is, as their author and first source] only to God the Trinity.

paras.t: Deinde Præcursor pandit unam rationem sui baptismi. Sed ut manifestetur in Israel, id est, ut Christus agnoscatur a populo Israel, propterea veni ego, Deo jubente, in aqua baptizans, id est, corpora lavans, non mentes sanctificans. Totum enim Joannis officium in prædicando et baptizando, ordinatum fuit ad hoc, ut homines inducerentur ad fidem, amorem atque notitiam Christi, sicut ostensum est plenius. De hac materia et baptismo dixi plura super Matthæum.
paras.en: Next the Forerunner sets out one reason for his baptism: [[1:31|but that he may be made manifest in Israel|Sed ut manifestetur in Israel]], that is, that Christ may be recognized by the people of Israel, [[1:31|therefore am I come|propterea veni ego]], at God's command, [[1:31|baptizing with water|in aqua baptizans]], that is, washing bodies, not sanctifying minds. For the whole office of John, in preaching and in baptizing, was ordered to this: that men might be led to faith in Christ, to love and knowledge of Him, as has been shown more fully. On this matter and on his baptism I have said more upon Matthew[[Matt 3:6||]].

paras.t: Denique quæ sequuntur, Joannes non dixit nisi Christo baptizato. Et testimonium perhibuit Joannes, dicens: Quia vidi Spiritum descendentem quasi columbam de cælo, id est Spiritum Sanctum in forma columbæ visibili: non quod Spiritus Sanctus, qui est verus, incircumscriptus, invariabilis atque immobilis Deus, essentialiter moveatur sive descendat; sed quoniam signum visibile in quo apparet, descendit, sicque Spiritus ratione sui effectus descendere perhibetur. Dum enim creatura subjecta apparet in persona Dei, eum repræsentans, vel in ejus persona loquens aut operans, hoc quandoque adscribitur Deo, quod facit hujusmodi creatura: quemadmodum Deus dicitur ore ad os locutus ad Moysen.
paras.en: What follows, finally, John did not say until Christ had been baptized. [[1:32|And John gave testimony, saying|Et testimonium perhibuit Joannes, dicens]]: [[1:32|I saw the Spirit coming down, as a dove from heaven|Quia vidi Spiritum descendentem quasi columbam de cælo]], that is, the Holy Ghost in the visible form of a dove: not that the Holy Ghost, who is true God, uncircumscribed, unchangeable and immovable, moves or descends in His essence; but because the visible sign in which He appears descends, and so the Spirit is said to descend by reason of His effect. For when a subject creature appears in the person of God, representing Him, or speaking or acting in His person, what such a creature does is sometimes ascribed to God: as God is said to have spoken to Moses [[Num 12:8|mouth to mouth|ore ad os]].

paras.t: Convenienter quoque Spiritus Sanctus, cui bonitas appropriatur, apparuit in forma columbæ, quæ est animal felle carens, simplex et innocens; et ut insinuaret Spiritus Sanctus, quod nemo possit ejus donis impleri, nisi columbinam simplicitatem studuerit imitari. Qui enim ambulat simpliciter, ambulat confidenter; et Dominus protegit gradientes simpliciter. In columbarum etiam osculis crebris ac mutuis patet, quod Spiritus Sanctus in specie columbæ rite apparuit, quoniam caritas appropriatur Spiritui Sancto, et illi Spiritu Sancto merentur repleri, qui satagunt caritative atque pacifice conversari. Non enim est Deus dissensionis, sed pacis, secundum Apostolum.
paras.en: Fittingly, too, the Holy Ghost, to whom goodness is appropriated [that is, attributed to Him in particular, though it is common to the whole Trinity], appeared in the form of a dove, which is an animal without gall, simple and innocent; and so the Holy Ghost would intimate that no one can be filled with His gifts unless he strives to imitate the simplicity of the dove. For [[Prov 10:9|He that walketh sincerely, walketh confidently|Qui ambulat simpliciter ambulat confidenter]] [simpliciter: literally "simply", the dove's simplicity just named]; and the Lord will [[Prov 2:7|protect them that walk in simplicity|protegit gradientes simpliciter]]. In the frequent and mutual kisses of doves, too, it is plain that the Holy Ghost rightly appeared in the likeness of a dove, since charity is appropriated to the Holy Ghost, and those deserve to be filled with the Holy Ghost who take pains to live together in charity and peace. [[1 Cor 14:33|For God is not the God of dissension, but of peace|Non enim est Deus dissensionis, sed pacis]], according to the Apostle.

paras.t: Et mansit super eum, id est, columba ista repræsentans Spiritum Sanctum ejusque habitationem in anima Christi, ad tempus sedit super caput Christi, ad insinuandum quod indesinenter semperque actualiter et æque perfecte requiesceret Spiritus Sanctus in Christo homine, juxta illud dictum Isaiæ: Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini. Sic autem non manet Spiritus Sanctus in aliis, quia mortali peccato perdere possunt Spiritum Sanctum; et venialibus culpis incurrunt quotidie quamdam debilitationem gratiæ Spiritus Sancti, quamvis quotidie per opera sancta magis proficiant quam decrescant.
paras.en: [[1:32|and he remained upon him|Et mansit super eum]], that is, that dove, representing the Holy Ghost and His dwelling in the soul of Christ, sat for a time upon the head of Christ, to intimate that the Holy Ghost would rest in Christ the man unceasingly, always actually and equally perfectly, according to that saying of Isaias: [[Is 11:2|the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him|Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini]]. But the Holy Ghost does not so remain in others, for they can lose the Holy Ghost by mortal sin; and by venial faults they daily incur a certain weakening of the grace of the Holy Ghost, though by holy works they daily advance more than they decline.

paras.t: In Christo quoque mansit Spiritus Sanctus, ita quod Christus indesinenter potens fuit ad exercenda omnia opera, tam gratiæ gratum facientis, quam gratiæ gratis datæ, in universis signis, virtutibus atque prodigiis. Hoc autem nulli competit aliorum. Unde et Eliseus sentiens sibi abesse spiritum prophetalem, jussit adduci psaltem. Nathan quoque putavit se loqui prophetico spiritu, quando consuluit regi David ædificare templum: Omnia, inquiens, quæ sunt in corde tuo, fac. Sed nocte sequenti instructus est a Spiritu Sancto persuadere oppositum. Postremo putandum non est, quod in descensu columbæ sit gratia aliqua infusa vel aucta in anima Christi, qui ab instanti conceptionis plenus fuit simpliciter omni gratia Spiritus Sancti; sed descensus mansioque columbæ in Christo, designavit perfectionem et efficaciam gratiæ Christi.
paras.en: The Holy Ghost also remained in Christ in this sense, that Christ was unceasingly able to perform all the works both of sanctifying grace and of gratuitous grace [gratia gratum faciens, the grace that makes its bearer pleasing to God; gratia gratis data, gifts such as prophecy and miracles given for the good of others], in all signs, mighty works and wonders. But this belongs to none of the others. Hence Eliseus, feeling that the prophetic spirit was absent from him, ordered a minstrel to be brought[[4 Kings 3:15||]]. Nathan, too, thought he was speaking by the prophetic spirit when he counselled King David to build the temple, saying: [[2 Kings 7:3|do all that is in they heart|Omnia, inquiens, quæ sunt in corde tuo, fac]]. But the following night he was instructed by the Holy Ghost to urge the opposite[[2 Kings 7:4||]]. Lastly, it is not to be thought that at the descent of the dove any grace was infused or increased in the soul of Christ, who from the instant of His conception was simply full of all the grace of the Holy Ghost; rather, the descent of the dove and its remaining upon Christ signified the perfection and the efficacy of Christ's grace.

paras.t: Et ego nesciebam eum: secundum sensus prætactos, quia ut dictum est, hoc tripliciter intelligi potest. Expositio tamen Augustini et Bedæ concurrit in idem. Sed qui misit me baptizare in aqua, id est Deus, qui mihi hoc jussit occulta inspiratione, vel manifesta atque sensibili apparitione angelica, ille mihi dixit per inspirationem internam, sive angelicam allocutionem: Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem, id est Spiritum Sanctum in forma columbæ venientem, et manentem super eum ad tempus in tali signo visibili, sicut expositum est; hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto, hoc est intus purgando a vitiis, præstando gratiam Spiritus Sancti. In Baptismate enim quod Christus instituit, datur Spiritus Sanctus. Christus autem baptizat efficienter et principaliter, sacerdos vero ministerialiter.
paras.en: [[1:33|And I knew him not|Et ego nesciebam eum]]: in the senses touched on before, for, as has been said, this can be understood in three ways. The exposition of Augustine and that of Bede, however, come to the same. [[1:33|but he who sent me to baptize with water|Sed qui misit me baptizare in aqua]], that is, God, who commanded me this by a hidden inspiration, or by a manifest and sensible apparition of an angel, [[1:33|said to me|ille mihi dixit]] by an inward inspiration, or by the speech of an angel: [[1:33|He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending|Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem]], that is, the Holy Ghost coming in the form of a dove, [[1:33|and remaining upon him|et manentem super eum]] for a time in such a visible sign, as has been explained, [[1:33|he it is that baptizeth with the Holy Ghost|hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto]], that is, by cleansing inwardly from vices and bestowing the grace of the Holy Ghost. For in the Baptism which Christ instituted the Holy Ghost is given. Christ baptizes as the efficient and principal cause, the priest as minister.

paras.t: Et ego vidi corporalibus oculis Spiritum Sanctum in forma columbæ descendentem modo præfato. Quæ columba, secundum quosdam doctores, fuit vera columba, angelico famulatu subito tunc formata, completoque suo ministerio, in præjacentem materiam resoluta. Aliqui tamen dubitant an hoc angelus posset. Quod relinquo disputantibus. Et testimonium perhibui coram turba, quia hic est Filius Dei naturalis et unicus, non adoptivus. Itaque, quod dicitur, Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem, dictum est Joanni, secundum Augustinum, ad agnoscendum quod Christo competeret potestas excellentiæ in Baptismo; secundum Chrysostomum vero ad agnoscendum determinate quod illa persona esset Christus in Spiritu Sancto baptizans.
paras.en: [[1:34|And I saw|Et ego vidi]] with bodily eyes the Holy Ghost descending in the form of a dove, in the manner described. This dove, according to some doctors, was a real dove, formed suddenly at that moment by the ministry of angels, and, its service done, dissolved into the matter that lay ready beforehand. Some, however, doubt whether an angel could do this. That I leave to the disputants. [[1:34|and I gave testimony|Et testimonium perhibui]] before the crowd, [[1:34|that this is the Son of God|quia hic est Filius Dei]], the natural and only-begotten Son, not an adopted one. So the words [[1:33|He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending|Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem]] were said to John, according to Augustine, that he might know that the power of excellence in Baptism [potestas excellentiæ: the power, proper to Christ, of giving the sacraments their effect and of conferring their effect without them] belonged to Christ; but according to Chrysostom, that he might know definitely that this was the person who was the Christ, baptizing in the Holy Ghost.

paras.t: Altera die, id est una die sequente diem prædictam, mediate vel immediate, iterum stabat Joannes ad fluenta Jordanis, tanquam paratus exsequi officium sibi commissum, in prædicando, baptizando et testificando de Christo. Spiritualiter quoque stabat in culmine perfectionis, in apice contemplationis, in stabilitate virtutum. Optimum enim est gratia stabiliri cor, secundum Apostolum. Et sapiens in sapientia permanet ut sol; stultus vero mutatur ut luna. Et ex discipulis ejus duo, conformantes se suo magistro. Et respiciens Jesum ambulantem, scilicet circa Jordanem. Christus namque suscepto baptismo ad tempus commoratus est in locis illis et cum Joanne conversatus: tamen non diu. Mansit enim, ut Joannes frequenter testaretur de ipso, et eum ostenderet, quatenus electi Judæi crederent, reprobi vero atque increduli inexcusabiles fierent. Dicit: Ecce Agnus Dei: qui, ut in Isaia scribitur, peccatum non fecit, nec dolus inventus est in ore ejus; qui etiam loquitur per Jeremiam: Ego quasi agnus mansuetus qui portatur ad victimam.
paras.en: [[1:35|The next day|Altera die]], that is, on a day following the day just mentioned, whether the very next or a later one, [[1:35|again John stood|iterum stabat Joannes]] by the streams of the Jordan, as one ready to carry out the office committed to him, in preaching, baptizing and bearing witness to Christ. Spiritually, too, he stood on the summit of perfection, on the height of contemplation, in the steadfastness of the virtues. For [[Heb 13:9|it is best that the heart be established with grace|Optimum enim est gratia stabiliri cor]], according to the Apostle. And the wise man [[Ecclus 27:12|continueth in wisdom as the sun: but a fool is changed as the moon|in sapientia permanet ut sol; stultus vero mutatur ut luna]]. [[1:35|and two of his disciples|Et ex discipulis ejus duo]], conforming themselves to their master. [[1:36|And beholding Jesus walking|Et respiciens Jesum ambulantem]], namely about the Jordan. For after receiving baptism Christ stayed for a time in those places and kept company with John, though not for long. He stayed so that John might often bear witness to Him and point Him out, in order that the elect among the Jews might believe, and the reprobate and unbelieving be left without excuse. [[1:36|he saith: Behold the Lamb of God|Dicit: Ecce Agnus Dei]]: who, as is written in Isaias[[Is 53:9||]], [[1 Pet 2:22|did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth|peccatum non fecit, nec dolus inventus est in ore ejus]] [the margin gives both Is. liii, 9 and 1 Pet. ii, 22: the words are those of St Peter, who is echoing Isaias]; who also speaks through Jeremias: [[Jer 11:19|I was as a meek lamb, that is carried to be a victim|Ego quasi agnus mansuetus qui portatur ad victimam]].

paras.t: Et audierunt eum duo discipuli Joannis loquentem, id est Joannem hæc de Christo testantem; et secuti sunt Jesum, ut ejus doctrina instruerentur, quem didicerunt majorem esse Joanne. Cupiebant enim sortiri charismata meliora, et optimo adhærere magistro. Per quod instruimur ut applicemus nos his quos videmus in sapientia et virtutibus præpollere.
paras.en: [[1:37|And the two disciples heard him|Et audierunt eum duo discipuli]] of John [[1:37|speak|loquentem]], that is, heard John bearing this witness to Christ; [[1:37|and they followed Jesus|et secuti sunt Jesum]], to be instructed by His teaching, since they had learned that He was greater than John. For they longed to obtain [[1 Cor 12:31|the better gifts|charismata meliora]] and to cleave to the best of masters. By this we are taught to attach ourselves to those whom we see excelling in wisdom and the virtues.

paras.t: Conversus autem Jesus, hoc est, vultum suum dulcissimum ad illos convertens, imo et pietatis suæ affectum super eos expandens, et videns eos sequentes se corporis gressu, et mente fideli, desiderio quoque proficiendi, dicit eis: Quid quæritis? id est, quare venitis post me? Non quasi ignorans quærit, sed ut illorum responsioni convenienter respondeat, atque ut illi suum desiderium exprimendo, amplius incalescant, et gratiæ præparatiores reddantur. Simili modo si nos cœperimus sequi et quærere Christum, convertet oculum pietatis suæ ad nos, et imbecillitatem nostram juvabit ac perducet ad thronum gratiæ suæ, si tamen constanter quæramus. Ideo monet Psalmista: Lætetur cor quærentium Dominum; quærite Dominum, et confirmamini, quærite faciem ejus semper. Et denuo: Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini.
paras.en: [[1:38|And Jesus turning|Conversus autem Jesus]], that is, turning His most sweet face towards them, and indeed spreading over them the affection of His loving-kindness, [[1:38|and seeing them following him|et videns eos sequentes se]] with the steps of the body and with a faithful mind, and with the desire to advance, [[1:38|saith to them: What seek you?|dicit eis: Quid quæritis?]], that is, why do you come after Me? He asks not as one who does not know, but so as to answer their reply fittingly, and so that they, by putting their desire into words, might grow warmer still and be made readier for grace. In the same way, if we begin to follow and to seek Christ, He will turn the eye of His loving-kindness upon us, and will help our weakness and lead us to the throne of His grace, provided we seek constantly. Therefore the Psalmist admonishes: [[Ps 104:3|let the heart of them rejoice that seek the Lord|Lætetur cor quærentium Dominum]]. [[Ps 104:4|Seek ye the Lord, and be strengthened: seek his face evermore|quærite Dominum, et confirmamini, quærite faciem ejus semper]]. And again: [[Ps 33:6|Come ye to him and be enlightened|Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini]].

paras.t: Qui dixerunt ei: Rabbi. Quod autem subditur, non est sermo eorum, sed verbum Evangelistæ exponentis quid significet verbum Hebraicum Rabbi. Quod dicitur interpretatum, id est, Latine expositum vocatur, magister. Ubi habitas, quasi in hospitio alieno, non quasi in propria domo? Christus enim non habuit propriam domum, quantum ad usum, quamvis ipsius esset terra et plenitudo ejus, orbis terrarum et universi qui habitant in eo. Propter quod ait apud Matthæum: Vulpes foveas habent, et volucres cæli nidos; Filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet. Hoc Jeremias prænoscens et vehementer admirans, ait: Quare quasi colonus venturus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum? Quare venturus es velut vir vagus?
paras.en: [[1:38|Who said to him: Rabbi|Qui dixerunt ei: Rabbi]]. What is added next is not their speech but the word of the Evangelist, explaining what the Hebrew word Rabbi means: [[1:38|which is to say, being interpreted|Quod dicitur interpretatum]], that is, which rendered in Latin is called, [[1:38|Master|magister]]. [[1:38|where dwellest thou?|Ubi habitas]], as in a lodging belonging to another, not as in a house of Thy own? For Christ had no house of His own, as far as use goes, though His were [[Ps 23:1|the earth|terra]] [[Ps 23:1|and the fulness thereof: the world, and all they that dwell therein|et plenitudo ejus, orbis terrarum et universi qui habitant in eo]]. Hence He says in Matthew: [[Matt 8:20|The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head|Vulpes foveas habent, et volucres cæli nidos; Filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet]]. Jeremias, foreseeing this and marvelling greatly, says: [[Jer 14:8|why wilt thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man turning in to lodge?|Quare quasi colonus venturus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum?]]? [[Jer 14:9|Why wilt thou be as a wandering man|Quare venturus es velut vir vagus?]]?

paras.t: Quæsierunt autem ubi Jesus habitaret, quoniam secum pernoctare optabant, quatenus ejus colloquio, præsentia et familiaritate fruerentur. Per quod implicite Christo responderunt quid quærerent. Quærebant enim instructionem salutarem et gratiam Salvatoris, scientes magistrum suum Joannem non mentiri, a quo audierunt quod Jesus esset Agnus Dei tollens peccata mundi, baptizans in Spiritu Sancto, et Filius Dei. Tota equidem vita Christi fuit satisfactoria pro piaculis mundi, et meritoria gratiæ cunctis hominibus; quamvis satisfactio illa et meritum terminabatur et consummabatur in passione et morte Christi. Propter quod Jesus pendens in cruce, et morti jam proximus, dixit: Consummatum est. Ideo Joannes non dixit, Ecce Agnus Dei qui tollet, videlicet in passione, sed, Qui tollit continuo peccata mundi.
paras.en: They asked where Jesus dwelt because they wished to spend the night with Him, so as to enjoy His conversation, His presence and His familiarity. By this they implicitly answered Christ what they were seeking. For they were seeking saving instruction and the grace of the Saviour, knowing that their master John did not lie, from whom they had heard that Jesus was the Lamb of God taking away the sins of the world, baptizing in the Holy Ghost, and the Son of God. Indeed the whole life of Christ was satisfactory for the sins of the world and meritorious of grace for all men [that is, it made satisfaction for sin and merited grace]; though that satisfaction and merit was completed and consummated in the passion and death of Christ. For this reason Jesus, hanging on the cross and now close to death, said: [[John 19:30|It is consummated|Consummatum est]]. Therefore John did not say, [[1:29|Behold the Lamb of God|Ecce Agnus Dei]] who shall take away, namely in the passion, but [[1:29|who taketh away|Qui tollit]], continually, [[1:29|the sin of the world|continuo peccata mundi]].

paras.t: Pariformiter et nos cum Sponsa quæramus ubi habitet Christus, dicentes illud in Canticis: Indica mihi, quem diligit anima mea, ubi pascas, ubi cubes in meridie. Studeamusque stabiliter Christo uniri, imo et actualiter ei quantum possibile est adhærere, exemplo dicentis: Unam petii a Domino, hanc requiram, ut inhabitem in domo Domini; et item, Adhæsit anima mea post te; rursusque, Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus ejus in ore meo.
paras.en: In like manner let us too, with the Bride, seek where Christ dwells, saying that verse of the Canticle: [[Cant 1:6|Shew me, O thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest, where thou liest in the midday|Indica mihi, quem diligit anima mea, ubi pascas, ubi cubes in meridie]]. And let us strive to be united to Christ steadfastly, and indeed to cleave to Him actually, as far as is possible, after the example of him who says: [[Ps 26:4|One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord|Unam petii a Domino, hanc requiram, ut inhabitem in domo Domini]]; and again, [[Ps 62:9|My soul hath stuck close to thee|Adhæsit anima mea post te]]; and once more, [[Ps 33:2|I will bless the Lord at all times, his praise shall be always in my mouth|Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus ejus in ore meo]].

paras.t: Dicit eis Jesus: Venite post me, et videte ubi habitem. Moraliter, secundum Origenem: Venite, bene agendo, ac de virtute in virtutem proficiendo; et videte, Deum deorum suaviter contemplando: quia in vita activa et via purgativa bene exercitati, ad vitam contemplativam, seu viam illuminativam, unitivamque cum Deo perfectionem, sunt apti. Unde et ait illustrissimus pater noster Joannes Cassianus: Oportet ethicam seu moralem præire theoricam. Venerunt duo isti Joannis discipuli, et viderunt ubi maneret Jesus, et apud eum manserunt die illo, id est ab illa hora diei qua cum Jesu domum intrabant, usque ad mane diei sequentis. Intraverunt tamen cum Jesu circa occasum solis, sicut subjungitur: Hora autem erat quasi decima, scilicet circa vesperam. Sic et nos, si venimus bene agendo, et videmus fideliter contemplando ubi habitet Christus, manebimus cum illo in die æternitatis.
paras.en: [[1:39|He saith to them|Dicit eis]] Jesus: [[1:39|Come|Venite]] after Me, [[1:39|and see|et videte]] where I dwell. Morally, according to Origen: Come, by doing well and advancing [[Ps 83:8|from virtue to virtue|de virtute in virtutem]]; and see, by sweetly contemplating [[Ps 83:8|the God of gods|Deum deorum]]: for those who have been well exercised in the active life and the purgative way are fit for the contemplative life, that is, for the illuminative way and the perfection of union with God [the purgative, illuminative and unitive ways: the three classic stages of the spiritual life]. Hence our most illustrious father John Cassian says: Ethics, that is, moral practice, must go before theory [theorica: contemplation]. [[1:39|They came|Venerunt]], those two disciples of John, [[1:39|and saw where he abode|et viderunt ubi maneret]], that is, Jesus, [[1:39|and they stayed with him that day|et apud eum manserunt die illo]], that is, from that hour of the day at which they went into the house with Jesus until the morning of the following day. They went in with Jesus, however, about sunset, as is added: [[1:39|Now it was about the tenth hour|Hora autem erat quasi decima]], that is, towards evening. So we too, if we come by doing well, and see by faithful contemplation where Christ dwells, shall abide with Him in the day of eternity.

paras.t: Erat autem Andreas frater Simonis Petri, unus ex duobus discipulis qui audierant a Joanne testimonium de Jesu, videlicet, Ecce Agnus Dei, et secuti fuerant eum, utpote Jesum. Quidam affirmant, quod alter fuit Joannes evangelista; sed nomen suum subticuit, quoniam consuetudo Scripturæ est, ut scriptores ejus proprium nomen non exprimant, ut frequenter. Vel exprimit nomen Andreæ, quoniam principalior exstitit alio.
paras.en: [[1:40|And Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two|Erat autem Andreas frater Simonis Petri, unus ex duobus]] disciples [[1:40|who had heard of John|qui audierant a Joanne]] the testimony concerning Jesus, namely, [[1:36|Behold the Lamb of God|Ecce Agnus Dei]], [[1:40|and followed him|et secuti fuerant eum]], that is, Jesus. Some affirm that the other was John the Evangelist; but he kept silent about his own name, since it is the custom of Scripture that its writers do not state their own name, as frequently happens. Or he states the name of Andrew because Andrew was the more important of the two.

paras.t: Invenit hic Andreas primum fratrem suum Simonem. Hoc quod ait, Primum, intelligi potest dupliciter: primo sic, Primum, id est primo; secundo sic, Primum, id est majorem et seniorem fratrem suum, Simonem Petrum, qui fuit Andrea antiquior. Et dicit ei Andreas: Invenimus Messiam. Quid autem hoc significet subdit Evangelista: quod nomen Messias, est interpretatum, Christus. Messias quippe est nomen Hebraicum, quod Græce dicitur Christus, et Latine unctus: et competit Salvatori, qui unctus fuit oleo spirituali, tanquam rex summus et sacerdos æternus, non oleo corporali. Unde Psalmista: Dilexisti justitiam, et odisti iniquitatem; propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ. Et Christus per Isaiam: Spiritus (inquit) Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me.
paras.en: [[1:41|He findeth first his brother Simon|Invenit hic Andreas primum fratrem suum Simonem]], Andrew, that is. What he says, *first*, can be understood in two ways: in the first way thus, *first*, that is, firstly; in the second way thus, *first*, that is, his greater and elder brother, Simon Peter, who was older than Andrew. [[1:41|and saith to him|Et dicit ei]] Andrew: [[1:41|We have found the Messias|Invenimus Messiam]]. And what this means, the Evangelist adds: the name Messias is, [[1:41|being interpreted, the Christ|interpretatum, Christus]]. For Messias is a Hebrew name, which in Greek is said *Christus*, and in Latin *unctus* [that is, anointed]; and it befits the Saviour, who was anointed with spiritual oil, as supreme king and eternal priest, not with bodily oil. Hence the Psalmist: [[Ps 44:8|Thou hast loved justice, and hated iniquity: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness|Dilexisti justitiam, et odisti iniquitatem; propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ]]. And Christ says through Isaias: [[Is 61:1|The spirit of the Lord is upon me|Spiritus (inquit) Domini super me]], [[Is 61:1|because the Lord hath anointed me|eo quod unxerit me]].

paras.t: Quemadmodum autem Andreas invenit Jesum, non casualiter, sed eum diligenter sequendo, sic invenit Simonem fratrem suum, non fortuitu, sed post inquisitionem sollicitam. Sentiens enim Andreas fructum et gratiam Christi, desideravit fratrem suum carnalem, quem spiritualiter diligebat, participem facere gratiæ sibi concessæ, ut essent fratres, non dumtaxat carnis propagine, sed fide quoque et religione. Et hæc est bona fraternitas naturæ, quam perficit gratia, et in qua spiritualis dilectio carnalem amorem exstinguit, naturalemque affectionem vincit ac ordinat.
paras.en: Now just as Andrew found Jesus not by chance but by following Him diligently, so he found Simon his brother, not by accident, but after careful search. For Andrew, feeling the fruit and grace of Christ, desired to make his brother in the flesh, whom he loved spiritually, a sharer in the grace granted to himself, so that they might be brothers not only by descent of the flesh but in faith and religion as well. And this is the good brotherhood of nature, which grace perfects, and in which spiritual love extinguishes carnal love, and overcomes and orders natural affection.

paras.t: Et adduxit eum, videlicet Andreas Simonem, ad Jesum. Sic et nos solliciti esse debemus secundum exigentiam nostræ vocationis et veræ caritatis, de salute confratrum et proximorum nostrorum, præcipue parentum, fratrum, sororum et cognatorum, sicut et Petrus admonet, Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, quatenus spiritualis dilectio naturalem informet et dirigat. Istud maxime pertinet ad prælatos, quibus quasi vicariis suis dicit Christus quod Joseph dixit fratribus suis in Genesi: Non videbitis faciem meam, nisi fratrem vestrum minimum adduxeritis ad me, videlicet faciendo pro ejus salvatione, quod in vobis est, et ad quod tenemini ratione officii.
paras.en: [[1:42|And he brought him|Et adduxit eum]], that is, Andrew brought Simon, [[1:42|to Jesus|ad Jesum]]. So we too ought to be solicitous, as our calling and true charity require, for the salvation of our brethren and neighbours, especially of our parents, brothers, sisters and kinsfolk, as Peter too admonishes: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another|Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes]]; so that spiritual love may inform and direct natural love. This pertains most of all to prelates, to whom, as to His vicars, Christ says what Joseph said to his brothers in Genesis: [[Gen 43:3|You shall not see my face, unless you bring your youngest brother|Non videbitis faciem meam, nisi fratrem vestrum minimum adduxeritis]] to me; that is, by doing for his salvation what lies in you, and what you are bound to by reason of your office.

paras.t: Intuitus autem eum, scilicet Simonem, Jesus, non solum oculis carnis, sed pietatis et caritatis respectu interno, sciens quantus esset futurus, et [quanta] pro Christo facturus atque passurus, dixit: Tu es Simon, non solum nomine, sed nominis interpretatione ac proprietate. Simon enim, obediens dicitur. Et Petrus obediens fuit Deo, quia nunquam manducavit omne commune et immundum; juniorique fratri consensit veniendo ad Christum; et postea, Christo vocante, cuncta reliquit, et ei adhæsit. Filius Joanna. Sic enim dictus est pater Petri. Joanna vero interpretatur gratia Dei, et Petrus filius fuit gratiæ Salvatoris. Tu vocaberis Cephas, quod interpretatur Petrus.
paras.en: [[1:42|And Jesus looking upon him|Intuitus autem eum]], that is, upon Simon, not only with the eyes of the flesh but with the inward regard of tenderness and charity, knowing how great he would become, and how much he would do and suffer for Christ, [[1:42|said: Thou art Simon|dixit: Tu es Simon]], not only in name, but in the meaning and property of the name. For Simon means obedient. And Peter was obedient to God, since he never ate [[Acts 10:14|any thing that is common and unclean|omne commune et immundum]]; and he gave way to his younger brother by coming to Christ; and afterwards, when Christ called him[[Matt 4:19||]], he left all things and clung to Him[[Matt 4:20||]]. [[1:42|The son of Jona|Filius Joanna]] [Denis reads *Joanna*, where the Douay-Rheims has Jona]: for so Peter's father was called. Now Joanna is interpreted the grace of God, and Peter was the son of the Saviour's grace. [[1:42|Thou shalt be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter|Tu vocaberis Cephas, quod interpretatur Petrus]].

paras.t: Cephas idem est quod caput vel capitaneus, et idem significat Petrus uno modo. Alio modo Petrus dicitur quasi firmus, a petra. Dicit ergo Salvator, quod Simon iste vocabitur Cephas, quia futurus fuit princeps Apostolorum. Postmodum vero, quum dixit Petrus ad Jesum, Tu es Christus, Filius Dei vivi; audivit a Christo, Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Verum, quoniam apud Marcum et Lucam scribitur, Jesum Simonem fratrem Andreæ vocasse Petrum in electione Apostolorum, ideo aliqui dubitant an Christus hac vice imposuit Simoni nomen istud, vel imponendum prædixit: et dicunt, quod si modo imposuisset, tunc posterior impositio fuisset confirmatio præcedentis. Videtur autem dici posse, quod nunc imposuit sibi nomen Cephæ, et per consequens nomen Petri, secundum unam significationem nominis Petri, et postea, secundum aliam: vel nunc, propter gratiam futuram; postea, propter gratiam tunc præsentem. Hæc enim mutatio nominum, variationem status et proprietatem gratiæ designavit.
paras.en: Cephas is the same as head or chief [as though from the Greek *kephalē*, “head”; the Aramaic *Cephas* means “rock”], and in one way Peter means the same. In another way Peter is so called as being firm, from *petra* [that is, rock]. The Saviour says, then, that this Simon shall be called Cephas, because he was to be the prince of the Apostles. But afterwards, when Peter said to Jesus, [[Matt 16:16|Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God|Tu es Christus, Filius Dei vivi]], he heard from Christ: [[Matt 16:18|thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church|Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam]]. But since it is written in Mark and Luke that Jesus called Simon, the brother of Andrew, Peter at the choosing of the Apostles[[Mark 3:16||]][[Luke 6:14||]], some therefore doubt whether Christ on this occasion gave Simon this name, or foretold that it would be given; and they say that if He gave it now, the later giving was a confirmation of the earlier. It seems, however, that one may say that He now gave him the name Cephas, and consequently the name Peter, according to one meaning of the name Peter, and afterwards according to the other; or now on account of the grace to come, afterwards on account of the grace then present. For this change of names signified a change of state and the property of grace.

paras.t: In crastinum autem, id est die sequenti post collocutionem Jesu et Andreæ ac Petri, voluit Jesus exire a loco prope Jordanem, in Galilæam, redeundo ad Matrem suam in Nazareth. Et invenit Philippum: non illum de quo in Actibus Apostolorum multa leguntur, qui et Simonem magum convertit, et unus fuit de septem diaconis; sed Philippum qui postea factus fuit apostolus. Invenit autem eum, non improvise aut casualiter; sed sic iter suum direxit, sicque Philippum ad sibi obviandum induxit, quod electum in apostolum S. Philippum cito invenit. Et dicit ei Jesus: Sequere me fide, affectu et opere, ac corporis gressu. Non mirum, si verba Verbi, seu sermo Christi, tantæ virtutis erant, quod exterioribus sensibus immutatis, etiam animas poterant immutare atque attrahere. Qui enim foris sonabat, intus movebat; et quoniam Deus verus fuit, in voluntatem aliorum potuit agere immediate, illam pro libitu afficiendo ac immutando. Hinc est quod quidam Apostolorum ad unam vocem Christi ipsum secuti sunt. Ex quibus patet insania Porphyrii ac Juliani redarguentium Apostolos de animi levitate, quod Christo vocante eum secuti sunt, quasi liceret quemlibet vocantem imitari. Erat autem Philippus oriundus a Bethsaida, civitate Andreæ et Petri, id est de qua hi duo nati fuerunt. Bethsaida autem fuit urbs Galilææ.
paras.en: [[1:43|On the following day|In crastinum]], that is, on the day after the conversation of Jesus with Andrew and Peter, Jesus [[1:43|would go forth|voluit exire]] from the place near the Jordan [[1:43|into Galilee|in Galilæam]], returning to His Mother in Nazareth. [[1:43|and he findeth Philip|et invenit Philippum]]: not the one of whom much is read in the Acts of the Apostles[[Acts 8:5||]] [the margin gives Acts viii, passim], who also converted Simon Magus[[Acts 8:13||]] and was one of the seven deacons[[Acts 6:5||]], but the Philip who was afterwards made an apostle[[Matt 10:3||]]. He found him, though, not unexpectedly or by chance; but He so directed His journey, and so led Philip to meet Him, that He soon found St Philip, who had been chosen for an apostle. [[1:43|And Jesus saith to him: follow me|Et dicit ei Jesus: Sequere me]], by faith, affection and deed, and with the steps of the body. No wonder if the words of the Word, or the speech of Christ, were of such power that, while they acted on the outward senses, they could also change and draw souls. For He who sounded without moved within; and since He was true God, He could act immediately upon the will of others, affecting and changing it as He pleased. Hence it is that some of the Apostles followed Him at a single word of Christ. From this the madness of Porphyry and Julian is plain, who charged the Apostles with fickleness of mind because they followed Christ when He called them, as though one might follow anyone at all who calls. [[1:44|Now Philip was of Bethsaida|Erat autem Philippus oriundus a Bethsaida]], [[1:44|the city of Andrew and Peter|civitate Andreæ et Petri]], that is, the city where these two were born. And Bethsaida was a city of Galilee.

paras.t: Invenit Philippus Nathanael fratrem suum carnalem. Quemadmodum dictum est de Andrea, quod Christo audito, accensus zelo salutis fraternæ, quæsivit et reperit Petrum, eumque adduxit ad Jesum, ita nunc legitur de Philippo. — Quæritur, si Philippus continuo sequebatur Jesum, ubi vel quomodo quæsivit ac reperit fratrem suum. Ad hoc facile est respondere. Forte enim reperit eum non longe a via qua ivit cum Jesu, vel alio die. Et dicit Philippus ei, videlicet Nathanaeli: Quem scripsit Moyses in lege, et Prophetæ, invenimus Jesum filium Joseph putativum, natum a Nazareth, ex parte Matris, et quia conceptus fuit in Nazareth, quamvis sit natus in Bethlehem.
paras.en: [[1:45|Philip findeth Nathanael|Invenit Philippus Nathanael]], his brother in the flesh. As was said of Andrew, that having heard Christ, and fired with zeal for his brother's salvation, he sought and found Peter and brought him to Jesus, so now it is read of Philip. — It is asked: if Philip followed Jesus straightaway, where or how did he seek and find his brother? To this it is easy to answer. For perhaps he found him not far from the road by which he went with Jesus, or on another day. [[1:45|and saith to him|Et dicit Philippus ei]], Philip, that is, to Nathanael: [[1:45|We have found him of whom Moses, in the law and the prophets did write|Quem scripsit Moyses in lege, et Prophetæ, invenimus]], [[1:45|Jesus the son of Joseph|Jesum filium Joseph]], His supposed son, [[1:45|of Nazareth|a Nazareth]], born on His Mother's side, and because He was conceived in Nazareth, though He was born in Bethlehem.

paras.t: Hæc verba Philippi plena sunt sensu. Itaque ait: Quem scripsit Moyses in lege, id est eum de quo Moyses scripsit in Pentateucho, et de quo scripserunt Prophetæ, invenimus ego aliique discipuli Joannis Baptistæ (fertur enim quod Petrus quoque et Philippus fuerunt Joannis discipuli), Jesum. Hunc invenerunt, non utique a casu, nec propria industria vel virtute, sed Joanne Baptista monstrante, et Christo se eis ostendente.
paras.en: These words of Philip are full of meaning. So he says: [[1:45|him of whom Moses, in the law|Quem scripsit Moyses in lege]] did write, that is, him of whom Moses wrote in the Pentateuch, and of whom the Prophets wrote, [[1:45|we have found|invenimus]], I and other disciples of John the Baptist (for it is said that Peter too and Philip were disciples of John), [[1:45|Jesus|Jesum]]. They found Him, not indeed by chance, nor by their own effort or power, but with John the Baptist pointing Him out and Christ showing Himself to them.

paras.t: Porro Moyses scripsit de Christo dupliciter: Uno modo verba aliorum narrando: quemadmodum in Genesi prædixit Jacob, Non auferetur (inquit) sceptrum de Juda, donec veniat qui mittendus est, et ipse erit exspectatio gentium; et iterum, Salutare tuum exspectabo, Domine. Alibi quoque scribit Deum dixisse ad Abraham: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Secundo, de ipso Christo prophetando: ut quum ait in Deuteronomio: Prophetam suscitabit vobis Dominus de fratribus vestris tanquam me; ipsum audietis. Quod autem Prophetæ scripserunt de Christo, non oportet speciali testimonio comprobare, quum certum sit, etiam secundum Judæorum magistros, quod omnes Prophetæ locuti sint super dies Messiæ. Propter quod in Actibus Apostolorum Petrus testatur: Omnes Prophetæ a Samuel et deinceps, annuntiaverunt dies istos, videlicet tempus gratiæ Christi. Hinc Christus dicit in Luca: Oportet impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt de me in lege, et Prophetis, et Psalmis.
paras.en: Now Moses wrote of Christ in two ways. In one way, by relating the words of others: as in Genesis Jacob foretold: [[Gen 49:10|The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda|Non auferetur (inquit) sceptrum de Juda]], he says, [[Gen 49:10|till he come that is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of nations|donec veniat qui mittendus est, et ipse erit exspectatio gentium]]; and again, [[Gen 49:18|I will look for thy salvation, O Lord.|Salutare tuum exspectabo, Domine]] Elsewhere too he writes that God said to Abraham: [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes]]. In the second way, by prophesying of Christ Himself: as when he says in Deuteronomy[[Deut 18:15||]]: [[Acts 3:22|A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me: him you shall hear|Prophetam suscitabit vobis Dominus de fratribus vestris tanquam me; ipsum audietis]] [Denis gives the words as St Peter cites them in Acts 3:22]. That the Prophets wrote of Christ need not be proved by particular testimony, since it is certain, even according to the masters of the Jews, that all the Prophets spoke of the days of the Messias. Wherefore in the Acts of the Apostles Peter testifies: [[Acts 3:24|all the prophets, from Samuel and afterwards|Omnes Prophetæ a Samuel et deinceps]], [[Acts 3:24|have told of these days|annuntiaverunt dies istos]], that is, the time of the grace of Christ. Hence Christ says in Luke: [[Luke 24:44|all things must needs be fulfilled which are written|Oportet impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt]] concerning me in the law, and [[Luke 24:44|in the prophets and in the psalms|et prophetis, et Psalmis]].

paras.t: Præterea, si Philippus fuit discipulus Joannis, vel eruditus in Prophetis, vel satis illustratus a Spiritu Sancto, tunc novit Jesum, quem credidit Christum, non esse filium Joseph sponsi Mariæ; sed loquebatur secundum opinionem vulgi. Probabile enim est, quod Præcursor docuit suos discipulos, Jesum Christum esse Virginis filium. Si vero nondum illuminatus fuit aliquo horum modorum, putavit sicut et ceteri, quod Jesus esset conceptus de viro. Nec mirum si ignorasset Christum esse filium Virginis, quum Joannes evangelista usque post resurrectionem Christi nescierit quod Christus resurrecturus fuit a mortuis. Imo Apostoli communiter ignoraverunt quod occidendus esset ab impiis, quum tamen Prophetæ hoc apertissime prænuntiaverint.
paras.en: Moreover, if Philip was a disciple of John, or learned in the Prophets, or sufficiently enlightened by the Holy Ghost, then he knew that Jesus, whom he believed to be the Christ, was not the son of Joseph, the spouse of Mary; but he was speaking according to common opinion. For it is probable that the Forerunner taught his disciples that Jesus Christ was the Virgin's son. But if he had not yet been enlightened in any of these ways, he thought, as the rest did, that Jesus had been conceived of a man. Nor is it any wonder if he did not know that Christ was the son of the Virgin, since John the Evangelist did not know until after Christ's resurrection that Christ was to rise from the dead[[John 20:9||]]. Indeed the Apostles in general did not know that He was to be killed by the wicked[[Luke 18:34||]] [the margin gives Luke xviii, 31–34], although the Prophets had foretold it most plainly.

paras.t: Et dixit ei Nathanael: A Nazareth potest aliquid boni esse? Non est certum an verba ista locutus sit Nathanael, asserendo, vel dubitando, vel abnegando. Augustinus enim sentit, quod dixit hæc verba assertive, tanquam diceret: Utique a Nazareth Christum venisse, non est incredibile. Aliter, secundum Augustinum, Christus non commendasset Nathanaelem, dicendo: Ecce vere Israelita in quo dolus non est. Et ad hoc potest adduci, quod Nathanael fuit excellens doctor in lege: et ergo novit Isaiam dixisse, quoniam Nazaræus vocabitur. Ubi enim nostra translatio habet in Isaia, Egredietur virga de radice Jesse et flos de radice ejus ascendet: Hebraica veritas continet: Egredietur virga de radice Jesse, et Nazaræus de radice ejus ascendet.
paras.en: [[1:46|And Nathanael said to him: Can any thing of good come from Nazareth?|Et dixit ei Nathanael: A Nazareth potest aliquid boni esse?]] It is not certain whether Nathanael spoke these words asserting, or doubting, or denying. For Augustine holds that he said these words by way of assertion, as if he said: It is indeed not incredible that the Christ should have come from Nazareth. Otherwise, according to Augustine, Christ would not have commended Nathanael, saying: [[1:47|Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile|Ecce vere Israelita in quo dolus non est]]. And in support of this it can be adduced that Nathanael was an excellent doctor of the law, and so he knew that Isaias had said: [[Matt 2:23|he shall be called a Nazarene|Nazaræus vocabitur]] [the words are those of Matt 2:23, where the Evangelist ascribes them to “the prophets”; Denis finds them in Isaias, as the next sentence shows]. For where our translation has in Isaias, [[Is 11:1|there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root|Egredietur virga de radice Jesse et flos de radice ejus ascendet]], the Hebrew truth has: There shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a Nazarene shall rise up out of his root [the Hebrew word for “flower” here is *netzer*, “shoot”, which was taken as the name behind *Nazareth* and *Nazarene*].

paras.t: Chrysostomus vero tenet oppositum, dicens, quod Nathanael dixit hæc negative, quoniam scivit scriptum in Michæa, quod nasceretur in Bethlehem. Alii dicunt, quod protulit verba ista dubitative, habens argumenta pro parte utraque. Puto autem quod dixit hæc cum quadam admiratione, cupiens plenius certificari: tanquam diceret, Mirum est si de civitate illa tam vili et modica, ortus sit Christus rex Israel. Ideo subditur: Dicit ei Philippus: Veni, et vide: id est, nolo ut meis verbis nudis fidem adhibeas absolute; sed accede ad Jesum, et tunc experieris qualis et quantus sit, sciesque me vera dixisse.
paras.en: Chrysostom, however, holds the opposite, saying that Nathanael said this by way of denial, since he knew it was written in Micheas that He would be born in Bethlehem[[Mich 5:2||]]. Others say that he uttered these words doubtfully, having arguments on both sides. But I think that he said this with a certain wonder, wishing to be more fully assured: as if he said, It is a wonder if Christ the King of Israel has sprung from that city, so mean and so small. Therefore it follows: [[1:46|Philip saith to him: Come and see|Dicit ei Philippus: Veni, et vide]]: that is, I do not want you to give credence absolutely to my bare words; but come to Jesus, and then you will find out by experience what and how great He is, and you will know that I have told the truth.

paras.t: Vidit Jesus Nathanael venientem ad se cum Philippo, qui eum adduxit; et dicit adstantibus de eo, audiente ipso Nathanael: qui tantæ perfectionis fuit, quod Christus novit sibi non obesse quod laudaret ipsum in sua præsentia. Pronis vero ad vanitatem, non expedit laus. Ecce vere Israelita, hoc est non solum nomine, sed et re, seu proprietate et gratia, filius Israelis, id est Jacob patriarchæ, qui alio nomine appellatus est Israel. Hoc est: Nathanael iste non solum est filius Jacob secundum carnem et nuncupationem, sed etiam secundum fidem, sapientiam, et virtutum sublimitatem. Israel interpretatur, vir videns Deum. Quoniam ergo Nathanael imitatus est beatissimum patriarcham Jacob, Deum fideliter contemplando, mysteria Christi sapienter intelligendo, et conversationem virtuosam ducendo, merito dicitur vere et verus Israelita. Est autem et alius Israelita secundum carnis originem solum, vel secundum litteram quæ occidit: de quo dicit Apostolus, Videte Israel secundum carnem. De vero autem et spirituali Israelita, disseruit: Pax super illos, et super Israel Dei.
paras.en: [[1:47|Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him|Vidit Jesus Nathanael venientem ad se]] with Philip, who had brought him; [[1:47|and he saith of him|et dicit adstantibus de eo]] to those standing by, in the hearing of Nathanael himself. He was of such perfection that Christ knew it would do him no harm to be praised in his own presence; but to those prone to vanity praise is not expedient. [[1:47|Behold an Israelite indeed|Ecce vere Israelita]]: that is, a son of Israel not only in name but in reality, that is, in character and in grace; a son of Israel, that is, of the patriarch Jacob, who by another name was called Israel[[Gen 32:28||]]. That is: this Nathanael is a son of Jacob not only according to the flesh and by name, but also according to faith, wisdom, and the loftiness of his virtues. Israel is interpreted ‘a man seeing God’. Since, then, Nathanael imitated the most blessed patriarch Jacob, by faithfully contemplating God, wisely understanding the mysteries of Christ, and leading a virtuous life, he is rightly called an Israelite indeed, and a true Israelite. But there is also another kind of Israelite, by fleshly descent alone, or according to the letter, which [[2 Cor 3:6|killeth|occidit]]; of whom the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 10:18|Behold Israel according to the flesh|Videte Israel secundum carnem]]. But of the true and spiritual Israelite he declared: [[Gal 6:16|peace on them|Pax super illos]], and [[Gal 6:16|upon the Israel of God|super Israel Dei]].

paras.t: Denique, sicut juxta doctrinam Apostoli ad Romanos et Galatas, quidam sunt filii Abrahæ secundum carnem, qui non reputantur in semine, quia non sunt digni vocari filii Abrahæ (quod verum est de filiis secundum carnem dumtaxat, puta Judæis incredulis et perversis); alii vero sunt filii Abrahæ spirituales, per fidei imitationem, qui dicuntur vere filii Abrahæ seu Abrahæitæ, quales sunt omnes gentiles electi tempore gratiæ: sic quidam sunt filii Israel secundum carnem tantummodo, qui non sunt vere Israelitæ; alii autem, secundum fidem et gratiam, qui sunt vere Israelitæ, videlicet omnes electi, Deum fide formata ac lucida intuentes. Electi quoque Judæi sunt filii Abrahæ et Jacob seu Israelis, secundum carnem et spiritualem imitationem. Inter quos unus de præcipuis fuit felix iste Nathanael, cui tam singulare atque magnificum testimonium perhibuit Filius Dei. Unde et subditur:
paras.en: Lastly, just as, according to the teaching of the Apostle to the Romans[[Rom 9:1||]] and the Galatians[[Gal 3:1||]] [the margin gives only the chapters, Rom. ix and Galat. iii (the numeral is hard to read); compare Rom 9:7–8 and Gal 3:7], some are sons of Abraham according to the flesh, who are not counted for the seed, because they are not worthy to be called sons of Abraham (which is true of those who are sons according to the flesh only, for instance the unbelieving and perverse Jews), while others are spiritual sons of Abraham, by imitation of his faith, who are called sons of Abraham indeed, or Abrahamites, such as are all the elect Gentiles in the time of grace: so some are sons of Israel according to the flesh only, who are not Israelites indeed; but others, according to faith and grace, are Israelites indeed, namely all the elect, who gaze upon God with a faith that is formed [that is, given its life and form by charity] and full of light. The elect Jews, too, are sons of Abraham and of Jacob, or Israel, both according to the flesh and by spiritual imitation. Among these, one of the foremost was this blessed Nathanael, to whom the Son of God bore so singular and so magnificent a testimony. Hence there follows:

paras.t: In quo dolus non est. De Christo testati sunt Isaias et Petrus, quod non est inventus dolus in ore ejus: quantus ergo fuit iste Nathanael, quem Christus eisdem verbis laudavit, quibus ipse prophetico fuit ore laudatus, apostolicoque laudandus? Non itaque fuit fraus, simulatio, hypocrisis, circumventio, in isto Nathanael, sicut communiter in aliis Scribis. Noverat quippe S. Nathanael, quod simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei; et quod, teste Isaia, fraudulenti vasa sunt pessima; imo, quod juxta Malachiam prophetam, maledictus dolosus. Siquidem virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus.
paras.en: [[1:47|in whom there is no guile|In quo dolus non est]]. Isaias[[Is 53:9||]] and Peter bore witness of Christ that [[1 Pet 2:22|neither was guile found in his mouth|non est inventus dolus in ore ejus]]: how great, then, was this Nathanael, whom Christ praised with the same words with which He Himself had been praised by the mouth of the prophet, and was to be praised by that of the apostle? There was, then, no fraud, pretence, hypocrisy or overreaching in this Nathanael, as there commonly was in the other Scribes. For St. Nathanael knew that [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei]]; and that, as Isaias witnesses, [[Is 32:7|The vessels of the deceitful are most wicked|fraudulenti vasa sunt pessima]]; nay more, that according to the prophet Malachias, [[Mal 1:14|Cursed is the deceitful man|maledictus dolosus]]. For indeed [[Ps 5:7|The bloody and the deceitful man the Lord will abhor|virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus]].

paras.t: Dicit ei Nathanael: Unde me nosti, non solum secundum faciem, sed insuper secundum interiora mea, et secundum cordis mei simplicitatem atque propositum? Forte Nathanael putavit se nunquam visum a Jesu corporali intuitu, et forsan sic erat. Verum, audiens Christum de sua interiori dispositione ea asserere de quibus ipse conscius sibi fuit, miratus est, dicens: Unde me nosti? id est, quis tibi hæc revelavit de me? Nam quis scit quid agatur in homine, nisi spiritus ejus, et Deus, et illuminatus a Deo? Respondit Jesus, et dixit ei: Priusquam te Philippus vocaret, ut venires ad me, quum esses sub ficu, ubi te Philippus invenit allocutusque fuit, dicendo me esse Messiam a Moyse et Prophetis prænuntiatum, vidi, id est cognovi, te, et secreta cordis tui perspexi.
paras.en: [[1:48|Nathanael saith to him: Whence knowest thou me|Dicit ei Nathanael: Unde me nosti]], not only by face, but also in my inward parts, and in the simplicity and purpose of my heart? Perhaps Nathanael thought he had never been seen by Jesus with bodily sight, and perhaps it was so. But hearing Christ assert things about his inward disposition of which he himself was conscious, he wondered, saying: [[1:48|Whence knowest thou me|Unde me nosti]]? that is, who revealed these things about me to Thee? For who knows what goes on within a man, but his own spirit[[1 Cor 2:11||]], and God, and one enlightened by God? [[1:48|Jesus answered and said to him|Respondit Jesus, et dixit ei]]: [[1:48|Before that Philip called thee|Priusquam te Philippus vocaret]], that thou mightest come to Me, [[1:48|when thou wast under the fig tree|quum esses sub ficu]], where Philip found thee and spoke with thee, saying that I am the Messias foretold by Moses and the Prophets, [[1:48|I saw thee|vidi]], that is, I knew thee, and looked into the secrets of thy heart.

paras.t: Respondit ei Nathanael, et ait: Rabbi, tu es Filius Dei, tu es Rex Israel, id est, ex istis signis agnosco, quod sis Christus rex Israeliticæ plebis. Nam cordium secreta et absentium verba, nullo narrante cognoscere, eos quoque et facta eorum spiritualiter cernere tam perfecte, qui corporaliter non videntur, Deo est proprium. Idcirco profiteor te Filium Dei, et Regem Israel, id est Deum et hominem. Scivit namque Nathanael, quod Christus non vidit eum sub ficu oculo corporali, nec verba ejus atque Philippi audivit auribus corporis; scivit quoque, quod nemo nuntiavit ea Christo: idcirco, auditis verbis Christi, confessus est quod esset Filius Dei.
paras.en: [[1:49|Nathanael answered him and said: Rabbi: Thou art the Son of God. Thou art the King of Israel|Respondit ei Nathanael, et ait: Rabbi, tu es Filius Dei, tu es Rex Israel]]: that is, from these signs I acknowledge that Thou art the Christ, the King of the Israelite people. For to know the secrets of hearts and the words of those who are absent, with no one telling of them, and to discern so perfectly in spirit those who are not seen in body, and their deeds, is proper to God. Therefore I confess Thee to be the Son of God and the King of Israel, that is, God and man. For Nathanael knew that Christ had not seen him under the fig tree with the eye of the body, nor heard his words and Philip's with the ears of the body; he knew too that no one had told these things to Christ: therefore, on hearing Christ's words, he confessed that He was the Son of God.

paras.t: Quidam dicit quod iste Nathanael, dicendo Jesum esse Filium Dei, intellexit hoc de filiatione adoptiva per gratiam excellentem, ita quod divinitatem Christi non videtur intellexisse; item, quod dicendo, Tu es Rex Israel, æstimavit eum temporaliter regnaturum, sicut communiter opinantur Judæi. Sed si Nathanael tam inconvenienter, imo et false, sensisset de Christo, nequaquam meruisset audire a Christo: Ecce vere Israelita in quo dolus non est. Tunc enim fuisset carnalis Israelita, aliosque decipiens, docendo de Christo futuro quod esset purus homo, et rex temporaliter regnaturus. Fuit enim legis doctor. Denique, quum fuerit valens legis doctor atque eximius, secundum Bedam, scrutabatur Scripturas de Christo. Quoniam ergo Prophetæ manifeste describunt Christi divinitatem (ut quum ait Jeremias: Hoc est nomen quod vocabunt eum, Dominus justus noster. In Hebræo autem habetur nomen Domini tetragrammaton, quod non convenit nisi vero Deo. Et Isaias: Vocabitur, inquit, nomen ejus, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis, Pater futuri sæculi, Princeps pacis); describunt quoque primum Christi adventum in omnimoda paupertate (dicente Zacharia: Ecce Rex tuus veniet tibi mansuetus, ipse pauper; et Jeremia, Quare quasi colonus venturus es in terra?): hinc igitur non est verisimile quod Nathanael æstimavit Messiam purum hominem, atque temporaliter regnaturum, sicut nunc somniant obtenebrati Judæi.
paras.en: A certain writer says that this Nathanael, in saying that Jesus is the Son of God, understood it of an adoptive sonship through surpassing grace, so that he does not seem to have understood the divinity of Christ; and likewise that in saying [[1:49|Thou art the King of Israel|Tu es Rex Israel]], he thought that He would reign in time, as the Jews commonly suppose. But if Nathanael had thought so unfittingly, nay so falsely, of Christ, he would never have deserved to hear from Christ: [[1:47|Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile|Ecce vere Israelita in quo dolus non est]]. For then he would have been a carnal Israelite, and one who deceived others, teaching of the Christ to come that He would be a mere man, and a king who would reign in time. For he was a doctor of the law. Indeed, since he was, according to Bede, an able and eminent doctor of the law, he searched the Scriptures concerning Christ. Since, then, the Prophets plainly describe the divinity of Christ (as when Jeremias says: [[Jer 33:16|this is the name that they shall call him, The Lord our just one|Hoc est nomen quod vocabunt eum, Dominus justus noster]]; and in the Hebrew there stands here the Tetragrammaton name of the Lord [the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH], which befits none but the true God. And Isaias: [[Is 9:6|his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God the Mighty, the Father of the world to come, the Prince of Peace|Vocabitur, inquit, nomen ejus, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis, Pater futuri sæculi, Princeps pacis]]), and since they also describe the first coming of Christ in utter poverty (as Zacharias says: [[Zach 9:9|BEHOLD THY KING will come to thee, the just and saviour: he is poor|Ecce Rex tuus veniet tibi mansuetus, ipse pauper]] [Denis has *mansuetus*, ‘meek’, as in Matt 21:5, where the Vulgate of Zacharias has ‘just and saviour’]; and Jeremias: [[Jer 14:8|why wilt thou be as a stranger in the land|Quare quasi colonus venturus es in terra]]?): it is therefore not likely that Nathanael thought the Messias a mere man, who would reign in time, as the benighted Jews now dream.

paras.t: Argumentum autem illius, quo arguit quod si Nathanael credidisset eum esse Filium Dei naturalem, non dixisset, Tu es Rex Israel, sed, Totius mundi, non convincit, nec apparentiam habet, præsertim quum in Isaia etiam Deus secundum naturam deitatis frequenter dicatur rex Jacob seu Israel. Unde in Isaia dicitur in persona Israelitici populi: Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster, Dominus rex noster, ipse veniet et salvabit nos. Quod ad litteram dictum est de Christo Filio Dei. Quamvis enim sit omnium rex, tamen specialiter appellatur Rex Israel: Primo, quoniam ex semine regum Israel natus. Secundo, quia populo illi specialiter promissus ac missus, quemadmodum ait: Non sum missus nisi ad oves perditas domus Israel. Ideo in Zacharia habetur: Exsulta satis, filia Sion, ecce Rex tuus. Non ait, Rex totius mundi; sed, Rex tuus. Et quid est, Rex tuus, nisi, Rex Israel?
paras.en: But his argument, by which he contends that if Nathanael had believed Him to be the natural Son of God, he would not have said [[1:49|Thou art the King of Israel|Tu es Rex Israel]], but ‘of the whole world’, does not convince, nor has it even the appearance of truth, especially since in Isaias, too, God, according to the nature of the Godhead, is often called the king of Jacob[[Is 41:21||]] or of Israel[[Is 44:6||]]. Hence it is said in Isaias in the person of the Israelite people: [[Is 33:22|the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king: he will save us|Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster, Dominus rex noster, ipse veniet et salvabit nos]] [Denis reads ‘he will come and save us’]. This was said, according to the letter, of Christ the Son of God. For although He is the King of all, yet He is especially called the King of Israel: first, because He was born of the seed of the kings of Israel; secondly, because He was especially promised and sent to that people, as He says: [[Matt 15:24|I was not sent but to the sheep, that are lost of the house of Israel|Non sum missus nisi ad oves perditas domus Israel]]. Therefore it is written in Zacharias: [[Zach 9:9|Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Sion|Exsulta satis, filia Sion]], [[Zach 9:9|BEHOLD THY KING|ecce Rex tuus]]. He does not say, ‘the King of the whole world’, but ‘thy King’. And what is ‘thy King’, but ‘the King of Israel’?

paras.t: Respondit Jesus, et dixit ei: Quia dixi tibi, Vidi te sub ficu: secundum sensum jam explanatum; credis me Filium Dei, et regem Israel. Majus his, id est signum evidentius meæ divinitatis, videbis, quam sint duo signa prædicta, videlicet, quod te vocavi vere Israelitam dolo carentem, et quod dixi me te vidisse sub ficu. Nam ceteris Prophetis sæpe concessum est, Deo illustrante, quod interiorem hominum dispositionem, actusque exteriores, certitudinaliter cognoverunt. Discipuli autem postea viderunt signa divinitatis Christi multo majora, ut erat suscitatio mortuorum, obscuratio solis tempore passionis, ingressus Christi in conclave januis clausis, ascensio Salvatoris, et missio Spiritus Sancti. Specialiter vero subjungitur de uno signo majori.
paras.en: [[1:50|Jesus answered and said to him: Because I said unto thee, I saw thee under the fig tree|Respondit Jesus, et dixit ei: Quia dixi tibi, Vidi te sub ficu]], in the sense already explained, [[1:50|thou believest|credis]] Me to be the Son of God and the King of Israel. [[1:50|greater things than these|Majus his]], that is, a clearer sign of My divinity, [[1:50|shalt thou see|videbis]], than are the two signs mentioned, namely that I called thee an Israelite indeed, free from guile, and that I said I had seen thee under the fig tree. For it has often been granted to the other Prophets, by God's enlightening, to know with certainty the inward disposition of men and their outward acts. But the disciples afterwards saw far greater signs of Christ's divinity, such as the raising of the dead[[Matt 9:25||]][[Luke 7:14||]][[John 11:43||]], the darkening of the sun at the time of the Passion[[Matt 27:45||]], Christ's entry into the room where they were gathered when the doors were shut[[John 20:19||]][[John 20:26||]], the Ascension of the Saviour[[Acts 1:9||]], and the sending of the Holy Ghost[[Acts 2:3||]]. And one greater sign in particular is now added.

paras.t: Et dicit ei Jesus: Amen, amen dico vobis, videlicet tibi, Nathanael, et fratri tuo Philippo, videbitis cælum apertum: non per scissuram, aut divisionem, vel aliquam corruptionem, quum corpora cælestia sint naturaliter incorruptibilia; sed per aliquam refulgentiam lucis, ob quam cælum quasi apertum apparet, ut in coruscatione. Vel dicitur cælum apertum, propter exitum civium supernorum. Et angelos Dei ascendentes et descendentes in corporibus assumptis, in quibus videri dicuntur, quum in propria natura incorporei invisibilesque consistant, supra Filium hominis, quasi ad ejus famulatum parati. Sed ubi viderunt istud discipuli? Dicendum, in ascensione, quando cum Christo multi angeli ascenderunt, quorum duo adstiterunt discipulis, dicentes: Viri Galilæi, quid statis adspicientes in cælum? Multa quoque fecit Christus miracula, et diversæ circa ipsum visiones apparuerunt, quæ non sunt ab aliquo Evangelistarum descriptæ.
paras.en: [[1:51|And he saith to him|Et dicit ei]], Jesus, that is: [[1:51|Amen, amen, I say to you|Amen, amen dico vobis]], namely to thee, Nathanael, and to thy brother Philip, [[1:51|you shall see the heaven opened|videbitis cælum apertum]]: not by any rending or division or any corruption, since the heavenly bodies are by nature incorruptible, but by some shining forth of light, on account of which the heaven appears as it were opened, as in a flash of lightning. Or the heaven is said to be opened because of the coming forth of its citizens on high. [[1:51|and the angels of God ascending and descending|Et angelos Dei ascendentes et descendentes]] in assumed bodies, in which they are said to be seen, since in their own nature they are incorporeal and invisible, [[1:51|upon the Son of man|supra Filium hominis]], as though ready to serve Him. But where did the disciples see this? It must be said: at the Ascension, when many angels ascended with Christ, two of whom stood by the disciples[[Acts 1:10||]], saying: [[Acts 1:11|Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven|Viri Galilæi, quid statis adspicientes in cælum]]? Christ also worked many miracles, and various visions appeared about Him, which have not been written down by any of the Evangelists.

paras.t: Circa præinducta, monemur advertere dispensationem sapientiæ Dei in electione Apostolorum: quomodo Christus sapientia Patris, attingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponens universa suaviter, potius elegit Petrum, Andream, Philippum, et alios idiotas in Apostolos, quam Nicodemum et Nathanael, qui erant doctores et legisperiti, ne prædicatio evangelicæ legis videretur virtute humanæ sapientiæ, seu auctoritate magnatum, invaluisse (nam teste Apostolo, Quæ stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes); item, ne propter excellentiam suam viderentur ad gratiam apostolatus promoti.
paras.en: On what has been set out above, we are admonished to consider the disposition of God's wisdom in the choosing of the Apostles: how Christ, the Wisdom of the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]], who [[Wis 8:1|reacheth, therefore, from end to end mightily, and ordereth all things sweetly|attingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponens universa suaviter]], chose Peter, Andrew, Philip and other unlettered men [*idiotas*: men without learning, not ‘idiots’] as Apostles, rather than Nicodemus and Nathanael, who were doctors and learned in the law; lest the preaching of the law of the Gospel should seem to have prevailed by the power of human wisdom, or by the authority of great men (for, as the Apostle witnesses, [[1 Cor 1:27|the foolish things of the world hath God chosen, that he may confound the wise|Quæ stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes]]); and again, lest they should seem to have been raised to the grace of the apostolate on account of their own eminence.

2.title: Explanatio capituli secundi: Et tertia die nuptiæ factæ sunt.
2.title_en: Explanation of the second chapter: “And the third day there was a marriage.”

paras.t: Subinde describitur miraculum Christi quo convertit aquam in vinum. Et tertia die nuptiæ factæ sunt in Cana villa Galilææ. Quidam exponunt hanc tertiam diem, de die sequente vocationem Philippi et Nathanaelis. Sed obviat, quod secundum Patres sanctos communiter, creditur quod Christus eodem die quo baptizatus est, convertit aquam in vinum, anno uno elapso. Vocatio autem prædictorum discipulorum, facta est statim post reditum Christi a deserto, in quod fuit ingressus statim suscepto baptismo. Propterea alii sic exponunt: Tertia die, id est die qui post dies prædictos tertio loco exprimitur. Et erat Mater Jesu ibi, videlicet invitata atque profecta ad nuptias istas. Hieronymus enim sentit quod sponsus fuit Joannes evangelista, filius sororis beatissimæ Virginis, Genitricisque Christi. Sicque Mater Jesu ivit ad nuptias sui nepotis.
paras.en: Next is described the miracle of Christ by which He turned water into wine. [[2:1|And the third day, there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee|Et tertia die nuptiæ factæ sunt in Cana villa Galilææ]]. Some explain this third day as the day following the calling of Philip and Nathanael. But against this stands the fact that, according to the holy Fathers generally, it is believed that Christ turned water into wine on the same day on which He was baptized, one year having passed. The calling of the aforesaid disciples, however, took place immediately after Christ's return from the desert, into which He had gone immediately on receiving baptism[[Mark 1:9||]][[Mark 1:12||]]. Therefore others explain it thus: [[2:1|the third day|tertia die]], that is, the day which is set down in the third place after the days mentioned before. [[2:1|and the mother of Jesus was there|Et erat Mater Jesu ibi]], namely invited to this wedding and gone there. For Jerome holds that the bridegroom was John the Evangelist, the son of the sister of the most blessed Virgin, the Mother of Christ. And so the Mother of Jesus went to the wedding of her nephew.

paras.t: Vocatus est autem, id est reverenter invitatus, et Jesus, et discipuli ejus: qui jam cœperant ejus magisterio adhærere, partim propter testimonium Joannis Baptistæ, et partim propter sapientiam et sanctitatem efficaciamque verborum Domini Jesu; itemque, propter signa ejus occulta, quemadmodum in præcedenti capitulo dictum est de Nathanael, quod credidit Jesum esse Christum Filium Dei, quoniam arcana sui cordis, et gesta ac verba sua in absentia Christi patrata ac dicta, ipse Christus manifestavit ipsi Nathanael. Ad nuptias. Quibus Christus interesse dignatus est: Primo, ut laudabilem consuetudinem, quæ habet vim legis, qua consanguinei et vicini tendunt ad nuptias cognatorum ac vicinorum suorum, approbaret. Secundo, ut demonstraret nuptias esse licitas atque divinitus institutas: cujus contrarium Tatianus et Marcion hæretici affirmabant, dicentes quod essent malæ et a diabolo traditæ.
