Tertio, ut occasione futuri defectus operaretur miraculum, ad propriæ majestatis declarationem, et discipulorum suorum confirmationem. Quarto, ut dicitur, quatenus nepotem suum Joannem, a statu conjugali ad statum sublimiorem vocaret. Unde et pro lege servatur, ut uterque conjugum libere possit religionem intrare, matrimonio nondum consummato, videlicet ante conjunctionem maritalem.
paras.en: [[2:2|And Jesus also was invited|Vocatus est autem]], that is, reverently invited, [[2:2|and his disciples|et Jesus, et discipuli ejus]], who had already begun to cleave to Him as their master, partly because of the testimony of John the Baptist, and partly because of the wisdom and holiness and the power of the words of the Lord Jesus; and also because of His hidden signs, as was said in the preceding chapter of Nathanael, that he believed Jesus to be the Christ, the Son of God[[John 1:49||]][[John 1:50||]], because Christ Himself made known to Nathanael the secrets of his heart, and the things he had done and said in Christ's absence. [[2:2|To the marriage|Ad nuptias]]. Christ deigned to be present at it: first, to approve the praiseworthy custom, which has the force of law, by which kinsmen and neighbours go to the weddings of their relatives and neighbours. Second, to show that marriage is lawful and instituted by God: the contrary of which the heretics Tatian and Marcion affirmed, saying that marriages were evil and handed down by the devil. Third, that on the occasion of the coming shortage He might work a miracle, to declare His own majesty and to confirm His disciples. Fourth, as is said, in order to call His nephew John from the married state to a higher state. Hence it is also kept as law that either spouse may freely enter religion [that is, a religious order] while the marriage is not yet consummated, namely before marital union.

paras.t: Et deficiente vino, vel quia totum fuerat epotatum, vel quia parum remansit, ita quod mox vinum omnino deesset, et sponsus de inopia confundendus exsisteret, dicit Mater Jesu ad eum: Vinum non habent ad sufficientiam sponsus et sponsa ad erogandum, et alii ad bibendum. Compassa est enim verecundiæ sponsi ac sponsæ, atque penuriæ seu indigentiæ convescentium, piissima, affectuosissima atque dulcissima Virgo. Et si illorum corporali inopiæ condolebat et succurrebat, etiam non rogata, quanto magis nostræ spirituali indigentiæ compatietur, auxiliumque præbebit, si fuerit fideliter invocata? quod utique facit ubertim, nondum petita. Porro, quum pudicissima ac prudentissima esset, paucissimis usa est verbis, et in voluntate Filii ac Domini sui relinquens quid agere vellet: de cujus bonitate et caritate eatenus confidebat, quod scivit desiderium suum ac precem non ab illo repelli posse. Quo docemur causam et indigentiam nostram, superioribus nostris simpliciter atque modeste insinuare, et in eorum potestate quid faciendum sit relinquere.
paras.en: [[2:3|And the wine failing|Et deficiente vino]], either because it had all been drunk, or because little remained, so that the wine would soon be gone altogether and the bridegroom would be put to shame by the want, [[2:3|the mother of Jesus saith to him|dicit Mater Jesu ad eum]]: [[2:3|They have no wine|Vinum non habent]], that is, not enough for the bridegroom and bride to serve and for the others to drink. For the most loving, most tender and sweetest Virgin had compassion on the embarrassment of the bridegroom and bride, and on the want or need of those feasting with them. And if she grieved over their bodily want and came to their help, even unasked, how much more will she have compassion on our spiritual need and give us help, if she is faithfully called upon? Which indeed she does abundantly, even before she is asked. Moreover, since she was most modest and most prudent, she used very few words, leaving it to the will of her Son and Lord what He would do: in whose goodness and love she trusted so far that she knew her desire and prayer could not be rejected by Him. By this we are taught to make known our cause and our need to our superiors simply and modestly, and to leave it in their power what is to be done.

paras.t: Et dicit ei Jesus: Quid mihi et tibi est, mulier? Quoniam dura videtur ista responsio, Manichæus dixit quod Christus non fuit verus filius Mariæ, nec habens corpus verum, sed phantasticum. Quod si ita se haberet, non subderet Evangelista: Dicit Mater ejus ministris. Cur ergo loquitur ita? Numquid quoniam verba Mariæ reprehensibilia erant, quam scimus nec mortaliter nec venialiter unquam peccasse? Non utique. Denique, si reprehensibiliter est locuta, cur Filius ejus mox fecit quod ipsa petivit? Sed loquitur sic, docens nos ne habeamus affectum nimis carnalem et mollem ad carnales parentes.
paras.en: [[2:4|And Jesus saith to her: Woman, what is that to me and to thee?|Et dicit ei Jesus: Quid mihi et tibi est, mulier?]] Since this answer seems harsh, Manichæus said that Christ was not the true son of Mary, and had no true body, but only a phantom one. If that were so, the Evangelist would not add: [[2:5|His mother saith to the waiters|Dicit Mater ejus ministris]]. Why then does He speak so? Was it because the words of Mary were blameworthy, she who, as we know, never sinned either mortally or venially? Certainly not. And besides, if she spoke blameworthily, why did her Son at once do what she asked? But He speaks so to teach us not to have too carnal and soft an affection for our parents according to the flesh.

paras.t: Exponitur autem locus iste dupliciter: Primo, secundum Augustinum, hoc modo: Quid mihi et tibi est, mulier? id est, nihil commune est mihi et tibi, cujus virtute conveniat mihi miracula facere, quia istud convenit mihi ratione divinæ naturæ, quam non sumpsi ex te. Ideo quantum ad hoc, videlicet ad facienda opera supernaturalia, non teneor tibi parere. Nondum venit hora mea, id est tempus persecutionis et passionis, in quo agam et patiar quæ mihi conveniunt ratione naturæ ex te sumptæ, et tunc ero sollicitus de te, committendo te discipulo prædilecto. Sed ista expositio videtur satis obscura.
paras.en: This passage is explained in two ways. First, according to Augustine, in this manner: [[2:4|Woman, what is that to me and to thee?|Quid mihi et tibi est, mulier?]] That is, there is nothing in common between Me and thee by virtue of which it befits Me to work miracles; for that befits Me by reason of the divine nature, which I did not take from thee. Therefore as to this, namely the doing of supernatural works, I am not bound to obey thee. [[2:4|My hour is not yet come|Nondum venit hora mea]], that is, the time of persecution and passion, in which I shall do and suffer what befits Me by reason of the nature taken from thee; and then I shall take care of thee, entrusting thee to the beloved disciple[[John 19:26||]][[John 19:27||]]. But this explanation seems rather obscure.

paras.t: Secundo ergo exponitur sic, secundum Chrysostomum: Quid mihi et tibi est, mulier? id est, in isto quod petis a me fieri, non convenis mecum quantum ad determinatam horam faciendi miraculum, nec est tibi mecum commune scire horam hujusmodi. Nondum venit hora mea, id est, adhuc non est tempus faciendi miraculum mutationis aquæ in vinum, seu alio modo supernaturaliter providendi de vino sufficienti. Virgo namque beata, secundum Chrysostomum, timens de futuro defectu vini et verecundia sponsi, optavit ut Jesus provideret de vino sufficienti, antequam vinum residuum ebiberetur. Christus vero scivit hoc non expedire, quia tunc miraculum fuisset minus notum et gratum. Quoniam ergo voluit suam divinitatem ostendere, discipulorumque fidem roborare, exspectavit quousque nihil de vino permansit: quo facto, miraculum provisionis de vino fuit magis gratum vescentibus, magis quoque manifestum præsentibus. Hæc expositio videtur aliquid ambiguitatis continere. Maria enim absolute dixit ad Jesum: Vinum non habent. Unde dubium est si aliquid vini superfuit.
paras.en: Secondly, then, it is explained thus, according to Chrysostom: [[2:4|Woman, what is that to me and to thee?|Quid mihi et tibi est, mulier?]] That is, in this which thou askest Me to do, thou art not at one with Me as to the appointed hour for working the miracle, nor is it for thee, together with Me, to know such an hour. [[2:4|My hour is not yet come|Nondum venit hora mea]], that is, it is not yet the time to work the miracle of changing water into wine, or to provide enough wine in some other supernatural way. For the blessed Virgin, according to Chrysostom, fearing the coming shortage of wine and the bridegroom's embarrassment, wished Jesus to provide enough wine before the remaining wine was drunk up. But Christ knew this was not expedient, because then the miracle would have been less known and less welcome. Since, then, He willed to show His divinity and to strengthen the faith of the disciples, He waited until none of the wine was left; and when that was done, the miracle of providing wine was more welcome to those eating, and also more evident to those present. This explanation seems to contain some ambiguity. For Mary said to Jesus without qualification: [[2:3|They have no wine|Vinum non habent]]. Hence it is doubtful whether any wine was left over.

paras.t: Propter quod videtur et sic exponi posse. Expositiones tamen prætactas nequaquam redarguo. Quid mihi et tibi est, mulier? id est, quid ad nos duos, qui pauperes sumus, et temporalium rerum sollicitudinem non habemus, in tantum pertinet providere istis de vino? Nondum venit hora mea, id est, necdum impletum est tempus ut manifeste ac passim agam miracula. Quamvis enim Christus ante incarcerationem Joannis Baptistæ, prædicavit, baptizavit, saltem suos Apostolos, et alios per illos, atque miracula aliqua fecit, hæc tamen non fecit ubertim, manifeste et passim, sed raro et coram paucis. Propter quod Matthæus, Marcus et Lucas talia omiserunt, incipientes ab operibus Christi et doctrinis post incarcerationem Joannis inceptis, prout manifeste patet in Matthæo, Marco et Luca.
paras.en: For this reason it seems it can also be explained in this way (though I by no means reject the explanations touched on above): [[2:4|Woman, what is that to me and to thee?|Quid mihi et tibi est, mulier?]] That is, what concern is it of us two, who are poor and have no care of temporal things, to provide these people with wine to such an extent? [[2:4|My hour is not yet come|Nondum venit hora mea]], that is, the time is not yet fulfilled for Me to work miracles openly and everywhere. For although Christ, before the imprisonment of John the Baptist, preached, baptized (at least His own Apostles, and others through them), and worked some miracles, yet He did not do these things abundantly, openly and everywhere, but seldom and before few. For this reason Matthew, Mark and Luke left such things out, beginning with the works and teachings of Christ begun after John's imprisonment, as plainly appears in Matthew[[Matt 4:12||]], Mark[[Mark 1:14||]] and Luke[[Luke 4:14||]].

paras.t: Dicit Mater ejus ministris, qui potum præbebant edentibus: Quodcumque dixerit vobis Filius meus Jesus, facite. Certissima equidem fuit amabilissima Virgo, se tantum amari ac honorari ab unico pignore ventris sui, a dilecto suo, a dilecto uteri sui, a dilecto votorum suorum, a quo nunquam aliquid austeritatis vel repulsæ fuit experta, quod incunctanter ageret id quod ipsa suggessit. Non enim accepit verba ejus quasi increpatorie dicta: quia et quod ait, Mulier, non sonat dure secundum idioma Hebræum, in quo omnis persona feminei sexus mulier appellatur.
paras.en: [[2:5|His mother saith to the waiters|Dicit Mater ejus ministris]], who were serving drink to those at table: [[2:5|Whatsoever he shall say to you|Quodcumque dixerit vobis]], my Son Jesus, [[2:5|do ye|facite]]. For the most lovable Virgin was entirely certain that she was so loved and honoured by the only pledge of her womb, by her beloved, the beloved of her womb, the beloved of her vows [an echo of Prov 31:2, “the beloved of my womb … the beloved of my vows”], from whom she had never met with any harshness or refusal, that He would without hesitation do what she herself suggested. For she did not take His words as spoken in rebuke: since even His saying [[2:4|Woman|Mulier]] does not sound harsh in the Hebrew idiom, in which every person of the female sex is called woman.

paras.t: Erant autem ibi lapideæ hydriæ, id est urnæ seu vasa pro receptione aquæ apta, sex positæ, secundum purificationem Judæorum, id est secundum consuetudinem, ritum, seu observationem quam habebant Judæi in purificando seu lavando se ipsos et utensilia sua, quando aliquam immunditiam incurrebant secundum legem; vel secundum seniorum suorum traditionem. Habebant enim consuetudinem ex traditione seniorum frequenter lavandi manus, et vasa, ac cetera multa: propter quod positæ erant ibi hydriæ, ut haberent aquam in promptu. Unde apud Marcum legitur: Pharisæi et omnes Judæi, nisi crebro laverint manus, non manducant, tenentes traditionem seniorum; et a foro nisi baptizentur, non comedunt; et alia multa sunt quæ tradita sunt illis servare, baptismata calicum, et urceorum, et æramentorum, et lectorum. Capientes singulæ, id est, quælibet hydria capiebat, metretas, id est mensuras decem sextariorum, binas vel ternas. Secundum Isidorum, metreta est mensura continens decem sextarios. Sextarius vero continet duas libras.
paras.en: [[2:6|Now there were set there six waterpots of stone|Erant autem ibi lapideæ hydriæ sex positæ]], that is, urns or vessels fit for holding water, [[2:6|according to the manner of the purifying of the Jews|secundum purificationem Judæorum]], that is, according to the custom, rite or observance which the Jews had in purifying or washing themselves and their utensils when they incurred some uncleanness according to the Law; or according to the tradition of their elders. For they had the custom, from the tradition of the elders, of often washing their hands and vessels and many other things: and for this reason the waterpots were set there, so that they might have water ready to hand. Hence we read in Mark: [[Mark 7:3|the Pharisees and all the Jews eat not without often washing their hands, holding the tradition of the ancients|Pharisæi et omnes Judæi, nisi crebro laverint manus, non manducant, tenentes traditionem seniorum]]; [[Mark 7:4|And when they come from the market, unless they be washed, they eat not: and many other things there are that have been delivered to them to observe, the washings of cups and of pots and of brazen vessels and of beds|et a foro nisi baptizentur, non comedunt; et alia multa sunt quæ tradita sunt illis servare, baptismata calicum, et urceorum, et æramentorum, et lectorum]]. [[2:6|containing|Capientes singulæ]], that is, each waterpot held, [[2:6|measures|metretas]], that is, measures of ten sextaries, [[2:6|two or three|binas vel ternas]] apiece. According to Isidore, a metreta is a measure containing ten sextaries. And a sextary holds two pounds [the *sextarius* was a Roman measure of a little under a pint; the *libra* is the pound weight].

paras.t: Dicit eis, puta ministris, Jesus: Implete hydrias aqua. Forsitan aliquid aquæ erat in hydriis; sed non erant repletæ, quia fortassis aliquid inde fuit sublatum pro lotione vasorum vel discumbentium. Et impleverunt eas usque ad summum earum, ita quod plus capere non valebant. Et dicit eis Jesus: Haurite, id est, vinum de hydriis sumite, nunc, quoniam divina virtute jam in instanti conversa est aqua in vinum, et ferte, id est, de vino isto portate, architriclino. Triclinium est locus seu domus sublimata, secundum Bedam, trino discumbentium ordine distincta, videlicet in quo sunt tres ordines mensarum. Architriclinus vero nominatur principalis inter convivas, vel dispensator ac ordinator convivii. Juxta Chrysostomum, voluit Christus ut ei primo vinum istud præberetur gustandum: primo, quia unusquisque honorandus est secundum exigentiam gradus atque officii sui; secundo, quoniam architriclini judicio magis credebatur ab omnibus; tertio, quia fortassis architriclinus propter curam suam in dispositione convivii parum comedit ac bibit, sicque propter sobrietatem suam aptior fuit aliis ad judicandum de valore vini. Et tulerunt ministri vinum ad architriclinum.
paras.en: [[2:7|Jesus saith to them|dicit eis Jesus]], that is, to the waiters: [[2:7|Fill the waterpots with water|Implete hydrias aqua]]. Perhaps there was some water in the waterpots; but they were not full, because perhaps some had been taken out of them for washing the vessels or those at table. [[2:7|And they filled them up to the brim|Et impleverunt eas usque ad summum]] of them, so that they could hold no more. [[2:8|And Jesus saith to them|Et dicit eis Jesus]]: [[2:8|Draw out|Haurite]], that is, take wine from the waterpots, [[2:8|now|nunc]], because by divine power the water has already been changed into wine in an instant, [[2:8|and carry|et ferte]], that is, bring some of this wine, [[2:8|to the chief steward of the feast|architriclino]]. A *triclinium*, according to Bede, is a raised place or room divided into three rows of those reclining at table, that is, one in which there are three rows of tables [hence *architriclinus*, “master of the triclinium”, the Douay-Rheims’ “chief steward of the feast”]. And he is called the *architriclinus* who is the chief among the guests, or the steward and ordainer of the feast. According to Chrysostom, Christ willed that this wine be given him to taste first: first, because each person is to be honoured according to what his rank and office require; secondly, because everyone trusted the judgment of the chief steward more; thirdly, because perhaps the chief steward, on account of his care in ordering the feast, ate and drank little, and so, on account of his sobriety, was fitter than the others to judge the worth of the wine. [[2:8|And they carried it|Et tulerunt]], the waiters, the wine to the chief steward.

paras.t: Ut autem, id est postquam, gustavit architriclinus aquam vinum factam, id est vinum in quod aqua fuit conversa. Ex aqua enim fuerat factum hoc vinum quasi ex causa materiali, forma aquæ corrupta. Et non sciebat architriclinus unde esset, id est, a quo adductum esset tam nobile vinum; ministri autem sciebant unde esset, qui hauserant aquam in hydrias fusam atque in vinum mutatam. Vocat sponsum architriclinus, ut arguat eum,
paras.en: [[2:9|And when|Ut autem]], that is, after, [[2:9|the chief steward had tasted the water made wine|gustavit architriclinus aquam vinum factam]], that is, the wine into which the water had been changed. For this wine had been made out of water as out of a material cause, the form of the water having been corrupted [in scholastic terms: the water was the matter, and its substantial form ceased to be when the form of wine came in its place]. [[2:9|and knew not whence it was|Et non sciebat architriclinus unde esset]], that is, by whom such noble wine had been brought; [[2:9|but the waiters knew|ministri autem sciebant]] whence it was, they [[2:9|who had drawn the water|qui hauserant aquam]] poured into the waterpots and changed into wine. [[2:9|the chief steward calleth the bridegroom|Vocat sponsum architriclinus]], to reprove him,

paras.t: Et dicit ei: Omnis homo primum bonum vinum ponit, et quum inebriati fuerint, tunc id quod deterius est. Distributio ista non est intelligenda simpliciter de universis hominibus, quia nec omnis homo habet vinum, nec omnis homo habens vinum ponit illud ante alios, nec omnis qui ponit ante alios vinum bonum, ponit bibentibus inebriatis vinum deterius. Est ergo distributio accommoda, et sermo secundum consuetudinem loquens, ut sit sensus: Omnis homo ponens vinum ante alios, primum, id est in principio potationis, et antequam aliud vinum ponat, bonum vinum ponit, dummodo humane, prudenter et rationabiliter agat, id est, saporosum et clarum vinum ponit coram bibentibus, ne reprehendatur ab illis de malitia vini. In principio enim epulationis sunt homines apti ad discernendum de vini valore. Et quum inebriati fuerint convivantes, tunc omnis homo ponit id quod deterius est, id est vilius vinum: quia sensus gustus est vivacior in sobrio quam in ebrio. Si autem quis ponat vinum deterius ante inebriatos, ut inordinatum lucrum sectetur ebriosque decipiat, sumendo tantam pecuniam pro vino deteriori sicut pro meliori, non excusaretur a culpa. Si vero sic faciat ad præcavendum ampliorem bibentium ebrietatem, nec quærat superfluum pretium pro vino, non facit male.
paras.en: [[2:10|And saith to him|Et dicit ei]]: [[2:10|Every man at first setteth forth good wine, and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse|Omnis homo primum bonum vinum ponit, et quum inebriati fuerint, tunc id quod deterius est]]. This distribution is not to be understood absolutely of all men, since not every man has wine, nor does every man who has wine set it before others, nor does everyone who sets good wine before others set worse wine before drinkers who are drunk. It is therefore an accommodated distribution [a *distribution* is the logicians’ term for the force of a universal word such as “every”; an *accommodated* one covers only the cases that fit, not absolutely all], and a way of speaking according to custom, so that the sense is: every man who sets wine before others, at first, that is, at the beginning of the drinking and before he sets out other wine, sets out good wine, provided he acts humanely, prudently and reasonably; that is, he sets savoury and clear wine before the drinkers, so as not to be blamed by them for the badness of the wine. For at the beginning of a feast men are able to judge the worth of wine. And when the guests are drunk, then every man sets out that which is worse, that is, cheaper wine: because the sense of taste is livelier in a sober man than in a drunken one. But if anyone were to set worse wine before men who are drunk in order to pursue inordinate gain and to deceive the drunken, taking as much money for the worse wine as for the better, he would not be excused from fault. If, however, he does so to guard against the drinkers becoming more drunk, and does not seek an excessive price for the wine, he does no wrong.

paras.t: Tu autem servasti bonum vinum usque adhuc, hoc est, contra laudabilem consuetudinem hoc fecisti, et meruisti redargui. Sic enim putavit architriclinus. Unde perpenditur quod vinum istud peroptimum fuit. Opera quippe Christi erant perfecta. Nam quos sanavit corporaliter, sanavit et spiritualiter; et in ceteris actibus Christi fuit eminentia quædam, ita quod terminabantur ad aliquid perfectius quam possit natura producere. Propterea hæc supernaturalis mutatio aquæ terminabatur ad vinum prævalidum.
paras.en: [[2:10|But thou hast kept the good wine until now|Tu autem servasti bonum vinum usque adhuc]], that is, you have done this against a praiseworthy custom, and deserve to be reproved. For so the chief steward thought. From this it is gathered that this wine was the very best. For the works of Christ were perfect[[Deut 32:4||]] [the margin gives only Deut. xxxii; cf. Deut 32:4, “The works of God are perfect”]. For those whom He healed in body He healed in spirit too; and in Christ’s other acts there was a certain excellence, so that they issued in something more perfect than nature could produce. Therefore this supernatural change of the water issued in wine of surpassing strength.

paras.t: Hoc fecit initium signorum Jesus, id est, prædicta mutatio aquæ in vinum fuit primum miraculum Christi quod fecit in carne; factumque est in Cana, quæ est villa Galilææ; et manifestavit, id est, aliis notificavit, gloriam suam, id est excellentiam, vel omnipotentiam, seu divinitatem suam in carne latentem.
paras.en: [[2:11|This beginning of miracles did Jesus|Hoc fecit initium signorum Jesus]], that is, the aforesaid change of water into wine was the first miracle that Christ worked in the flesh; and it was done [[2:11|in Cana|in Cana]], which is a town of Galilee; [[2:11|and manifested|et manifestavit]], that is, made known to others, [[2:11|his glory|gloriam suam]], that is, His excellence, or omnipotence, or His Godhead hidden in the flesh.

paras.t: Quæritur, an mutatio aquæ in vinum fuerit primum miraculum factum a Salvatore. Et apparet primo, quod non, per ea quæ in evangelio Nazaræorum, et in libro de Infantia Salvatoris scribuntur. Secundo: nam Christus miraculose exivit de utero Virginis. Dicitur quoque apparuisse tribus Magis in somnis, admonuisseque eos ut per aliam viam reverterentur in terram suam. Denique in præcedenti capitulo patuit, quod prædixit Petro prophetice: Tu vocaberis Cephas. Philippum quoque supernaturaliter intus attraxit, ut sequeretur se. Et Nathanael confessus est Jesum esse Filium Dei propter duo signa: primo, quoniam secreta cordis sui cognovit; secundo, quoniam absentis verba cognovit, et dixit, Antequam Philippus vocaret te, quum esses sub arbore fici, vidi te; eique prophetando prædixit, Videbitis angelos Dei ascendentes et descendentes supra Filium hominis. Quæ omnia erant super naturam. Et secundum Apostolum, prophetiæ in signum sunt non infidelibus. Jejunavit quoque Salvator quadraginta diebus et noctibus, nihil prorsus manducans. Sed et in Luca habetur quod Jesus, quum esset annorum duodecim, sedit in medio doctorum, interrogans illos et audiens, quum tamen litteras non didicerit. Et tam sapienter respondit, ut asserat Evangelista: Stupebant omnes super prudentia et responsis ejus.
paras.en: It is asked whether the change of water into wine was the first miracle done by the Saviour. And it seems, first, that it was not, from what is written in the Gospel of the Nazarenes and in the book of the Infancy of the Saviour. Secondly: for Christ came forth miraculously from the Virgin’s womb. He is also said to have appeared to the three Magi in their sleep and to have warned them to return to their own country by another way[[Matt 2:12||]]. Lastly, it was shown in the preceding chapter that He foretold to Peter prophetically: [[John 1:42|Thou shalt be called Cephas|Tu vocaberis Cephas]]. He also drew Philip inwardly, in a supernatural way, to follow Him[[John 1:43||]]. And Nathanael confessed Jesus to be the Son of God[[John 1:49||]] because of two signs: first, because He knew the secrets of his heart[[John 1:47||]]; secondly, because He knew his words while absent, and said: [[John 1:48|Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee|Antequam Philippus vocaret te, quum esses sub arbore fici, vidi te]]; and prophesying He foretold to him: You shall see [[John 1:51|the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man|angelos Dei ascendentes et descendentes supra Filium hominis]]. All of which were above nature. And according to the Apostle, [[1 Cor 14:22|prophecies, not to unbelievers|prophetiæ in signum sunt non infidelibus]] are for a sign [the OCR is unclear at *non*; the Apostle’s words are “prophecies, not to unbelievers but to believers”]. The Saviour also fasted forty days and nights, eating nothing at all[[Matt 4:2||]][[Luke 4:2||]]. And in Luke too we have that Jesus, when He was twelve years old[[Luke 2:42||]], sat in the midst of the doctors, asking them questions and hearing them[[Luke 2:46||]], though He had not learned letters[[John 7:15||]]. And He answered so wisely that the Evangelist declares: All [[Luke 2:47|were astonished at his wisdom and his answers|Stupebant omnes super prudentia et responsis ejus]].

paras.t: Ad hanc quæstionem dicendum, quod potestas faciendi miracula inerat Christo a principio suæ incarnationis. Quum autem asserit evangelista Joannes prædictum opus fuisse initium signorum Domini Jesu, non est sic intelligendum quod Christus non habuit nec egit aliquem actum supernaturalem ante hoc signum; sed quod non fecit in aliis rebus opera supernaturalia per se ipsum immediate, quibus ratio miraculi proprie sumpti conveniat, videlicet prout miraculum dicit quid manifestativum. Miraculum quippe sic debet esse opus evidens, valens ad fidei confirmationem. Propter quod patet ad argumenta solutio. Liber autem de Infantia Salvatoris reprobatur in decreto Gelasii Papæ, tanquam ab hæreticis editus et confictus. Similiter evangelium Nazaræorum inter falsa a doctoribus computatur.
paras.en: To this question it must be said that the power of working miracles was in Christ from the beginning of His incarnation. But when John the Evangelist asserts that the aforesaid work was the beginning of the signs of the Lord Jesus, it is not to be understood that Christ had or did no supernatural act before this sign; but that He did not, in other things, work by Himself and immediately supernatural works to which the nature of a miracle properly so called belongs, that is, a miracle as it signifies something that makes manifest [Latin *ratio miraculi proprie sumpti*: a miracle in the strict sense is a sign that shows something openly to others]. For a miracle taken in this way must be an evident work, able to confirm faith. And from this the answer to the arguments is plain. The book of the Infancy of the Saviour, moreover, is rejected in the decree of Pope Gelasius as published and fabricated by heretics [the so-called Gelasian Decree, a list of books received and rejected by the Church]. Likewise the Gospel of the Nazarenes is counted by the doctors among false writings.

paras.t: Postremo, post descriptionem miraculi præinducti, subdit Evangelista: Et crediderunt in eum, puta in Jesum, discipuli ejus, qui secum fuerunt vocati ad nuptias. Sed quoniam, teste Philosopho, addiscentem oportet credere, et Isaias testatur, Nisi credideritis non intelligetis: constat quod isti discipuli crediderunt Christo; sed non tam perfecte ut postea, viso tanto miraculo. Firmiter namque tunc crediderunt quod missus esset a Deo, et veram doctrinam ac salutarem proponeret, atque divina virtute operaretur in omnibus. An tamen credebant explicite quod esset Deus verus, Unigenitus Patris, certum non arbitror.
paras.en: Lastly, after the description of the miracle set out above, the Evangelist adds: [[2:11|And his disciples believed in him|et crediderunt in eum discipuli ejus]], that is, in Jesus, those who had been invited with Him to the marriage. But since, on the testimony of the Philosopher, the learner must believe, and Isaias testifies, [[Is 7:9|If you will not believe|Nisi credideritis]], you shall not understand [Denis quotes the Septuagint reading *non intelligetis*, as the margin notes; the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have “you shall not continue”]: it is certain that these disciples believed in Christ already; but not as perfectly as afterwards, when they had seen so great a miracle. For then they firmly believed that He was sent by God, that He set forth true and saving doctrine, and that He worked all things by divine power. But whether they believed explicitly that He was true God, the Only-begotten of the Father, I do not think certain.

paras.t: Circa moralizationem evangelii hujus, multa pulcherrima posuit Augustinus. Nec tanta dicta sunt, quin plura dici possint. Fit enim mentio in Scripturis de multiplicibus nuptiis, scilicet: carnalibus, quæ dum legitime fiunt, sacramentales dicuntur, et in ecclesia celebrantur. Secundo, de nuptiis spiritualibus, quæ duplices sunt, videlicet: Verbi cum humana natura, quæ dicuntur nuptiæ incarnationis, celebratæ in utero Virginis (unde et dicitur: Ipse tanquam sponsus procedens de thalamo suo); et item, Christi cum militanti Ecclesia, quæ secundum Apostolum, est Christi sponsa: quæ dicuntur nuptiæ spiritualis conjunctionis, celebranturque in cubili conscientiæ purioris. Tertio, de nuptiis beatificæ fruitionis: quæ dicuntur æternales, et celebrantur in palatio majestatis. Unde habetur in Apocalypsi: Beati qui ad cœnam nuptiarum Agni vocati sunt.
paras.en: On the moral sense of this Gospel, Augustine has set down many very beautiful things. Yet not so much has been said that more cannot be said. For Scripture speaks of several kinds of marriage. First, of carnal marriage, which, when it is lawfully contracted, is called sacramental and is celebrated in the church. Secondly, of spiritual marriage, which is twofold: that of the Word with human nature, which is called the marriage of the Incarnation, celebrated in the womb of the Virgin (whence it is said: [[Ps 18:6|he as a bridegroom coming out of his bridechamber|Ipse tanquam sponsus procedens de thalamo suo]]); and again, that of Christ with the Church militant, which, according to the Apostle, is the bride of Christ[[Eph 5:23||]] [the margin gives Eph. v, 23 and following]: this is called the marriage of spiritual union, and it is celebrated in the bridal chamber of a purer conscience. Thirdly, of the marriage of beatific fruition [that is, the enjoyment of God seen face to face in heaven], which is called eternal, and is celebrated in the palace of the divine majesty. Hence we have in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 19:9|Blessed are they that are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb|Beati qui ad cœnam nuptiarum Agni vocati sunt]].

paras.t: Celebremus ergo spirituales nuptias in conscientia nostra, uniendo et intime copulando animas nostras Verbo seu Filio Dei, sponso animarum sanctarum, qui ait per Osee, Sponsabo te mihi in fide, ut animæ nostræ fecundentur et impregnentur cælesti semine, id est lumine gratiæ copiosæ, quatenus indesinenter producant fructus spirituales, seu actus virtuosos.
paras.en: Let us therefore celebrate a spiritual marriage in our conscience, uniting and closely joining our souls to the Word or Son of God, the Bridegroom of holy souls, who says through Osee: [[Osee 2:20|I will espouse thee to me in faith|Sponsabo te mihi in fide]]; so that our souls may be made fruitful and may conceive by the heavenly seed, that is, by the light of abundant grace, and so bring forth without ceasing spiritual fruits, or virtuous acts.

paras.t: Si hoc facimus, celebramus nuptias in Cana Galilææ, hoc est in zelo transmigrationis, seu desiderio eundi ac perveniendi ad nuptias æternales. Cana enim, zelus, Galilæa autem, transmigratio interpretatur. Debemus igitur zelum ferventem habere transmigrandi de via ad patriam, de exsilio isto ad paradisum cælestem. Porro, celebrando has nuptias, aderit Mater Jesu, dulcis et mitis Maria. Tunc vocabimus magno fervore potius quam oris clamore, Jesum: non quasi absentem, quum ipse sit sponsus, sed quasi nondum perfecte præsentem, atque per speciem apparentem. Rogabimus itaque eum, ut de his nuptiis imperfectis, interruptis et suspiriosis, perducat nos ad nuptias consummatas, continuas, gaudio plenas, ubi non est desiderium boni futuri quoad præmium essentiale, sed perfectissimus […] superlibenter celebrat Christus modo in anima devota nuptias spirituales! Ipse nempe est qui ait per Salomonem in Proverbiis: Deliciæ meæ, esse cum filiis hominum; et in Apocalypsi: Ego sto ad ostium, et pulso; si quis aperuerit mihi, intrabo et cœnabo cum illo, et ipse mecum. Dicat ergo anima nostra Christo sponso cælesti, illud Canticorum: Veniat dilectus meus in hortum suum, et comedat fructum pomorum suorum; et illud, Omnia poma nova et vetera, dilecte mi, servavi tibi. Poma ista, sunt sancta desideria patriæ, fervidi motus in Deum, contemplationes sinceræ cælestium: quibus certum est Christum præcipue delectari.
paras.en: If we do this, we celebrate a marriage [[2:1|in Cana of Galilee|in Cana Galilææ]], that is, in the zeal of transmigration, or the desire of going forth and coming to the eternal marriage. For Cana is interpreted "zeal", and Galilee "transmigration" [that is, a passing over from one place to another]. We ought therefore to have a fervent zeal to pass over from the way to the fatherland, from this exile to the heavenly paradise. Moreover, as we celebrate this marriage, [[2:1|the mother of Jesus|Mater Jesu]] will be there, sweet and gentle Mary. Then we shall call Jesus, with great fervour rather than with the clamour of the mouth: not as though He were absent, since He Himself is the Bridegroom, but as not yet perfectly present and appearing by sight [per speciem: seen face to face, and no longer by faith]. We shall ask Him, then, to lead us from this marriage, imperfect, interrupted and full of sighs, to the marriage that is consummated, unbroken and full of joy, where there is no desire of a good still to come as regards the essential reward [the essential reward of heaven is the vision and enjoyment of God Himself, as distinct from the accidental joys added to it], but the most perfect […] [about two lines are unreadable in the OCR here] most gladly does Christ even now celebrate a spiritual marriage in the devout soul! For it is He who says through Solomon in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:31|my delights were to be with the children of men|Deliciæ meæ, esse cum filiis hominum]]; and in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:20|I stand at the gate and knock|sto ad ostium, et pulso]]; if any man open to me, [[Apoc 3:20|I will come in to him and will sup with him: and he with me|intrabo et cœnabo cum illo, et ipse mecum]]. Let our soul, then, say to Christ, the heavenly Bridegroom, that word of the Canticle: [[Cant 5:1|Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat the fruit of his apple trees|Veniat dilectus meus in hortum suum, et comedat fructum pomorum suorum]]; and that other: [[Cant 7:13|all fruits: the new and the old, my beloved, I have kept for thee|Omnia poma nova et vetera, dilecte mi, servavi tibi]] [the margin gives only "Ibid.", that is, Cant 5; these words are those of Cant 7:13]. These fruits are holy desires for the fatherland, fervent movements toward God, pure contemplations of heavenly things: and it is certain that Christ delights in these above all.

paras.t: Quemadmodum autem in nuptiis illis corporalibus, deficiente vino, dixit Mater Jesu ad eum, Vinum non habent; sic in præmemoratis animæ nuptiis, deficiente vino, hoc est spirituali consolatione, devotionis sapore, mystico intellectu, perfectionisque gratia, advocata ac domina nostra intercedet pro nobis ad Christum, ut desideratam dulcedinis suæ præsentiam, consolationem internam, solidum cibum, stabilem puritatem, nobis conferre dignetur. Si autem fecerimus quod dixit Virgo beata ministris, Quodcumque (inquiens) dixerit vobis, facite; tunc Jesus faciet nobis quidquid Mater ejus pro nobis rogaverit.
paras.en: And as in that bodily marriage, [[2:3|the wine failing, the mother of Jesus saith to him: They have no wine|deficiente vino, dixit Mater Jesu ad eum, Vinum non habent]]; so in the marriage of the soul spoken of above, when the wine fails, that is, spiritual consolation, the savour of devotion, mystical understanding, and the grace of perfection, our advocate and Lady will intercede for us with Christ, that He may deign to grant us the longed-for presence of His sweetness, inward consolation, solid food, and steadfast purity. And if we do what the blessed Virgin told the waiters, saying: [[2:5|Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye|Quodcumque (inquiens) dixerit vobis, facite]]; then Jesus will do for us whatever His Mother asks for us.

paras.t: Per sex quoque lapideas hydrias, intelligo sex principales animæ vires: quarum tres sunt in parte intellectiva, videlicet ratio, memoria, et voluntas; et tres in parte sensitiva, scilicet appetitus concupiscibilis, irascibilis, et virtus cogitativa, quæ dicitur a Philosopho, intellectus passivus et ratio particularis. Istæ quippe potentiæ sunt subjecta scientiæ seu virtutum: idcirco implendæ sunt aquis scientiæ salutaris, et humore ac rore virtutum, ut omnes in suis actionibus ordinate se habeant, rationis censuram sequendo, ne passiones appetitus concupiscibilis et irascibilis rationi repugnent et prævaleant, sed sensualitas rationis imperio […]
paras.en: By the [[2:6|six waterpots of stone|lapideas hydrias]], too, I understand the six principal powers of the soul: three of them are in the intellective part, namely reason, memory and will; and three in the sensitive part, namely the concupiscible appetite, the irascible, and the cogitative power, which the Philosopher calls the passive intellect and particular reason [the cogitative power is the inner sense that judges particular things, as reason judges universals]. For these powers are the subjects of knowledge or of the virtues [that is, the powers in which knowledge and the virtues reside]: therefore they are to be filled with the waters of saving knowledge, and with the moisture and dew of the virtues, so that all of them may act in due order, following the judgement of reason, lest the passions of the concupiscible and irascible appetite resist reason and prevail over it, but that sensuality may be subject to the command of reason […] [the verb is lost in the OCR, and about two lines are unreadable here; "be subject" is supplied from the sense]

paras.t: […]tet has aquas in vinum, infundendo animæ septem dona Spiritus Sancti, cum exuberantia quadam, ita ut ratio et voluntas, quæ sunt subjecta septem donorum, sint prompte ac delectabiliter mobiles a Spiritu Sancto, præsertim in actibus theologicarum virtutum, in ordine ad ultimum finem, qui est beatitudo supernaturalis. Tunc per donum sapientiæ, sortietur anima dulcem gustum in contemplatione divinorum, et impellente eam amoris sancti fervore, faciet corde promptissimo quidquid noverit Creatori placere, et pro ejus reverentia esse. Sic animalis homo fit spiritualis, introductus in cellam vinariam, atque inebriatus vino Spiritus Sancti, ita ut memoriam abundantiæ suavitatis Dei eructet, dicens: Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine!
paras.en: […] [the beginning of this sentence is lost in the OCR; the sense is that Christ then] will turn these waters into wine, pouring into the soul the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost with a certain overflowing abundance, so that reason and will, which are the subjects of the seven gifts, may be readily and delightfully moved by the Holy Ghost, above all in the acts of the theological virtues, in order to the last end, which is supernatural beatitude. Then through the gift of wisdom the soul will receive a sweet taste in the contemplation of divine things, and, driven on by the fervour of holy love, will do with a most ready heart whatever it knows to be pleasing to the Creator and to belong to His honour. Thus the animal man becomes spiritual [animalis homo: the natural man, ruled by sense, as opposed to the spiritual man], being brought into the cellar of wine[[Cant 2:4||]] and inebriated with the wine of the Holy Ghost, so that he utters the memory of the abundance of God's sweetness[[Ps 144:7||]], saying: [[Ps 30:20|O how great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord|Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine!]]!

paras.t: Post hæc, videlicet post nuptiarum in Cana factarum, et prædicti miraculi perpetrationem, descendit Capharnaum, urbem Galilææ metropolim atque maritimam, ipse, et Mater ejus, et fratres ejus, hoc est consanguinei et affines ex parte virgineæ Genitricis. Non enim fuerunt filii Mariæ, ut dixit infelicissimus ille Helvidius hæreticus, asserens Christo nato, Matrem ejus cognitam esse a Joseph. Aliqui vero dixerunt, quod erant filii Joseph ex alia conjuge. Sed probabilius est quod etiam Joseph virgo fuit: quia non decuit tantam virginem, nisi a sponso virgine, a pudicissimo atque castissimo viro custodiri. Et item, quum Christus in cruce erectus, non commendavit Matrem suam jam provectæ ætatis, nisi discipulo virgini, verisimile est quod juvenculam non commisit custodiendam, nisi virgineo viro. Dicuntur itaque fratres, juxta consuetudinem sacræ Scripturæ, quæ sæpissime homines ejusdem genealogiæ nominat fratres: sicut in Genesi, Lot dicitur frater Abrahæ, et Jacob dicitur frater Laban; Ismael quoque coram cunctis fratribus suis fertur obiisse; et Joab dixit ad Amasam, Salve, mi frater.
paras.en: [[2:12|After this|Post hæc]], that is, after the marriage held in Cana and the working of the miracle just described, [[2:12|he went down to Capharnaum|descendit Capharnaum]], the chief city of Galilee, lying by the sea, [[2:12|he and his mother and his brethren|ipse, et Mater ejus, et fratres ejus]], that is, His kinsmen and relations on the side of His virgin Mother. For they were not sons of Mary, as that most wretched heretic Helvidius said, asserting that after Christ was born His Mother was known by Joseph. Others again have said that they were sons of Joseph by another wife. But it is more probable that Joseph too was a virgin: for it was not fitting that so great a virgin should be kept by any but a virgin spouse, a most modest and most chaste man. And again, since Christ, raised upon the cross, commended His Mother, then already advanced in years, to none but a virgin disciple[[John 19:27||]], it is likely that He did not entrust her, when a young maiden, to the keeping of any but a virgin man. They are called brethren, therefore, after the custom of sacred Scripture, which very often calls men of the same family brethren: as in Genesis Lot is called the brother of Abraham[[Gen 13:8||]][[Gen 14:14||]], and Jacob the brother of Laban[[Gen 29:15||]] [the margin is hard to read here; Gen 29:15 is where Laban calls Jacob his brother]; Ismael, too, is said to have died [[Gen 25:18|in the presence of all his brethren|coram cunctis fratribus suis]]; and Joab said to Amasa: [[2 Kings 20:9|God save thee, my brother|Salve, mi frater]].

paras.t: Et discipuli ejus. Et ibi manserunt non multis diebus. Causa hujus habitationis insinuatur in Matthæo, quo scribitur: Relicta civitate sua Nazareth, venit et habitavit in civitate Capharnaum in finibus Zabulon et Nephthali, ut impleretur quod dictum est per Isaiam prophetam: Populus qui ambulabat in tenebris, vidit lucem magnam, etc. Voluit quippe Salvator majestatem suam paulatim manifestare: idcirco accessit ad urbem suæ provinciæ principalem, ubi a pluribus audiretur ac nosceretur.
paras.en: [[2:12|and his disciples|Et discipuli ejus]]. [[2:12|and they remained there not many days|Et ibi manserunt non multis diebus]]. The cause of this stay is indicated in Matthew, where it is written: [[Matt 4:13|leaving the city Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capharnaum|Relicta civitate sua Nazareth, venit et habitavit in civitate Capharnaum]] [[Matt 4:13|in the borders of Zabulon and of Nephthalim|in finibus Zabulon et Nephthali]], [[Matt 4:14|That it might be fulfilled which was said by Isaias the prophet|ut impleretur quod dictum est per Isaiam prophetam]]: [[Is 9:2|The people that walked in darkness, have seen a great light|Populus qui ambulabat in tenebris, vidit lucem magnam]], etc. [Denis gives the prophecy in the words of Isaias himself rather than as Matthew quotes it (Matt 4:16, "sat in darkness"); the margin's "Is. ix" is followed by a misread verse number.] For the Saviour willed to make His majesty known little by little: and therefore He went to the chief city of His province, where He might be heard and known by more people.

paras.t: Et prope erat Pascha, id est paschalis solennitas, Judæorum; et ascendit Jerosolymam Jesus. Non dubium quin secum ascenderunt qui cum eo Capharnaum intraverunt, videlicet Mater ejus, fratres atque discipuli. Cur ascendit Jerusalem? Primo, ut legem impleret. Fuit enim præceptum in Exodo, ut omne masculinum Judæorum ter in anno appareret coram Domino, in loco quo licuit sacrificia fieri, scilicet in festo Paschæ, Pentecostes, et Tabernaculorum. Et licet interdum dispensabatur cum longe habitantibus, quantum ad ultima duo festa, tamen in festivitate paschali maxime tenebantur Judæi legis præceptum servare. Secundo, ut dicit Beda, ut sacrificia offerret, et orationum vota persolveret, quemadmodum lex præcepit. Tertio, ut futurorum hæreticorum dicentium legem Mosaicam a diabolo traditam, errorem destrueret. Quarto, ut nobis exemplum daret cum omni vigilantia cordis et reverentia obediendi divinis præceptis.
paras.en: [[2:13|And the pasch|Et prope erat Pascha]], that is, the paschal solemnity, [[2:13|of the Jews was at hand: and Jesus went up to Jerusalem|Judæorum; et ascendit Jerosolymam Jesus]]. There is no doubt that those who had entered Capharnaum with Him went up with Him, namely His Mother, His brethren and His disciples. Why did He go up to Jerusalem? First, to fulfil the law. For it was commanded in Exodus that every male of the Jews should appear before the Lord three times a year[[Ex 23:17||]][[Ex 34:23||]], in the place where sacrifices might lawfully be offered[[Deut 12:5||]], namely at the feasts of the Pasch, of Pentecost and of Tabernacles. And though a dispensation was sometimes given to those who lived far off as regards the last two feasts, yet at the paschal festival above all the Jews were bound to keep the precept of the law. Secondly, as Bede says, to offer sacrifices and to pay His vows of prayer, as the law commanded[[Deut 12:6||]]. Thirdly, to destroy the error of future heretics who would say that the Mosaic law was given by the devil[[Ex 21:1||]] [the margin here reads ‘Exod. xxi, passim’, that is, the laws given by God throughout Exodus; the chapter number is uncertain]. Fourthly, to give us an example of obeying the divine precepts with all watchfulness of heart and with reverence.

paras.t: Hoc ipsum quod Christus Filius Dei, Deus incarnatus, cum ceteris Jerosolymam tenderet in solennitate paschali, prædictum fuit per Zachariam, dicentem: Hæc dicit Dominus exercituum: Usquequo veniant populi, et vadant habitatores, unusquisque ad alterum dicentes, Eamus et deprecemur faciem Domini? Vadam etiam ego, et venient populi multi, ad quærendum Dominum exercituum in Jerusalem. Hoc quod dicitur hic, Vadam etiam ego, non dicitur in persona Zachariæ prophetæ, sed Dei per ipsum loquentis, ut patet diligenter intuenti seriem textus. Ire autem non competit Deo nisi ratione naturæ assumptæ: ideo in his verbis innuebat se Dominus exercituum incarnandum. Et quoniam scripturæ veteris Testamenti loquuntur de Deo mittente, et Christo mittendo seu misso, quasi de distinctis personis, patet quod Moyses et Prophetæ insinuaverunt personalem esse distinctionem in simplici Deitate.
paras.en: This very thing, that Christ the Son of God, God incarnate, should make His way to Jerusalem with the rest at the paschal solemnity, was foretold by Zacharias, who says: [[Zach 8:20|Thus saith the Lord of hosts, until people come|Hæc dicit Dominus exercituum: Usquequo veniant populi]], [[Zach 8:21|And the inhabitants go one to another, saying: Let us go, and entreat the face of the Lord|et vadant habitatores, unusquisque ad alterum dicentes, Eamus et deprecemur faciem Domini?]]? [[Zach 8:21|I also will go|Vadam etiam ego]], [[Zach 8:22|And many peoples, and strong nations shall come to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem|et venient populi multi, ad quærendum Dominum exercituum in Jerusalem]]. What is said here, [[Zach 8:21|I also will go|Vadam etiam ego]], is not said in the person of the prophet Zacharias but in that of God speaking through him, as is plain to anyone who looks carefully at the sequence of the text. But to go does not befit God except by reason of the nature He assumed; and so in these words the Lord of hosts was hinting that He would become incarnate. And since the Scriptures of the Old Testament speak of God who sends, and of Christ who is to be sent or has been sent, as of distinct persons, it is plain that Moses and the Prophets gave hints that there is a distinction of persons in the simple Godhead.

paras.t: Et invenit Jesus in templo, hoc est in quodam anteriori atrio templi, ubi vulgus orabat et doctores docebant, non in atrio sacerdotum continente altare holocaustorum, vendentes boves, et oves, et columbas. Sacerdotes enim, quum essent avari, posuerunt in templo ministros suos, vel filios, qui animalia immolaticia venderent, ne de longe venientes possent se excusare ab immolatione animalium, propter difficultatem adducendi ea secum ob prolixitatem itineris. Invenit quoque et nummularios, id est campsores quosdam, sedentes in templo. Ne enim pauperes se excusarent per hoc quod non haberent pecuniam ad emenda animalia requisitam, posuerunt sacerdotes in templo campsores, qui egenis sub cautione accommodarent pecuniam.
paras.en: [[2:14|And he found in the temple|Et invenit Jesus in templo]], that is, in a certain outer court of the temple, where the common people prayed and the doctors taught, not in the court of the priests which held the altar of holocausts, [[2:14|them that sold oxen and sheep and doves|vendentes boves, et oves, et columbas]]. For the priests, being covetous, had placed in the temple their servants, or their sons, to sell animals for sacrifice, so that those who came from far off could not excuse themselves from sacrificing animals on the ground of the difficulty of bringing them along on so long a journey. He found also [[2:14|the changers of money|nummularios]], that is, certain money-changers, [[2:14|sitting|sedentes]] in the temple. For so that the poor should not excuse themselves on the ground that they had not the money needed to buy the animals, the priests placed money-changers in the temple, who lent money to the needy on security.

paras.t: Et quum fecisset quasi flagellum de funiculis, omnes venditores præfatos ejecit de templo, minando et expellendo eos cum tali flagello; oves quoque et boves ejecit; et nummulariorum effudit æs, id est pecuniam, et mensas super quas ponebantur pecuniæ, subvertit. Et his qui columbas vendebant, dixit: Auferte ista animalia hinc, et nolite facere domum Patris mei cœlestis ac naturalis, domum negotiationis, vendendo ibi animalia ista, quæ in foro solent venundari.
paras.en: [[2:15|And when he had made, as it were, a scourge of little cords|Et quum fecisset quasi flagellum de funiculis]], He drove all the aforesaid sellers [[2:15|out of the temple|ejecit de templo]], driving and chasing them out with that scourge; [[2:15|the sheep also and the oxen|oves quoque et boves]] He drove out; [[2:15|and the money of the changers he poured out|et nummulariorum effudit æs]], that is, their coins, [[2:15|and the tables|et mensas]] on which the coins were laid [[2:15|he overthrew|subvertit]]. [[2:16|And to them that sold doves he said|Et his qui columbas vendebant, dixit]]: [[2:16|Take these things|Auferte ista]] (these animals) [[2:16|hence|hinc]], [[2:16|and make not the house of my Father|et nolite facere domum Patris mei]], My heavenly and natural Father, [[2:16|a house of traffic|domum negotiationis]], by selling here these animals, which are usually sold in the market.

paras.t: Satis mirandum videtur, quomodo Christo hæc faciente, qui nondum miraculis multis coruscavit, neque fama magna innotuit, nullus Judæorum præsumpsit resistere. Et respondendum, quod Jesus divina sua virtute, potuit corda eorum terrere quos alloquebatur. Potuit quoque ex vultu et oculis suis igneum splendidumque ac deiformem fulgorem, seu radios luciformes emittere, quo omnes videntes eum, timore concussi sunt. Corpus enim suum fuit animæ suæ omnino subjectum, ita quod qualificabatur in vultu et corpore secundum imperium animæ. Sed et humanitas Christi erat instrumentum animatum, conjunctum, ac proprium deitatis unitæ, quæ operabatur per illam ut voluit. Et quid miramur, si nunc nondum capiendus et occidendus, ejecit omnes flagello, qui postmodum mox capiendus et crucifigendus, solo verbo universam cohortem armatam, et ministros furentes ac gladiis cinctos, prostravit in terram? Nihilo minus, secundum Origenem, ejectio ista fuit magis miraculosa, quam conversio aquæ in vinum: quoniam ibi inanimata subservit materia; hic vero tot millium compescuntur ingenia.
paras.en: It seems quite astonishing that, when Christ did these things, though He had not yet shone forth with many miracles nor become known by any great fame, none of the Jews dared to resist. The answer must be that Jesus, by His divine power, could strike terror into the hearts of those He spoke to. He could also send forth from His face and eyes a fiery, shining and godlike brightness, or rays of light, so that all who saw Him were struck with fear. For His body was wholly subject to His soul, so that it took on qualities in face and body as the soul commanded. Moreover, the humanity of Christ was the living, conjoined and proper instrument of the Godhead united to it [a conjoined instrument is one united to the agent, as the hand is to a man, unlike a separate tool such as a pen], and the Godhead worked through it as It willed. And why do we wonder if now, when He was not yet to be taken and killed, He drove them all out with a scourge, when afterwards, about to be taken and crucified, by a word alone He threw to the ground the whole armed band[[Matt 26:47||]] and the raging servants girt with swords[[John 18:6||]] [the margin prints Joann. xv, 6; the falling to the ground is John 18:6]? Nevertheless, according to Origen, this casting out was more miraculous than the changing of water into wine: for there it was lifeless matter that obeyed, but here the minds of so many thousands are held in check.

paras.t: Recordati sunt vero discipuli ejus, quia scriptum est in Psalmo, in persona Christi: Zelus domus tuæ, id est magna affectio honorandi templum tuum, o Pater, comedit, id est, spiritualiter absorbuit me. Et etiam zelus iste fuit occasio occisionis Christi, et ita comedit, id est, consumpsit seu interfecit eum. Per hunc etenim zelum, bis ejecit vendentes de templo: semel in primo anno suæ prædicationis, unde nunc sermo; et in die Palmarum, ut patet in Luca. Per quod maxime offendit, odiumque incurrit sacerdotum, qui eum ex invidia occiderunt.
paras.en: [[2:17|And his disciples remembered, that it was written|Recordati sunt vero discipuli ejus, quia scriptum est]] in the Psalm[[Ps 68:10||]], in the person of Christ: [[2:17|The zeal of thy house|Zelus domus tuæ]], that is, a great desire to honour Thy temple, O Father, [[2:17|hath eaten me up|comedit]], that is, has spiritually swallowed Me up. And this zeal was also the occasion of Christ’s being put to death, and so it ate Him up, that is, consumed or killed Him. For through this zeal He twice drove the sellers out of the temple: once in the first year of His preaching, of which we are now speaking; and on Palm Sunday, as is plain in Luke[[Luke 19:45||]][[Luke 19:46||]]. By this above all He gave offence and incurred the hatred of the priests[[Luke 19:47||]], who put Him to death out of envy[[Mark 15:10||]] [the margin prints Marc. xv, 40; the envy of the chief priests is in Mark 15:10].

paras.t: Zelus proprie sumptus, est fervor quidam, seu intensa affectio ex amore procedens: per quem zelum homo conatur ea excludere quæ consecutionem boni optati impediunt. Quemadmodum autem amor est duplex, puta carnalis et spiritualis; sic duplex est zelus, videlicet carnalis, de quo dicit Apostolus: Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis vos? Et Psalmista: Neque zelaveris facientes iniquitatem. Alter est zelus spiritualis, divinus et caritativus, quo nititur homo ea excludere quæ divino honori aut proximorum contrariantur saluti. De quo Elias: Zelo (inquit) zelatus sum pro Domino exercituum. Hoc zelo zelatus est Phinees, pugione perfodiens Zambri et Cozbi concumbentes: pro quo meruit pactum sacerdotii sempiterni. Hoc zelo accendi debemus, Dei honorem, proximorum correctionem, justitiæ observationem cordialiter affectantes, atque impedimenta eorum pro viribus dissipantes. Sed omnino oportet ut incipiat homo a semetipso, totis præcordiis Deum amans, et omni posse honorans; et tunc idem optet ac procuret ab aliis fieri. Nam et zelus animarum est sacrificium acceptissimum Deo. — Præterea, secundum Glossam, zelus iste est fervor animi quo mens abjecto humano timore, pro defensione veritatis accenditur. Et secundum Augustinum, ille zelo domus Dei comeditur, qui universa mala quæ videt in ea, studet corrigere; quod si non potest, tolerat et gemit. Dum ergo discipuli viderunt Christum exercuisse hunc zelum pro honore Patris sui, et emundatione domus suæ, ac populi correctione, attenderunt præfatam Scripturam, intellexeruntque eam in hoc facto Christi impletam.
paras.en: Zeal, taken properly, is a certain fervour, or intense affection proceeding from love, by which a man strives to shut out whatever hinders his attaining the good he desires. And just as love is twofold, namely carnal and spiritual, so zeal is twofold. There is carnal zeal, of which the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 3:3|whereas there is among you envying and contention, are you not carnal|Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis vos?]]? And the Psalmist: [[Ps 36:1|nor envy them that work iniquity|Neque zelaveris facientes iniquitatem]]. [Here the Latin has zelus and zelare, ‘zeal’ and ‘to be zealous’, which also mean envy; the Douay-Rheims renders them ‘envying’ and ‘envy’.] The other is spiritual zeal, divine and charitable, by which a man strives to shut out whatever is contrary to the honour of God or the salvation of his neighbours. Of this Elias says: [[3 Kings 19:10|With zeal have I been zealous for the Lord God of hosts|Zelo (inquit) zelatus sum pro Domino exercituum]][[3 Kings 19:14||]]. With this zeal Phinees was zealous, piercing with a dagger Zambri and Cozbi as they lay together[[Num 25:7||]][[Num 25:8||]][[Num 25:14||]][[Num 25:15||]]; for which he merited the covenant of an everlasting priesthood[[Num 25:13||]]. With this zeal we ought to be kindled, heartily desiring the honour of God, the correction of our neighbours and the keeping of justice, and scattering with all our strength whatever hinders them. But a man must by all means begin with himself, loving God with his whole heart and honouring Him with all his power; and then let him desire and see to it that the same be done by others. For zeal for souls is a sacrifice most acceptable to God. — Further, according to the Gloss, this zeal is a fervour of spirit by which the mind, casting off human fear, is kindled for the defence of the truth. And according to Augustine, he is eaten up by zeal for the house of God who strives to correct all the evils he sees in it, and if he cannot, bears them and groans. So when the disciples saw that Christ had exercised this zeal for the honour of His Father, the cleansing of His house and the correction of the people, they turned their minds to the Scripture just mentioned, and understood that it was fulfilled in this deed of Christ.

paras.t: Responderunt ergo Judæi incorrigibiles et superbi, et dixerunt ei: Quod signum, id est quale divinum miraculum, ostendis nobis quia hæc facis, id est, per quod sciamus tibi licitum esse hæc facere? tanquam dicerent: Ejectio ista non spectat ad te, nec tuum est corrigere nos et facta sacerdotum, quum non habeas auctoritatem, nec sis sacerdos, neque propheta; et si dicis quod imo tuum sit hoc, ostende signum quo sciamus tibi divinitus commissam potestatem.
paras.en: [[2:18|The Jews, therefore, answered|Responderunt ergo Judæi]], incorrigible and proud, [[2:18|and said to him|et dixerunt ei]]: [[2:18|What sign|Quod signum]], that is, what kind of divine miracle, [[2:18|dost thou shew unto us, seeing thou dost these things|ostendis nobis quia hæc facis]]? that is, by which we may know that it is lawful for thee to do these things? As though they said: This casting out is no business of thine, nor is it for thee to correct us and the doings of the priests, since thou hast no authority and art neither priest nor prophet; and if thou sayest that it is indeed thy business, show a sign by which we may know that the power has been committed to thee by God.

paras.t: Respondit Jesus, et dixit eis: Solvite templum hoc, id est, mortem violentam mihi inferendo, solvetis, occidetis, dissipabitis, et a naturalibus juncturis separabitis corpus meum, quod est templum Verbi in eo habitantis. In passione enim solutum est corpus Christi ab anima ejus, et sanguis a corpore, universaque membrorum compago præ nimia corporis distentione soluta est. Propter quod ait in Psalmo: Sicut aqua effusus sum, et dispersa sunt omnia ossa mea; et rursus, Dinumeraverunt omnia ossa mea. Porro, quod ait Salvator, Solvite, non dicit exhortando et licentiando quasi rem bonam ex parte facientium, quia maximum erat peccatum; sed prænuntiando, quomodo dixit ad Judam in Cœna, Quod facis, fac citius.
paras.en: [[2:19|Jesus answered and said to them: Destroy this temple|Respondit Jesus, et dixit eis: Solvite templum hoc]]: that is, by inflicting a violent death on Me you will destroy, kill and scatter My body, and sever it at its natural joints, the body which is the temple of the Word dwelling in it. [The Latin solvite means both ‘destroy’ and ‘loose’, which Denis goes on to apply to the loosening of the body.] For in the Passion the body of Christ was loosed from His soul, and the blood from the body, and the whole framework of the limbs was loosened by the excessive stretching of the body. Therefore He says in the Psalm: [[Ps 21:15|I am poured out like water; and all my bones are scattered|Sicut aqua effusus sum, et dispersa sunt omnia ossa mea]]; and again, [[Ps 21:18|They have numbered all my bones|Dinumeraverunt omnia ossa mea]]. Moreover, when the Saviour says, [[2:19|Destroy|Solvite]], He does not say it by way of exhortation and permission, as though it were a good thing on the part of those who did it, for it was the greatest of sins; but by way of foretelling, as He said to Judas at the Supper, [[John 13:27|That which thou dost, do quickly|Quod facis, fac citius]].

paras.t: Dicitur autem corpus Christi et anima ejus, seu tota sua humanitas, templum Verbi et unitæ Deitatis: Primo, quoniam Verbum fuit in eis per immediatam personalemque unionem: unde secundum Apostolum, in Christo habitat omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter. Secundo, quoniam habitavit in eis per excellentissimam gratiam. Tertio, quoniam habitavit in anima Christi per fruitionem claram ac beatificam. Quarto, quia sicut in templo materiali orationes Domino offeruntur, et ab ipso exaudiuntur; sic preces Ecclesiæ porriguntur Deo in Christo et per Christum, per quem etiam exaudiuntur. Et in tribus diebus, id est intra tres dies naturales, videlicet tertia die, repente excitabo, id est, a morte suscitabo, illud, animam ei reuniendo. Divinitas enim mansit semper unita corpori et animæ Christi.
paras.en: Now the body of Christ and His soul, that is, His whole humanity, is called the temple of the Word and of the Godhead united to it: first, because the Word was in them by an immediate and personal union; whence, according to the Apostle, in Christ [[Col 2:9|dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead corporeally|habitat omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter]]. Secondly, because He dwelt in them by the most excellent grace. Thirdly, because He dwelt in the soul of Christ by clear and beatific fruition [that is, the enjoyment of God seen face to face]. Fourthly, because, as in a material temple prayers are offered to the Lord and are heard by Him, so the prayers of the Church are offered to God in Christ and through Christ, through whom they are also heard. [[2:19|And in three days|Et in tribus diebus]], that is, within three natural days, namely on the third day, suddenly [[2:19|I will raise|excitabo]], that is, raise from death, [[2:19|it up|illud]], by reuniting the soul to it. For the Godhead remained ever united to the body and to the soul of Christ.

paras.t: His verbis ostendit se Christus esse Deum omnipotentem, cui omnia licent. Nam se ipsum resuscitare a morte, non competit nisi Deo mortali natura induto. Merito autem perversis, induratis incredulisque Judæis, datur signum obscurum, rememorativum præteriti, sicut et regi Achaz ejusque populo datum est signum futuræ incarnationis, ut in Isaia habetur: Propter hoc dabit Dominus ipse vobis signum: Ecce virgo concipiet et pariet filium.
paras.en: By these words Christ shows that He is God almighty, to whom all things are lawful. For to raise oneself from death befits none but God clothed in mortal nature. And rightly is an obscure sign given to the perverse, hardened and unbelieving Jews, a sign that recalls what is past [that is, one understood only when it is remembered after the event, as in v. 22], just as a sign of the future incarnation was given to King Achaz and his people, as we read in Isaias: [[Is 7:14|Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign. Behold a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son|Propter hoc dabit Dominus ipse vobis signum: Ecce virgo concipiet et pariet filium]].

paras.t: Dixerunt ergo Judæi irridentes et redarguere cupientes verba Christi, quæ carnaliter intellexerunt de templo illo lapideo, inanimato et manufacto: Quadraginta et sex annis ædificatum est templum hoc secundum, a Nehemia atque Zorobabel, prophetantibus Aggæo et Zacharia. Templum vero primum a Salomone constructum, intra septem annos fuit completum.
paras.en: [[2:20|The Jews then said|Dixerunt ergo Judæi]], mocking, and wishing to refute the words of Christ, which they understood carnally of that temple of stone, lifeless and made with hands: [[2:20|Six and forty years was this temple in building|Quadraginta et sex annis ædificatum est templum hoc]], this second temple, by Nehemias and Zorobabel[[1 Esd 3:2||]][[1 Esd 3:8||]], while Aggeus and Zacharias prophesied[[1 Esd 5:1||]]. But the first temple, built by Solomon, was completed within seven years[[3 Kings 6:38||]].

paras.t: Verba vero prætacta non sunt sic intelligenda, quod Judæi quadraginta et sex annis continue fabricaverunt hoc templum, sed quia a tempore quo cœperunt, usque ad templi consummationem, fluxerunt tot anni. Sed interim frequenter retardabantur, et sæpe cessabant ad tempus ab ædificatione incepta, propter gentiles vicinos et prohibitionem regis, ut patet in libro Esdræ. A primo siquidem anno Cyri regis Persarum, qui dedit Judæis licentiam a Babylonia revertendi et templum ædificandi, usque ad sextum annum Darii regis, quando consummatum est templum, leguntur anni quadraginta sex fluxisse. Et tamen non est magna vis verificandi hæc verba Judæorum, qui multa falsa dixerunt arguendo contra Christum. Et tu in tribus diebus excitabis, id est, solutum seu dissipatum reparabis, illud? quasi dicant: Hoc tibi impossibile esset, quum domus hæc sit tanto tempore fabricata. Certum est, si Christus aperte dixisset, In tribus diebus resurgam, vel, Resuscitabo corpus meum, quod non credidissent, sed derisissent.
paras.en: These words, however, are not to be understood to mean that the Jews worked at building this temple for forty-six years without a break, but that so many years passed from the time they began until the temple was completed. Meanwhile they were often held back, and often ceased for a time from the building they had begun, because of the Gentiles round about and the prohibition of the king[[1 Esd 4:1||]], as is plain in the book of Esdras. For from the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, who gave the Jews leave to return from Babylon and to build the temple[[1 Esd 1:1||]], to the sixth year of King Darius, when the temple was completed[[1 Esd 6:15||]], forty-six years are said to have passed. And yet there is no great need to verify these words of the Jews, who said many false things in arguing against Christ. [[2:20|and wilt thou raise it up in three days|Et tu in tribus diebus excitabis]], that is, repair it once destroyed or scattered? As though they said: This would be impossible for thee, since this house was built over so long a time. It is certain that if Christ had said openly, I shall rise in three days, or, I will raise up My body, they would not have believed Him, but would have mocked.

paras.t: Ille autem dicebat, id est, Jesus prædicta verba intellexit, de templo corporis sui, id est de corpore proprio, quod fuit templum Divinitatis. Quod igitur ait Evangelista, De templo corporis sui, sumendum est intransitive, sicut ad Colossenses dicit Apostolus, In exspoliatione corporis carnis, hoc est corporis quod est caro. — Hæc verba Domini Jesu, tenuerunt Judæi memoriter, tanquam falsa prolata. Unde et in nocte passionis, surgentes duo falsi testes, dixerunt: Nos audivimus eum dicentem: Possum destruere templum Dei, et in tribus diebus reædificare illud.
paras.en: [[2:21|But he spoke|Ille autem dicebat]], that is, Jesus meant the aforesaid words, [[2:21|of the temple of his body|de templo corporis sui]], that is, of His own body, which was the temple of the Godhead. So when the Evangelist says, [[2:21|of the temple of his body|De templo corporis sui]], it is to be taken intransitively [that is, the genitive names the same thing as the word it depends on: the temple which is His body], as the Apostle says to the Colossians, [[Col 2:11|in despoiling of the body of the flesh|In exspoliatione corporis carnis]], that is, of the body which is flesh. — These words of the Lord Jesus the Jews kept in mind, as though they had been spoken falsely. Hence on the night of the Passion two false witnesses rose up and said: [[Mark 14:58|We heard him say|Nos audivimus eum dicentem]]: [[Matt 26:61|I am able to destroy the temple of God and after three days to rebuild it|Possum destruere templum Dei, et in tribus diebus reædificare illud]].

paras.t: Quum ergo resurrexisset a mortuis, recordati sunt discipuli ejus, quia hoc dicebat Jesus de futura solutione, passione et resuscitatione corporis sui. Recordati autem sunt discipuli verborum istorum, non statim post resurrectionem, quia nec statim credebant eum resurrexisse; sed postquam apparuit eis, et aperuit eis sensum ut intelligerent Scripturas. Unde etiam constat, quod discipuli non intellexerunt verba Christi quæ ait, Solvite templum hoc, etc., tunc quando protulit ea, sed post resurrectionem, ut dictum est. Et crediderunt Scripturæ Prophetarum loquenti de Christi passione et resurrectione, et sermoni præmemorato quem dixit Jesus, videlicet: Solvite templum hoc. Quamvis discipuli ante resurrectionem non intellexerunt hæc verba, nec Prophetarum eloquia, tamen credebant ea vera esse; sed post resurrectionem idem credebant magis perfecte, tanquam notitiam verborum sortiti.
paras.en: [[2:22|When therefore he was risen again from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this|Quum ergo resurrexisset a mortuis, recordati sunt discipuli ejus, quia hoc dicebat]], namely Jesus, of the future destruction, passion and raising of His body. Now the disciples remembered these words not immediately after the resurrection, for neither did they believe at once that He had risen; but after He had appeared to them and [[Luke 24:45|opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures|aperuit eis sensum ut intelligerent Scripturas]]. Hence it is also clear that the disciples did not understand the words of Christ in which He said, [[2:19|Destroy this temple|Solvite templum hoc]], etc., at the time when He spoke them, but after the resurrection, as has been said. [[2:22|and they believed the scripture|Et crediderunt Scripturæ]] of the Prophets, which speaks of Christ’s passion and resurrection, [[2:22|and the word that Jesus had said|et sermoni præmemorato quem dixit Jesus]], namely: [[2:19|Destroy this temple|Solvite templum hoc]]. Although before the resurrection the disciples did not understand these words, nor the sayings of the Prophets, yet they believed them to be true; but after the resurrection they believed the same more perfectly, as having gained an understanding of the words.

paras.t: Quum autem esset Jerosolymis in Pascha, videlicet in die festo paschali. Non solum die uno seu ultimo festivitatis paschalis, quæ septem duravit diebus; sed forte toto tempore illo, vel pluribus diebus, ibi fuit. Multi crediderunt in nomine ejus, id est in ipso per nomen nominans designato, credentes quod esset Christus, vel saltem vir sanctus atque Propheta. Non tamen crediderunt nec suspicabantur quod esset Filius Dei naturalis, verusque Deus, nisi forte ante agnovissent per Scripturas quod Christus in lege promissus esset Deus. Causa credulitatis subjungitur: videntes signa ejus quæ faciebat tempore isto: quæ non sunt in speciali descripta, nisi quod ejecit vendentes in templo, etc. Fecit tamen magna miracula. Propter quod Nicodemus dixit ad eum: Nemo potest hæc signa facere quæ tu facis, nisi Deus fuerit cum eo. Supernaturalis quippe doctrina, supernaturalibus argumentis seu divinis miraculis fuerat comprobanda, ut tam certa sit fidei veritas, quam certum est Deum falsitatis non esse confirmatorem, cooperatorem, vel assertorem.
paras.en: [[2:23|Now when he was at Jerusalem, at the pasch|Quum autem esset Jerosolymis in Pascha]], that is, on the paschal feast day. Not only on one day, or on the last day, of the paschal festival, which lasted seven days; but perhaps He was there for that whole time, or for several days. [[2:23|many believed in his name|Multi crediderunt in nomine ejus]], that is, in Him who is designated by the name, believing that He was the Christ, or at least a holy man and a Prophet. Yet they did not believe, nor even suspect, that He was the natural Son of God [that is, Son by nature, not by adoption] and true God, unless perhaps they had already learned from the Scriptures that the Christ promised in the law was God. The cause of their belief is added: [[2:23|seeing his signs which he did|videntes signa ejus quæ faciebat]] at that time. These are not described one by one, except that He cast out those who sold in the temple, etc. Yet He did great miracles; for which reason Nicodemus said to Him: [[John 3:2|no man can do these signs which thou dost, unless God be with him|Nemo potest hæc signa facere quæ tu facis, nisi Deus fuerit cum eo]]. For a supernatural doctrine had to be proved by supernatural arguments, that is, by divine miracles, so that the truth of the faith may be as certain as it is certain that God is not the confirmer, the co-worker or the asserter of falsehood.

paras.t: Ipse autem Jesus non credebat semetipsum eis. Hoc quoad superficiem litteræ, sonat ac si Jesus Dominus virtutum, cui potestatem omnis carnis dedit Pater, timuisset aliquid mali sibi posse ab istis inferri. Sed certum est quod non timuit hoc, nec eos qui corpus occidunt. Augustinus ergo et Beda exponunt hoc modo, quod ideo Jesus non se credidit eis, quoniam nondum baptizati et plena fide imbuti fuerunt, gerentes formam catechumenorum: quibus Christus dicitur se ipsum non credere, quia non datur eis Sacramentum corporis Christi. Hæc autem expositio videtur tendere ad moralitatem; et posset aliquis ei objicere, quod discipuli Jesu necdum fuerant baptizati, ut patet in sequenti capitulo, nec plene credentes, saltem explicite. — Lyra vero exponit, affirmans quod Jesus non se credebat eis, quia non revelavit eis altiora mysteria fidei, eo quod essent incapaces. Verum nec discipuli capaces jam fuerant mysteriorum sublimium: quibus infra ait Salvator, Multa habeo vobis dicere, sed non potestis portare modo. Et tamen Jesus credebat se eis.
paras.en: [[2:24|But Jesus did not trust himself unto them|Ipse autem Jesus non credebat semetipsum eis]] [the Latin *credere* means both 'to believe' and 'to entrust': many believed in Him, but He did not entrust Himself to them]. On the surface of the letter this sounds as if Jesus, [[Ps 23:10|the Lord of hosts|Dominus virtutum]], to whom the Father gave [[John 17:2|power over all flesh|potestatem omnis carnis]], had feared that some harm could be done to Him by these men. But it is certain that He did not fear this, nor [[Matt 10:28|them that kill the body|eos qui corpus occidunt]].
