Augustine and Bede therefore explain it in this way: Jesus did not trust Himself to them because they were not yet baptized and filled with full faith, but were in the condition of catechumens; and Christ is said not to trust Himself to such, because the Sacrament of the Body of Christ is not given to them. But this explanation seems to lean toward the moral sense; and someone could object to it that the disciples of Jesus had not yet been baptized either, as is clear in the following chapter[[John 3:7||]] [the margin reference is hard to read, apparently John iii, 7], nor did they yet believe fully, at least explicitly. — Lyra, on the other hand, explains it by saying that Jesus did not trust Himself to them because He did not reveal to them the higher mysteries of the faith, since they were incapable of them. But neither were the disciples yet capable of the sublime mysteries; to them the Saviour says below, [[John 16:12|I have yet many things to say to you: but you cannot bear them now|Multa habeo vobis dicere, sed non potestis portare modo]]. And yet Jesus trusted Himself to them.

paras.t: Apparet igitur quod possit litteraliter sic exponi: Jesus non credebat, id est, non committebat, semetipsum eis, tanquam fidelibus constantibusque amicis, nec voluit conversari inter eos quasi inter veros discipulos, quia non bene sensit de eis, nec ipsi habuerunt fidem formatam, aut stabilem. Ideo non credebat se eis, non quia verebatur circumveniri vel pati ab eis, sed quoniam scivit quod non adhærerent sibi constanter, et nec cor eorum rectum fuerat cum ipso. Isti enim sic credebant in Jesum, quemadmodum illi de quibus infra habetur: Ex principibus multi crediderunt in eum, sed propter Pharisæos non confitebantur. Dilexerunt enim gloriam hominum magis quam gloriam Dei. Tales autem non credunt vere atque salubriter: sicut ait Salvator, Quomodo potestis vos credere, qui gloriam ab invicem accipitis, et gloriam quæ a solo Deo est, non quæritis? Loquitur ergo Evangelista secundum communem modum loquendi, quo aliquis dicitur se ipsum alteri credere, quoniam fidei illius se committit, certus de fidelitate vel amicitia ejus. Si vero sumatur credere, prout est actus fidei quæ est virtus theologica, sic Christus non credidit, nec aliquis debet sic in purum hominem credere. Denique huic expositioni concordant sequentia, in quibus tangitur ratio quare Christus non credebat se illis.
paras.en: It appears, then, that it can be explained literally thus: Jesus [[2:24|did not trust|non credebat]], that is, did not commit, [[2:24|himself unto them|semetipsum eis]] as to faithful and steadfast friends, and did not wish to live among them as among true disciples, because He did not think well of them, nor did they have formed faith [that is, faith given its form by charity, living faith] or steadfast faith. So He did not trust Himself to them, not because He was afraid of being deceived or of suffering at their hands, but because He knew that they would not cling to Him steadfastly, and [[Ps 77:37|their heart was not right with him|cor eorum rectum fuerat cum ipso]]. For these believed in Jesus in the same way as those of whom we read below: [[John 12:42|many of the chief men also believed in him: but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him|Ex principibus multi crediderunt in eum, sed propter Pharisæos non confitebantur]]. [[John 12:43|For they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God.|Dilexerunt enim gloriam hominum magis quam gloriam Dei.]] And such men do not believe truly and to their salvation, as the Saviour says: [[John 5:44|How can you believe, who receive glory one from another: and the glory which is from God alone, you do not seek?|Quomodo vos potestis credere, qui gloriam ab invicem accipitis, et gloriam quæ a solo Deo est, non quæritis?]] The Evangelist therefore speaks according to the common way of speaking, in which someone is said to trust himself to another because he commits himself to that man's good faith, being sure of his faithfulness or friendship. But if 'believe' is taken as the act of the faith which is a theological virtue, then Christ did not believe in that way, nor ought anyone to believe in that way in a mere man. Finally, what follows agrees with this explanation, for there the reason is touched upon why Christ did not trust Himself to them.

paras.t: Eo quod ipse nosset omnes, id est, certitudinaliter cognosceret omnium corda, et per consequens corda istorum, sciens quanta esset eorum interna defectio; et quia opus, id est necesse, ei non erat, ut quis testimonium perhiberet de homine quocumque, ad manifestandum Christo aliquid prius ei ignotum. Ipse enim sciebat, præsertim per scientiam increatam, secundum quod Deus, et item per scientiam infusam, ut homo, vel in Verbo, quid esset in homine, hoc est omnia interiora secretaque hominis cujuscumque, videlicet desideria, cogitationes, intentiones. Per quod innuit Evangelista divinitatem Salvatoris, quia Scripturæ testantur Deo proprium esse, universorum cordium scire arcana. Nam licet Christus sciverit illa, etiam ut homo, per scientiam concreatam, ut dictum est, hoc tamen non fuit nisi secundum quod homo talis, utpote habens humanitatem Verbo hypostatica unione conjunctam. Hinc in libris Regum Salomon loquitur: Tu, Domine, solus nosti corda omnium hominum. Et in Apocalypsi Dominus protestatur: Scient omnes Ecclesiæ, quia ego sum scrutans corda et renes.
paras.en: [[2:24|for that he knew all men|Eo quod ipse nosset omnes]], that is, knew with certainty the hearts of all, and consequently the hearts of these men, knowing how great was their inward failing; and [[2:25|because he needed not|quia opus]], that is, it was not necessary for Him, [[2:25|that any should give testimony of man|ut quis testimonium perhiberet de homine]], of any man whatever, to make known to Christ something He did not know before; [[2:25|for he knew|Ipse enim sciebat]], above all by His uncreated knowledge, as God, and also by infused knowledge, as man, or in the Word [that is, by the vision of the Word which His human soul enjoyed], [[2:25|what was in man|quid esset in homine]], that is, all the inward and secret things of any man whatever, namely his desires, thoughts and intentions. By this the Evangelist hints at the divinity of the Saviour, since the Scriptures testify that it is proper to God to know the secrets of all hearts. For although Christ knew these things also as man, by concreated knowledge [knowledge given to His soul together with its creation], as has been said, yet this was only by reason of His being such a man, namely one having a humanity joined to the Word by hypostatic union [the union of the two natures in the one Person of the Word]. Hence in the books of Kings Solomon says: [[3 Kings 8:39|thou only knowest the heart of all the children of men|Tu, Domine, solus nosti corda omnium hominum]]. And in the Apocalypse the Lord declares: [[Apoc 2:23|all the churches shall know that I am he that searcheth the reins and hearts|Scient omnes Ecclesiæ, quia ego sum scrutans corda et renes]].

paras.t: Nunc aliquid de moralitate hujus evangelicæ lectionis tractandum est. Instante festo paschali Judæorum, ascendit Jesus Jerosolymam. Sic et nos, appropinquante Pascha Christianorum, qui sunt veri Judæi, non carne et littera, sed spiritu confitentes, ascendere debemus ecclesiam toto tempore quadragesimali, præparando nos ad devotam paschalis festivitatis celebrationem, per opera pœnitentiæ et exercitia devotionis atque compunctionis interna.
paras.en: Now something must be said of the moral sense of this Gospel reading. When the paschal feast of the Jews was at hand, [[2:13|Jesus went up to Jerusalem|ascendit Jesus Jerosolymam]]. So we too, when the Pasch of the Christians draws near (for they are the true Jews, confessing not in the flesh and the letter but in the spirit [*Judæus* was taken to mean 'one who confesses', from the name Juda, interpreted 'confession']), ought to go up to the Church throughout the whole season of Lent, preparing ourselves for the devout celebration of the paschal feast by works of penance and by the inward exercises of devotion and compunction.

paras.t: Quotidie quoque visitat Christus Ecclesiam, quæ per Jerusalem designatur; et invenit ibi vendentes oves et boves, id est clericos temporalibus negotiis implicatos, sacerdotes, religiosos atque prælatos avaritiæ deditos, propria lucra, non Christi honorem et gregis dominici salutem, quærentes. Quocontra dicit Apostolus: Nemo militans Deo, implicat se sæcularibus negotiis. Demum columbas vendunt, qui spiritualia bona pro temporalibus exhibent; qui non excutiunt manus suas ab omni munere. Contra quos ait Salvator: Gratis accepistis, gratis date.
paras.en: Christ also visits the Church daily, which is signified by Jerusalem; and He finds there [[2:14|them that sold oxen and sheep|vendentes oves et boves]], that is, clerics entangled in temporal business, and priests, religious and prelates given over to avarice, seeking their own gain[[1 Pet 5:2||]], not the honour of Christ and the salvation of the Lord's flock. Against this the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 2:4|No man, being a soldier to God, entangleth himself with secular businesses|Nemo militans Deo, implicat se sæcularibus negotiis]]. Then those sell [[2:14|doves|columbas]] who give out spiritual goods in return for temporal ones; who do not shake their hands free from all bribes[[Is 33:15||]]. Against these the Saviour says: [[Matt 10:8|freely have you received, freely give|Gratis accepistis, gratis date]].

paras.t: Omnes tales ejicit Christus de templo, id est, a corpore suo mystico, a consortio electorum separat eos nunc voto ac merito; postea vero separabit istos ab illis, loco et præmio, sicut segregat pastor oves ab hædis, quando hi ibunt in ignem æternum, illi vero in paradisum cœlestem. Ejicit autem, flagellat et punit eos Christus, flagello facto de funiculis, id est pœna quam merentur propriis vitiis, quæ sunt funes seu vincula quibus impius irretitur, ligatur, atque constringitur, ne Deum sequatur, ne in viam vitæ proficiscatur, sed dæmonis potestati, jugo et obsequio subditus maneat, prout ad Timotheum ait Apostolus: Resipiscant a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem. De talibus nempe funiculis Salomon loquitur in Proverbiis: Iniquitates suæ capiunt impium, et funibus peccatorum suorum constringitur. Talibus funiculis se constringunt, et restem infernalis suspensionis sibimet texunt, quicumque in vitiis perseverant; qui adjiciunt ad peccandum; quorum iniquitates sicut onus grave gravantur super eos; qui non elevant oculos suos ut videant cœlum. Quibus dictum est per Isaiam: Væ qui trahitis iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis, et quasi vinculum plaustri peccatum.
paras.en: All such Christ casts [[2:15|out of the temple|de templo]], that is, out of His mystical body: He separates them now from the fellowship of the elect in will and in merit; but afterwards He will separate the one from the other in place and in reward, [[Matt 25:32|as the shepherd separateth the sheep from the goats|sicut segregat pastor oves ab hædis]], when these shall go into eternal fire, and those into the paradise of heaven[[Matt 25:46||]] [Denis joins Matt 25:46, 'these shall go', and 25:41, 'into everlasting fire']. And Christ casts them out, scourges and punishes them with [[2:15|a scourge of little cords|flagello facto de funiculis]], that is, with the punishment they deserve by their own vices, which are the cords or bonds by which the wicked man is ensnared, bound and held fast, so that he may not follow God nor set out on the way of life, but may remain subject to the power, yoke and service of the devil; as the Apostle says to Timothy: that [[2 Tim 2:26|they may recover themselves from the snares of the devil by whom they are held captive at his will|Resipiscant a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem]]. Of such cords indeed Solomon speaks in Proverbs: [[Prov 5:22|His own iniquities catch the wicked, and he is fast bound with the ropes of his own sins.|Iniquitates suas capiunt impium, et funibus peccatorum suorum constringitur.]] With such cords they bind themselves, and weave for themselves the rope of the hanging of hell, all who persevere in vices; who add to their sinning[[Ecclus 3:29||]]; whose iniquities weigh upon them as a heavy burden[[Ps 37:5||]]; who do not lift up their eyes to see heaven. To them it is said through Isaias: [[Is 5:18|Woe to you that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as the rope of a cart.|Væ qui trahitis iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis, et quasi vinculum plaustri peccatum!]]

paras.t: Possumus insuper per templum intelligere animam rationalem, quæ capax est Dei per cognitionem ac dilectionem, in qua habitat Deus per fidem, caritatem et gratiam. Hanc visitat Christus sapientia Patris, qui in animas sanctas se transfert, statque ad ostium cordis, et pulsat. Sed dum anima concupiscentiis superatur, dum jumentis insipientibus comparatur, bestiales motus sequendo, peccatis et passionibus serviendo (a quo enim quis victus est, hujus et servus est), tunc vendit oves et boves, videlicet stultos ac irrationabiles motus, diabolo, cui talia serviendo impendit, ut per hæc voluptates consequatur, quas velut pretium pro fine intendit. Sed utinam Christus faciat nunc flagellum paternæ correctionis, omnesque hujusmodi motus et vitia expellat ab anima nostra, corripiendo nos temporaliter, ut resipiscamus, nec æternaliter pereamus. Quidam enim non corriguntur nisi flagellis seu adversitatibus, qui quodammodo compelluntur intrare, et dicere possunt: Castigans castigavit me Dominus, et morti non tradidit me. Sic conversus est Paulus.
paras.en: Moreover, by the temple we can understand the rational soul, which is capable of God by knowledge and love, and in which God dwells by faith[[Eph 3:17||]], charity and grace. This soul Christ visits, the wisdom of the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]], who [[Wis 7:27|conveyeth herself into holy souls|in animas sanctas se transfert]] [in the book of Wisdom this is said of Wisdom, hence 'herself'], and stands at the door of the heart and knocks[[Apoc 3:20||]]. But when the soul is overcome by its concupiscences, when it [[Ps 48:13|is compared to senseless beasts|jumentis insipientibus comparatur]] by following bestial impulses and serving sins and passions ([[2 Pet 2:19|by whom a man is overcome, of the same also he is the slave|a quo enim quis victus est, hujus et servus est]]), then it sells sheep and oxen, namely foolish and irrational impulses, to the devil, on whom it spends such things by serving him, in order to obtain pleasures through them, which it seeks as its price and its end. But would that Christ might now make [[2:15|a scourge|flagellum]] of fatherly correction and drive all such impulses and vices out of our soul, chastising us in time, that we may come to our senses and not perish eternally. For some are not corrected except by scourges, that is, by adversities; they are in a way compelled to come in[[Luke 14:23||]] [the margin seems to read Luke xv; the words are those of Luke 14:23], and can say: [[Ps 117:18|The Lord chastising hath chastised me: but he hath not delivered me over to death.|Castigans castigavit me Dominus, et morti non tradidit me.]] So was Paul converted[[Acts 9:3||]].

paras.t: Præterea, non faciamus domum Dei, puta ecclesiam materialem, nec animam propriam, domum negotiationis, confabulationis, distractionis, sæcularia in eis tractando; sed potius emundemus nos ab omni inquinamento carnis et spiritus, ut mente quieta, tranquilla ac pura, Christum suscipere, retinere, et possidere mereamur. Ipse etenim dicit: Super quem requiescet spiritus meus, nisi super quietum et humilem?
paras.en: Furthermore, let us not make the house of God, whether the material church or our own soul, [[2:16|a house of traffic|domum negotiationis]], of idle talk and distraction, by dealing with worldly matters in them; but rather let us [[2 Cor 7:1|cleanse ourselves from all defilement of the flesh and of the spirit|emundemus nos ab omni inquinamento carnis et spiritus]], so that with a quiet, tranquil and pure mind we may deserve to receive, keep and possess Christ. For He Himself says: Upon whom shall My spirit rest, but upon him that is quiet and humble?[[Is 66:2||]] [the margin compares Is 66:1–2; Denis gives the saying in the form long current among Latin writers, not in the words of the Vulgate]

paras.t: Quemadmodum autem Judæi a Christo correpti dixerunt, Quod signum ostendis quia hæc facis? quasi dicant, Quis te constituit principem aut judicem super nos? Sic multi impatientes et inverecundi, duri atque rebelles et animosi, dum fraternaliter admonentur, vel paternaliter arguuntur, aut juste corriguntur, indignando seu murmurando respondent: Quod signum ostendis? id est, quid ad te pertinet? et, Numquid ego tibi commissus sum? Corrige temetipsum, nec ingeras te factis aut sermonibus meis. Tales vero miserrimi sunt obtenebrati et vitiosi. Unde in Proverbiis loquitur Salomon: Viro qui corripientem dura cervice contemnit, repentinus ei superveniet interitus; et alibi: Qui abjicit disciplinam, despicit animam suam; qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis.
paras.en: And just as the Jews, when Christ rebuked them, said, [[2:18|What sign dost thou shew unto us, seeing thou dost these things?|Quod signum ostendis quia hæc facis?]] as if to say, [[Ex 2:14|Who hath appointed thee prince and judge over us|Quis te constituit principem aut judicem super nos?]]? so many who are impatient and shameless, hard, rebellious and headstrong, when they are admonished as by a brother, or reproved as by a father, or justly corrected, answer with indignation or grumbling: [[2:18|What sign dost thou shew|Quod signum ostendis]]? that is, what business is it of yours? and, Am I committed to your charge? Correct yourself, and do not meddle in my deeds or words. But such men are most wretched, darkened and vicious. Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: [[Prov 29:1|The man that with a stiff neck despiseth him that reproveth him, shall suddenly be destroyed|Viro qui corripientem dura cervice contemnit, repentinus ei superveniet interitus]]; and elsewhere: [[Prov 15:32|He that rejecteth instruction, despiseth his own soul: but he that yieldeth to reproof, possesseth understanding.|Qui abjicit disciplinam despicit animam suam; qui autem acquiescit increpationibus possessor est cordis.]] [Latin *possessor est cordis*, literally 'is master of his heart'].

3.title: Expositio capituli tertii: Erat autem homo ex Pharisæis, Nicodemus nomine.
3.title_en: Explanation of the third chapter: “And there was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus.”

paras.t: Post hæc, Evangelista plenius prosequitur atque describit doctrinam et prodigia Salvatoris, ea præsertim quæ ab aliis Evangelistis erant omissa. Et quia in fine præcedentis capituli dixit multos Judæorum credidisse in nomine Jesu, nunc specialiter tractat de uno illorum. Erat autem homo, rationabiliter agens, dignus nomine hominis, tanquam rationis judicium, non sensualitatis impetum, sequens. Optimum enim hominis est esse secundum rationem, juxta Dionysium. Ex Pharisæis, id est de secta et numero Pharisæorum, quorum secta fuit solennior. Eratque homo iste, Nicodemus nomine, re et nomine Pharisæus, hoc est ab aliis divisus, tanquam veraciter religiosus in anima, sicut nomen et habitus ejus exterior prætendebant: sicut nunc aliquis dicitur veraciter monachus, qui soli Deo et sibi ipsi digne intendit atque sinceriter vacat. Ceteri vero Pharisæorum, ut communiter, erant solo nomine, habitu et apparenti sanctitate seu simulata æquitate Pharisæi: sicut nunc sunt multi claustrales solo nomine, apparatu et habitu monachi, religiosi ac spirituales. Princeps Judæorum, id est unus de principalibus doctoribus atque rectoribus Judaicæ plebis, quæ primo regebatur per judices, deinde per reges usque ad captivitatem Babylonicam, exinde per doctores et sacerdotes, quorum multi fuerunt Pharisæi. Non tamen fuit hic Nicodemus summus princeps vel pontifex Judæorum.
paras.en: After this the Evangelist goes on to set out and describe more fully the teaching and the wonders of the Saviour, especially those which the other Evangelists had left out. And because at the end of the preceding chapter he said that many of the Jews believed in the name of Jesus[[John 2:23||]], he now treats in particular of one of them. [[3:1|And there was a man|Erat autem homo]], acting according to reason, worthy of the name of man, as one who follows the judgement of reason, not the impulse of sensuality. For the best thing for man is to live according to reason, as Dionysius says. [[3:1|of the Pharisees|Ex Pharisæis]], that is, of the sect and number of the Pharisees, whose sect was the more distinguished. And this man, [[3:1|named Nicodemus|Nicodemus nomine]], was a Pharisee in fact and in name, that is, set apart from others, as one truly religious in soul, just as his name and his outward habit professed: as now a man is truly called a monk who worthily attends to God alone and to himself and sincerely gives himself up to them. But the rest of the Pharisees, as commonly happens, were Pharisees only in name, habit and outward holiness or feigned righteousness: as now there are many cloistered men who are monks, religious and spiritual only in name, outward show and habit. [[3:1|a ruler of the Jews|Princeps Judæorum]], that is, one of the chief teachers and rulers of the Jewish people, which was governed first by judges, then by kings until the Babylonian captivity, and from then on by teachers and priests, many of whom were Pharisees. Yet this Nicodemus was not the supreme ruler or high priest of the Jews.

paras.t: Hic venit ad Jesum, cujus jam signa vidit, et documenta audivit; et ex utroque perpendit aliquid magnæ excellentiæ esse in Jesu, cujus tantam potestatem et sapientiam, tantam demum justitiam imperterritamque constantiam fuit expertus, ita ut, neminem metuens et pro Deo zelans, omnes vendentes in templo expelleret, suamque doctrinam confirmaret miraculis. Hinc Nicodemus, zelo agnoscendæ veritatis et spiritualis profectus accensus, venit ad Jesum ut plenius doceretur ab eo. Venit autem nocte. Vel quia aliorum Pharisæorum ac sacerdotum offensam incurrere formidavit (quemadmodum Gedeon nocte confregit statuam Baal, timens suos concives): et hic timor fuit imperfectionis, quem plena dilectio mittit foras. Vel quia, quum esset nominatus doctor ac magister in Israel, aliqualiter erubescebat publice se submittere informationi Jesu, qui sciebatur litteras non didicisse: et hoc fuisset alicujus elationis. Vel, ut secrete, silenter ac libere loqueretur cum Jesu. Convenit quoque tempus cum mysterio. Nam quia in tenebris mentis quodammodo fuit, imperfecte credendo in Christum, et spiritualium mysteriorum notitiam non habendo, recte asseritur nocte venisse: quemadmodum Maria Magdalene venit ad monumentum quum adhuc tenebræ essent, putans Christum non resurrexisse.
paras.en: [[3:2|This man came to Jesus|Hic venit ad Jesum]], whose signs he had already seen and whose teachings he had heard; and from both he judged that there was something of great excellence in Jesus, whose great power and wisdom, and great justice too and fearless constancy, he had come to know: so that, fearing no one and zealous for God, He drove out all who sold in the temple[[John 2:15||]], and confirmed His teaching with miracles[[John 2:23||]]. Hence Nicodemus, fired with zeal to know the truth and to make spiritual progress, came to Jesus to be taught by Him more fully. And he came [[3:2|by night|nocte]]. Either because he was afraid of incurring the displeasure of the other Pharisees and of the priests (as Gedeon broke down the statue of Baal by night, fearing his fellow citizens[[Judg 6:27||]]): and this fear was a fear of imperfection, which perfect love casts out[[1 John 4:18||]]. Or because, being a renowned doctor and master in Israel, he was somewhat ashamed to submit publicly to the instruction of Jesus, who was known never to have learned letters[[John 7:15||]]: and this would have been a mark of some pride. Or so as to speak with Jesus in secret, quietly and freely. The time also fits the mystery. For because he was in a way in darkness of mind, believing imperfectly in Christ and having no knowledge of spiritual mysteries, he is rightly said to have come by night: as Mary Magdalene came to the tomb [[John 20:1|when it was yet dark|adhuc tenebræ essent]], thinking that Christ had not risen.

paras.t: Et dixit ei: Rabbi, scimus quia a Deo venisti, id est, divinitus missus es in mundum, magister veritatis. De quo magistro dicitur in Osee: Tempus requirendi Dominum, quum venerit qui docebit vos justitiam; et per Joelem: Exsultate in Domino Deo vestro, quia dedit vobis doctorem justitiæ. Per quid vero Nicodemus id scierat, subditur: Nemo enim potest hæc signa facere quæ tu facis, nisi fuerit Deus cum eo, cooperando et gratiam miraculorum præstando. Solus quippe omnipotens Deus facit miracula proprie dicta tanquam principalis effector; servi autem ipsius faciunt ea solum ministerialiter: juxta illud in Psalmo, Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus.
paras.en: [[3:2|and said to him: Rabbi, we know that thou art come a teacher from God|Et dixit ei: Rabbi, scimus quia a Deo venisti]], that is, Thou art sent by God into the world, a teacher of truth. Of which teacher it is said in Osee: [[Osee 10:12|the time to seek the Lord is, when he shall come that shall teach you justice|Tempus requirendi Dominum, quum venerit qui docebit vos justitiam]]; and by Joel: [[Joel 2:23|rejoice, and be joyful in the Lord your God: because he hath given you a teacher of justice|Exsultate in Domino Deo vestro, quia dedit vobis doctorem justitiæ]]. How Nicodemus knew this is added next: [[3:2|for no man can do these signs which thou dost, unless God be with him|Nemo enim potest hæc signa facere quæ tu facis, nisi fuerit Deus cum eo]], working together with him and granting the grace of miracles. For almighty God alone works miracles properly so called, as their principal cause; His servants work them only as ministers, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 71:18|Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone doth wonderful things.|Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus]]

paras.t: Porro miraculum proprie dictum, est effectus totam virtutem et legem naturæ creatæ excedens. Et talia erant aliqua Christi miracula, ut illuminatio cæci nati, suscitatio mortuorum, eclipsis solis in plenilunio tempore passionis. Et ista miracula sunt certa ac sufficientia argumenta, quod actor eorum sit vera docens, et divina virtute agens. Unde ait infra: Si opera non fecissem in eis, quæ nullus alius fecit, peccatum non haberent. — Aliqua vero miracula fieri possunt cooperatione diaboli, sicut de Antichristo dicit Apostolus: Cujus adventus est secundum operationem Satanæ, in omni seductione et virtute, in signis et prodigiis. Quamvis autem talia sint miracula quantum ad modum agendi, non tamen excedunt facultatem totius naturæ creatæ, sed per occultas naturalium rerum virtutes aguntur: quemadmodum magi Pharaonis, Jannes et Mambres, projecerunt virgas suas, quæ mox in dracones conversæ sunt; produxerunt etiam ranas, et maleficiis suis converterunt aquam in sanguinem, ut legitur in Exodo.
paras.en: Now a miracle properly so called is an effect that exceeds the whole power and law of created nature. And some of Christ's miracles were of this kind, such as the giving of sight to the man born blind[[John 9:1||]], the raising of the dead[[Matt 9:25||]][[Luke 7:15||]], and the eclipse of the sun at the full moon at the time of the Passion[[Matt 27:45||]] [an eclipse of the sun cannot happen naturally at the full moon; the margin here is only partly legible: it seems to give John 9, Matt 9:25, Luke 7 and Matt 27:45]. And these miracles are certain and sufficient proofs that their author teaches what is true and acts by divine power. Hence He says further on: [[John 15:24|If I had not done among them the works that no other man hath done, they would not have sin|Si opera non fecissem in eis, quæ nullus alius fecit, peccatum non haberent]]. — But some miracles can be done with the cooperation of the devil, as the Apostle says of Antichrist: [[2 Thess 2:9|Whose coming is according to the working of Satan|Cujus adventus est secundum operationem Satanæ]], in all seduction and power, in signs and wonders. But though such things are miracles as to the manner of working, they do not exceed the capacity of the whole of created nature, but are done through the hidden powers of natural things: as Pharao's magicians, Jannes and Mambres, cast down their rods, which were straightway turned into serpents[[Ex 7:12||]]; they also brought forth frogs[[Ex 8:7||]], and by their enchantments turned water into blood[[Ex 7:22||]], as we read in Exodus.

paras.t: Talia vero miracula etiam multa fecit Christus, convertendo aquam in vinum, quod facit natura paulatim in vitibus; et illuminando cæcos, quod interdum fit arte medicinæ. Et ista non sunt sufficientia argumenta fidei et cooperationis divinæ, quum sint bonis malisque communia. Verumtamen eo modo quo a Christo et ejus ministris peracta sunt, sunt utique sufficientia fidei argumenta. Christus enim fecit ea imperialiter, et in instanti. Fideles quoque faciunt ea per invocationem nominis Dei, cum exsecratione omnis communionis diaboli. — Facit præterea Deus quandoque signa per reprobos seu injustos: quæ licet non probent quod operatores hujusmodi sint boni et Deo accepti, probant tamen quod vera sit fides qua invocant Deum, et vera doctrina ad cujus confirmationem efficit Deus talia signa. Propter quod dicit Salvator apud Matthæum: Multi dicent mihi in die illa: Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetavimus, et in nomine tuo dæmonia ejecimus, et virtutes multas fecimus? Et tunc confitebor illis: Quia nunquam novi vos.
paras.en: Christ too worked many miracles of this second kind, turning water into wine[[John 2:9||]], which nature does gradually in the vines, and giving sight to the blind[[Matt 9:30||]][[Matt 20:34||]][[Mark 8:25||]][[John 9:7||]], which is sometimes done by the art of medicine. And these are not sufficient proofs of the faith and of divine cooperation, since they are common to good and wicked alike. Yet in the way in which they were performed by Christ and His ministers, they are indeed sufficient proofs of the faith. For Christ worked them as one who commands, and in an instant. The faithful, too, work them by calling on the name of God, renouncing all fellowship with the devil. — Moreover, God sometimes works signs through the reprobate or the unjust: and though these do not prove that such workers are good and acceptable to God, they do prove that the faith by which they call upon God is true, and that the teaching in confirmation of which God works such signs is true. For this reason the Saviour says in Matthew: [[Matt 7:22|Many will say to me in that day: Lord, Lord, have not we prophesied in thy name, and cast out devils in thy name, and done many miracles in thy name?|Multi dicent mihi in die illa: Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetavimus, et in nomine tuo dæmonia ejecimus, et virtutes multas fecimus?]] [[Matt 7:23|And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you|Et tunc confitebor illis: Quia nunquam novi vos]].

paras.t: Et quoniam Christus novit intentionem ac desiderium Nicodemi, qui venit ut instrueretur, idcirco incipit eum Christus instruere. Et primo instruit eum de primo sacramento novæ legis maxime necessario, videlicet de Baptismo, quod est spiritualis regeneratio, porta vitæ. Respondit Jesus, et dixit ei: Amen, amen dico tibi. Repetitio, confirmationis indicium est et provocatio advertentiæ diligentis. Nisi quis natus fuerit denuo, id est regeneratus, videlicet per spiritualem generationem esse gratiæ, caritatis et fidei, puta esse supernaturale ac deiforme adeptus, non potest videre oculis cordis, clare, per speciem, regnum Dei, id est patriam Beatorum, seu Deum regnantem in cælis. Quum enim ultimus finis hominis, seu ipsa felicitas, quæ est visio Dei per speciem, sit supernaturalis, nullus potest ad eam pertingere per pura naturalia, sed oportet naturam adjuvari ac perfici per fidem et gratiam ceteraque dona Spiritus Sancti. Quemadmodum autem dicitur homo primo nasci, quando per generationem carnalem ac naturalem parentum producitur in esse naturali specifico, contrahendo a parentibus esse naturæ; sic dicitur nasci denuo vel renasci, quando per operationem divinam acquirit esse gratiæ, quod est esse divinum, supernaturale et meritorium: quia, ut dicit Dionysius, Sicut intellectualis creatura ponitur in esse specifico per naturam, per quam est apta ac potens ad operationes naturales; sic per gratiam ponitur in esse divino, per quod est idonea ad operandum opera meritoria.
paras.en: And since Christ knew the intention and desire of Nicodemus, who had come to be instructed, Christ therefore begins to instruct him. And first He instructs him about the first sacrament of the new law, the most necessary one, namely Baptism, which is spiritual regeneration, the gate of life. [[3:3|Jesus answered and said to him: Amen, amen, I say to thee|Respondit Jesus, et dixit ei: Amen, amen dico tibi]]. The repetition is a sign of confirmation and a call to careful attention. [[3:3|unless a man be born again|Nisi quis natus fuerit denuo]], that is, regenerated: having gained, namely, through a spiritual generation, the being of grace, charity and faith, that is, a supernatural and deiform being, [[3:3|he cannot see|non potest videre]] with the eyes of the heart, clearly, by sight [per speciem: face to face, as opposed to by faith], [[3:3|the kingdom of God|regnum Dei]], that is, the fatherland of the Blessed, or God reigning in heaven. For since the last end of man, or happiness itself, which is the vision of God face to face, is supernatural, no one can attain to it by his natural powers alone; but nature must be helped and perfected by faith and grace and the other gifts of the Holy Ghost. And as a man is said to be born the first time when, through the carnal and natural generation of his parents, he is brought forth into his natural specific being [that is, the being proper to his species], receiving from his parents the being of nature, so he is said to be born again, or reborn, when through God's working he acquires the being of grace, which is a divine, supernatural and meritorious being: for, as Dionysius says, as the intellectual creature is set in its specific being by nature, through which it is fit and able for natural operations, so by grace it is set in divine being, through which it is fit to do meritorious works.

paras.t: Si sic accipimus, Nasci denuo, tunc nunquam potuit aliquis salvari, nisi rursus nascendo. Omnes namque nati sunt filii iræ, contrahendo peccatum originale secundum communem legem: sicque oportebat eos intus renasci, recipiendo gratiam reformantem, et conferentem esse divinum. Verum, quia Salvator ad litteram loquitur de regeneratione Baptismatis, ut patet in subditis, idcirco, quod dicit de regeneratione ista, intelligendum est pro tempore novi Testamenti. Temporibus vero legis naturæ et legis scriptæ, fuerunt alia contra originale peccatum remedia, scilicet circumcisio, et fides parentum.
paras.en: If we take “to be born again” in this sense, then no one could ever have been saved except by being born anew. For all are born [[Eph 2:3|children of wrath|filii iræ]], contracting original sin according to the common law; and so they had to be reborn inwardly, receiving the grace that reforms them and confers divine being. But since the Saviour is speaking literally of the regeneration of Baptism, as is clear from what follows, what He says of this regeneration is to be understood of the time of the New Testament. In the times of the law of nature and of the written law, there were other remedies against original sin, namely circumcision and the faith of the parents.

paras.t: Dicit ad eum Nicodemus, arguens contra verba Christi, quæ male atque carnaliter intellexit, quia in lege assuetus non fuit spiritualibus modis loquendi: Quomodo potest homo nasci quum sit, id est, quando est, senex? Christus non dixit simpliciter, Nisi quis natus fuerit, non potest videre regnum Dei; sed, Nisi quis natus fuerit denuo. Sed quia renasci includit nasci, et Nicodemus non novit nisi unam nativitatem, ideo sic resumit: Quomodo potest homo nasci quum sit senex? Quod non est sic intelligendum, quasi secundum intentionem Nicodemi infans vel juvenis possit renasci; sed quoniam de se ipso sollicitus fuit, et ipse jam vetulus exstitit, idcirco sic fatur: Quomodo potest homo nasci quum sit senex? Et probat quod non possit: Numquid potest in ventrem matris suæ iterato introire et renasci? præsertim quum matres communiter mortuæ sint tempore senectutis natorum.
paras.en: [[3:4|Nicodemus saith to him|Dicit ad eum Nicodemus]], arguing against the words of Christ, which he understood wrongly and carnally, because under the law he had not been used to spiritual ways of speaking: [[3:4|How can a man be born|Quomodo potest homo nasci]] when he is, that is, at the time when he is, [[3:4|old|senex]]? Christ did not say simply, “Unless a man be born, he cannot see the kingdom of God,” but, “Unless a man be born again.” But because to be reborn includes being born, and Nicodemus knew of only one birth, he therefore takes it up in this way: [[3:4|How can a man be born when he is old?|Quomodo potest homo nasci quum sit senex?]] This is not to be understood as though, in Nicodemus's mind, an infant or a youth could be reborn; but because he was anxious about himself, and was already an old man, he therefore speaks thus: [[3:4|How can a man be born when he is old?|Quomodo potest homo nasci quum sit senex?]] And he proves that it cannot be: [[3:4|Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born again?|Numquid potest in ventrem matris suæ iterato introire et renasci?]] Especially since mothers have commonly died by the time their children are old.

paras.t: Respondit Jesus, solvendo instantiam Nicodemi, et exponendo verba quæ dixit: Amen, amen dico tibi, nisi quis renatus fuerit, id est spiritualiter regeneratus in fonte Baptismatis, ex aqua, quæ est materiale elementum corpus lavans, et dispositive regenerans, et Spiritu Sancto, qui est invisibilis actor intus mentem purificans et efficienter regenerans, gratiam influendo, quæ est res sacramenti et causa formalis intrinseca hujus regenerationis: non potest introire in regnum Dei, quod est triumphans Ecclesia, vita æterna, seu patria electorum. Quod intelligendum est, dummodo adsit facultas recipiendi sacramentum Baptismi: alias sufficeret baptismus Flaminis, id est interior mundatio Sancti Spiritus, et baptismus sanguinis, puta martyrium, cum voto seu desiderio baptismi fluminis. In Baptismo quippe conformamur Christo et ei incorporamur, quemadmodum ad Romanos testatur Apostolus: Quicumque baptizati sumus in Christo Jesu, in morte ipsius baptizati sumus: consepulti enim sumus cum illo per Baptismum in mortem, ut quomodo resurrexit Christus a mortuis per gloriam Patris, ita et nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus.
paras.en: Jesus answered, resolving Nicodemus's objection [instantia: in the schools, an objection raised against what has been said] and explaining the words He had spoken: [[3:5|Amen, amen, I say to thee, unless a man be born again|Amen, amen dico tibi, nisi quis renatus fuerit]], that is, spiritually regenerated in the font of Baptism, [[3:5|of water|ex aqua]], which is the material element, washing the body and regenerating dispositively [that is, by preparing the subject for grace, not by producing it], [[3:5|and the Holy Ghost|et Spiritu Sancto]], who is the invisible agent within, purifying the mind and regenerating efficiently by pouring in grace, which is the reality of the sacrament [res sacramenti: the inward effect that the outward sign signifies and brings about] and the intrinsic formal cause of this regeneration: [[3:5|he cannot enter into the kingdom of God|non potest introire in regnum Dei]], which is the Church triumphant, eternal life, the fatherland of the elect. This is to be understood provided there is the possibility of receiving the sacrament of Baptism; otherwise the baptism of the Spirit would suffice, that is, the inward cleansing of the Holy Spirit, and the baptism of blood, namely martyrdom, together with the vow or desire of the baptism of water [Denis plays on baptismus flaminis, 'of the breath', that is, of the Spirit, and baptismus fluminis, 'of the stream', that is, of water]. For in Baptism we are conformed to Christ and incorporated into Him, as the Apostle testifies to the Romans: [[Rom 6:3|all we who are baptized in Christ Jesus are baptized in his death?|Quicumque baptizati sumus in Christo Jesu, in morte ipsius baptizati sumus]] [[Rom 6:4|For we are buried together with him by baptism into death: that, as Christ is risen from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also may walk in newness of life.|consepulti enim sumus cum illo per Baptismum in mortem, ut quomodo resurrexit Christus a mortuis per gloriam Patris, ita et nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus]]

paras.t: Sed quum Baptismus detur in nomine sanctæ Trinitatis, a qua est effectus Baptismi seu gratia sacramentalis, cur potius dicit Salvator, Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu, quam, Ex aqua et Patre, vel, Ex aqua et Filio? Dicendum, quod Baptismus est effectus præcipuus liberalitatis ac pietatis divinæ. Liberalitas vero et pietas appropriantur Spiritui Sancto, quemadmodum amor et bonitas.
paras.en: But since Baptism is given in the name of the Holy Trinity[[Matt 28:19||]], from whom comes the effect of Baptism, or sacramental grace, why does the Saviour say, [[3:5|unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost|Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu]], rather than 'of water and the Father', or 'of water and the Son'? The answer is that Baptism is the chief effect of the divine liberality and loving-kindness; and liberality and loving-kindness are appropriated to the Holy Spirit [appropriation: ascribing to one divine Person what is common to all three, because of its likeness to what is proper to that Person], as are love and goodness.

paras.t: Deinde Christus ostendit ordinem spiritualis regenerationis, eamque a carnali generatione distinguit. Quod natum est ex carne, caro est; et quod natum est ex spiritu, spiritus est. Verba hæc intricata et difficilia sunt, et multipliciter intelligi possunt. Primo sic: Quod natum est ex carne, id est corpus filii propagatum ac natum ex semine patris, caro est; et quod natum est ex spiritu, id est anima rationalis creata a Deo, qui spiritus appellatur, spiritus est, id est spiritualis substantia. Hoc tamen non est sic accipiendum, quasi corporalia non sint immediate creata a Deo; sed in homine sunt duæ partes, quarum una est caro, a patre carnali contracta, alia est spiritus, a patre spirituali producta. Juxta hunc sensum dicit Apostolus ad Hebræos: Patres carnis nostræ habuimus eruditores, et reverebamur eos: non multo magis obtemperabimus Patri spirituum, et vivemus? — Secundo sic: Quod natum est ex carne, id est a carnali parente, caro est, id est res carnalis, non habens nisi esse carnale ac naturale, virtute generationis carnalis: unde ut talis, non potest salvari; et quod natum est ex spiritu, id est spiritualiter regeneratum ac positum in esse spirituali vitaque gratiæ, ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, in Baptismatis lavacro, spiritus est, id est, spirituale efficitur, scilicet homo invisibiliter intus renatus et Deo conjunctus, cum quo, secundum Apostolum, unus est spiritus. Ex quo patet, quod ista regeneratio non sit impossibilis, sed necessaria, et a carnali generatione distincta. De qua ait Joannes in sua Canonica: Omne quod natum est ex Deo, vincit mundum.
paras.en: Next Christ shows the order of spiritual regeneration, and distinguishes it from carnal generation: [[3:6|That which is born of the flesh is flesh: and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.|Quod natum est ex carne, caro est: et quod natum est ex spiritu, spiritus est.]] These words are involved and difficult, and can be understood in many ways. First thus: [[3:6|That which is born of the flesh|Quod natum est ex carne]], that is, the son's body, propagated and born of the father's seed, [[3:6|is flesh|caro est]]; [[3:6|and that which is born of the Spirit|et quod natum est ex spiritu]], that is, the rational soul created by God, who is called spirit[[John 4:24||]], [[3:6|is spirit|spiritus est]], that is, a spiritual substance. Yet this is not to be taken as though bodily things were not created immediately by God; but in man there are two parts, one of which is the flesh, contracted from the carnal father, and the other the spirit, produced by the spiritual Father. In this sense the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:9|we have had fathers of our flesh for instructors, and we reverenced them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live?|Patres carnis nostræ habuimus eruditores, et reverebamur eos: non multo magis obtemperabimus Patri spirituum, et vivemus?]] Secondly thus: [[3:6|That which is born of the flesh|Quod natum est ex carne]], that is, of a carnal parent, [[3:6|is flesh|caro est]], that is, a carnal thing, having only a carnal and natural being, by virtue of carnal generation; and so, as such, it cannot be saved; [[3:6|and that which is born of the Spirit|et quod natum est ex spiritu]], that is, spiritually regenerated and set in spiritual being and the life of grace, of water and the Holy Spirit, in the laver of Baptism, [[3:6|is spirit|spiritus est]], that is, is made spiritual: namely the man invisibly reborn within and joined to God, with whom, according to the Apostle, he is [[1 Cor 6:17|one spirit|unus est spiritus]]. From this it is plain that this regeneration is not impossible, but necessary, and distinct from carnal generation. Of it John says in his Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 5:4|whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world|Omne quod natum est ex Deo, vincit mundum]].

paras.t: Hinc subdit Salvator: Non mireris eo modo quo hucusque miratus es, videlicet admiratione incredulitatis, vel ex malo intellectu procedentis, vel animum opprimentis ac tædio afficientis. Sic enim mirabatur Nicodemus, quasi sermo Christi impossibilitatem contineret. Potest tamen de doctrina Christi admiratio ordinata haberi, quum dicat Psalmista: Mirabilia testimonia tua. Non ergo inordinate mireris, quia dixi tibi: Oportet necessitate conditionata, non absoluta, videlicet, si debeatis salvari, vos nasci denuo: secundum modum nunc præostensum.
paras.en: Hence the Saviour adds: [[3:7|Wonder not|Non mireris]] in the way you have wondered until now, that is, with the wonder of unbelief, whether it proceeds from a wrong understanding or weighs down the mind and fills it with weariness. For so Nicodemus wondered, as though Christ's words contained an impossibility. Yet a well-ordered wonder may be had at Christ's teaching, since the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:129|Thy testimonies are wonderful|Mirabilia testimonia tua]]. So do not wonder in a disordered way [[3:7|that I said to thee|quia dixi tibi]]: [[3:7|You must|Oportet]], by a conditional, not an absolute, necessity, namely, if you are to be saved, [[3:7|be born again|vos nasci denuo]], in the manner just now shown.

paras.t: Insuper Christus ostendit ordinem spiritualis regenerationis per simile. Spiritus, ut puta Spiritus Sanctus, ubi vult spirat, id est, potestative ac libere gratiam præstat cui placuerit, sicut fatetur Apostolus: Omnia operatur unus atque idem Spiritus, dividens singulis prout vult. Deus namque operatur in creaturis, non necessitate naturæ, sed liberrima voluntate, prout ad Ephesios ait Apostolus: Qui omnia operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ. Et vocem ejus audis, id est verba sacræ Scripturæ divinitus revelata. Vel, Vocem ejus, id est internam allocutionem, audis: eo modo quo ait Psalmographus, Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus. Est enim auditus interior, quo divinus instinctus percipitur, dum sentit se homo interius tangi, doceri, accendi, rapi, resolvi et absorberi. Unde ait Dominus per Osee: Ducam eam in solitudinem, et loquar ad cor ejus. Nunquam Nicodemus salubriter venisset ad Jesum, nisi hanc vocem Spiritus Sancti internam audisset.
paras.en: Further, Christ shows the order of spiritual regeneration by a comparison. [[3:8|The Spirit|Spiritus]], namely the Holy Spirit, [[3:8|breatheth where he will|ubi vult spirat]], that is, bestows grace with power and freely on whom He pleases, as the Apostle declares: [[1 Cor 12:11|all these things, one and the same Spirit worketh, dividing to every one according as he will|Omnia operatur unus atque idem Spiritus, dividens singulis prout vult]]. For God works in creatures not by necessity of nature but by a most free will, as the Apostle says to the Ephesians: [[Eph 1:11|who worketh all things according to the counsel of his will|Qui omnia operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ]] [Denis reads 'according to the purpose of His will']. [[3:8|And thou hearest his voice|Et vocem ejus audis]], that is, the words of Holy Scripture, divinely revealed. Or: [[3:8|his voice|Vocem ejus]], that is, His inward speaking, [[3:8|thou hearest|audis]], in the way the Psalmist says: [[Ps 84:9|I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me|Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus]]. For there is an inward hearing by which the divine prompting is perceived, when a man feels himself inwardly touched, taught, kindled, rapt, dissolved and absorbed. Hence the Lord says through Osee: I [[Osee 2:14|will lead her into the wilderness: and I will speak to her heart|Ducam eam in solitudinem, et loquar ad cor ejus]]. Nicodemus would never have come to Jesus to his salvation, had he not heard this inward voice of the Holy Spirit.

paras.t: Sed non scis unde veniat Spiritus Sanctus, id est, quomodo mentem ejus ubi spirat et loquitur ingrediatur, non percipis, aut quo vadat, id est, qualiter recedat ignoras. Unde per Job inducitur: Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum; et si recesserit a me, non intelligam. Imo nullus viator scit certitudinaliter absque revelatione, an Spiritus Sanctus sit in ipso per gratiam gratum facientem, quia tunc sciret se dignum amore. Ideo hoc modo Spiritus Sanctus imperceptibiliter venit, imperceptibiliterque recedit. Vel sic: Vocem ejus audis, sed non scis unde veniat vox ista, aut quo vadat ipsa, id est, id a quo inspirata est, scilicet principium ejus, quod est Spiritus Sanctus, id quoque ad quod tendit, videlicet æterna felicitas, quæ est finis in quem tendit seu ordinatur Scriptura, sunt tibi ignota, quoniam sola fide tenentur, nec possunt in hac vita secundum essentiam sciri, quum tamen vox ista sensibiliter percipiatur.
paras.en: [[3:8|But thou knowest not whence he cometh|Sed non scis unde veniat]], the Holy Spirit: that is, you do not perceive how He enters the mind of the one in whom He breathes and speaks; [[3:8|and whither he goeth|aut quo vadat]], that is, you do not know how He withdraws. Hence Job is made to say: [[Job 9:11|If he come to me, I shall not see him: if he depart, I shall not understand|Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum; et si recesserit a me, non intelligam]]. Indeed no wayfarer [viator: a man still on the way, in this life, as against the blessed in heaven] knows with certainty, without a revelation, whether the Holy Spirit is in him by sanctifying grace [gratia gratum faciens: the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God], since then he would know himself worthy of love. So in this way the Holy Spirit comes imperceptibly and imperceptibly withdraws. Or thus: [[3:8|thou hearest his voice|Vocem ejus audis]], [[3:8|but thou knowest not whence he cometh|sed non scis unde veniat]], this voice, [[3:8|and whither he goeth|aut quo vadat]]: that is, that from which it is inspired, namely its principle, which is the Holy Spirit, and also that to which it tends, namely eternal happiness, which is the end towards which Scripture tends or is ordered, are unknown to you, since they are held by faith alone and cannot be known in their essence in this life, although the voice itself is perceived by the senses.

paras.t: Sic est omnis qui natus est ex spiritu: id est, in homine spiritualiter renato, est aliquid scitum ac manifestum, videlicet ipsa persona secundum se, et aliquid ignotum, quia intus invisibiliter reformatur, et de carnali ac perdito, spiritualis et filius adoptivus efficitur imperceptibili gratiæ infusione. Quod enim aliquis in Baptismo sic melioratur, sola fide tenemus. Vel sic: Sic est omnis qui natus est ex spiritu: id est, in regeneratione hominis talis, est aliquid evidens, scilicet aqua et forma verborum; et aliquid abditum, puta principium effectivum regenerationis, quod est Spiritus Sanctus; et item finis ejus, quæ est beatitudo æterna.
paras.en: [[3:8|So is every one that is born of the Spirit|Sic est omnis qui natus est ex spiritu]]: that is, in a man spiritually reborn there is something known and manifest, namely the person himself as he is in himself, and something unknown, because he is invisibly reformed within, and from carnal and lost is made spiritual and an adopted son by the imperceptible infusion of grace. For that anyone is thus bettered in Baptism we hold by faith alone. Or thus: [[3:8|So is every one that is born of the Spirit|Sic est omnis qui natus est ex spiritu]]: that is, in the regeneration of such a man there is something evident, namely the water and the form of words; and something hidden, namely the effective principle of the regeneration, which is the Holy Spirit, and likewise its end, which is eternal beatitude.

paras.t: Istæ expositiones procedunt secundum intentionem Augustini. Chrysostomus vero exponit de vento, ita quod secundum eum, Christus inducit exemplum sensibile ad intelligentiam prædictorum. Spiritus, id est ventus (de quo in Psalmo: Flabit spiritus ejus, et fluent aquæ; et rursus, Et stetit spiritus procellæ), ubi vult, id est, in quo inclinatur, spirat, id est, flat; et vocem, id est sonum, ejus audis, sed non scis unde veniat, aut quo vadat ventus, id est certum locum ubi flare incipiat, vel desistat. Hæc expositio non videtur multum conveniens aliis: Primo et maxime, quoniam Christus hoc loco frequenter per spiritum, intellexit Spiritum Sanctum, vel spiritualem essentiam. Unde non est verisimile quod nunc in eodem loco, nomine spiritus, designet rem materialem, seu ventum. Secundo, quoniam vento non competit proprie voluntas. Tertio, quoniam vento proprie non convenit vox, quum sit res inanimata, sed sonus. Quarto, quoniam scimus quod ventus venit ab aquilone, vel austro, et recte procedat, non tendens in partem oppositam. Verumtamen ista tria argumenta solvi possent, quia Scriptura frequenter adscribit voluntatem rebus inanimatis, ut quum dicitur in Josue: Quid sibi volunt lapides isti? Similiter vocem, ut quum ad Corinthios dicit Apostolus: Quæ sine anima sunt vocem dantia. Item nescimus determinatum principium certumque finem, unde incipit et ubi desinit ventus flare, quamvis sciamus in generali quod ab aliqua parte plaga australis vel alterius inchoetur.
paras.en: These expositions follow the mind of Augustine. Chrysostom, however, explains it of the wind, so that according to him Christ brings in a sensible example to make what has been said understood. [[3:8|The Spirit|Spiritus]], that is, the wind [the Latin spiritus means 'spirit', 'breath' and 'wind'] (of which it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 147:7|his wind shall blow, and the waters shall run|Flabit spiritus ejus, et fluent aquæ]]; and again, [[Ps 106:25|there arose a storm of wind|stetit spiritus procellæ]]), [[3:8|where he will|ubi vult]], that is, where it is inclined, [[3:8|breatheth|spirat]], that is, blows; [[3:8|and thou hearest his voice|et vocem ejus audis]], that is, its sound, [[3:8|but thou knowest not whence he cometh and whither he goeth|sed non scis unde veniat, aut quo vadat]], the wind: that is, the definite place where it begins or ceases to blow. This exposition does not seem to agree very well with the others. First and chiefly, because in this place Christ has repeatedly understood by 'spirit' the Holy Spirit, or a spiritual essence; so it is not likely that now, in the same place, He means by the name 'spirit' a material thing, the wind. Secondly, because will does not properly belong to the wind. Thirdly, because a voice does not properly belong to the wind, since it is an inanimate thing, but only a sound. Fourthly, because we know that the wind comes from the north or the south, and goes straight on, not turning towards the opposite quarter. Yet the last three arguments could be answered, since Scripture often ascribes will to inanimate things, as when it is said in Josue: [[Jos 4:6|What means these stones|Quid sibi volunt lapides isti?]]? Likewise a voice, as when the Apostle says to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 14:7|things without life that give sound|Quæ sine anima sunt vocem dantia]]. Again, we do not know the determinate beginning and the certain end, where the wind begins and where it ceases to blow, although we know in general that it starts from some quarter, the southern or another.

paras.t: Respondit Nicodemus, et dixit ei: Quomodo possunt hæc, quæ de spirituali regeneratione et Spiritus libera spiratione disseruisti, fieri, id est, taliter se habere ut asseris? Nicodemus in litterali sensu legis ac Prophetarum instructus et usitatus, ad spiritualem ac mysticum intellectum erigi facile non valebat: quoniam usus est velut altera natura. Ideo satis audacter sciscitatur quomodo queant hæc fieri.
paras.en: [[3:9|Nicodemus answered and said to him|Respondit Nicodemus, et dixit ei]]: [[3:9|How can these things|Quomodo possunt hæc]], which you have set out concerning spiritual regeneration and the free breathing of the Spirit, [[3:9|be done|fieri]], that is, be so as you assert? Nicodemus, instructed and practised in the literal sense of the Law and the Prophets, could not easily be raised to the spiritual and mystical understanding, since custom is like a second nature. So he asks rather boldly how these things can be done.

paras.t: Christus vero qui corda cognoscit, cernens doctorem de suo magisterio aliqualiter tumidum, ad humilitatem eum reducit quatenus instrui mereatur. Quemadmodum enim superbia excæcationem diabolicam, sic humilitas illuminationem divinam meretur. Propter quod Salomon protestatur: Ubi fuerit humilitas, ibi et sapientia. Tu es magister in Israel, id est doctor Judæorum, et hæc de Baptismo prolata ignoras? Quæ tamen in libris Moysis et Prophetarum figuraliter et litteraliter describuntur: ideoque, quum sis legis doctor, deberes hæc scire, vel saltem faciliter intelligere. Doctoris quippe est mysteria et figuras atque difficillima loca Scripturarum sanctarum cognoscere. Baptismus autem Christi, per transitum maris Rubri et per ablutiones legales præfigurabatur, dicente Apostolo: Omnes in Moyse baptizati sunt in nube et in mari. Prophetæ vero ad litteram locuti sunt de Christi Baptismate, ut quum per Zachariam dicitur: In die illa erit fons patens domui David et habitantibus Jerusalem, in ablutionem peccatoris. De quo accipi potest et illud Joelis: Fons de domo Domini egredietur, et irrigabit torrentem spinarum, videlicet corda vitiosa, spinis ac tribulis spiritualibus plena. Hinc per Ezechielem multa dicuntur de aquis redundantibus templi, quæ de aquis Baptismatis exponuntur. Quod ergo ait Salvator, Tu es magister in Israel, et hæc ignoras? non dicit insultando, sed potius miserendo, eumque humiliando, et ad meliora provocando.
paras.en: But Christ, who knows hearts, seeing the teacher somewhat puffed up by his mastership, brings him back to humility, so that he may deserve to be instructed. For as pride merits the blindness of the devil, so humility merits divine illumination. Wherefore Solomon declares: [[Prov 11:2|where humility is, there also is wisdom|Ubi fuerit humilitas, ibi et sapientia]]. [[3:10|Art thou a master in Israel|Tu es magister in Israel]], that is, a teacher of the Jews, [[3:10|and knowest not these things|et hæc ignoras?]], these things spoken about Baptism? Yet they are described, in figure and in the letter, in the books of Moses and the Prophets; and so, since you are a doctor of the Law, you ought to know them, or at least understand them easily. For it belongs to a teacher to know the mysteries and figures and the most difficult passages of the holy Scriptures. Now the Baptism of Christ was prefigured by the crossing of the Red Sea and by the washings of the Law, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 10:2|all in Moses were baptized, in the cloud and in the sea|Omnes in Moyse baptizati sunt in nube et in mari]]. And the Prophets spoke of Christ's Baptism in the literal sense, as when it is said through Zacharias: [[Zach 13:1|In that day there shall be a fountain open to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem: for the washing of the sinner|In die illa erit fons patens domui David et habitantibus Jerusalem, in ablutionem peccatoris]]. Of it may also be taken that saying of Joel: [[Joel 3:18|a fountain shall come forth of the house of the Lord, and shall water the torrent of thorns|Fons de domo Domini egredietur, et irrigabit torrentem spinarum]], namely vicious hearts, full of spiritual thorns and briars. Hence many things are said through Ezechiel of the waters overflowing from the temple[[Ezech 47:1||]] [the margin gives Ezech. xlvii throughout], which are expounded of the waters of Baptism. So when the Saviour says, [[3:10|Art thou a master in Israel, and knowest not these things?|Tu es magister in Israel, et hæc ignoras?]]? He does not say it to insult him, but rather in pity, humbling him and calling him on to better things.

paras.t: Deinceps pandit Salvator quam certa sit sua doctrina: propter quod ei humiliter est credendum. Amen, amen dico tibi, quia quod scimus nos rex Messias, unigenitus Filius Dei, Dominus universorum: quod, inquam, scimus, id est, clare cognovimus ab æterno secundum quod Deus (eadem enim est sapientia idemque numero intellectus Patris et Filii), loquimur nunc vobis Judæis, de sacramentis et documentis evangelicæ legis. Et quod vidimus oculo mentis, id est, certissime novimus, testamur, id est, firmiter affirmamus, hominibus prædicando. Potest quoque intelligi de scientia Christi creata, per quam omnia scivit ab instanti incarnationis, quæ scit Deus scientia visionis: sicque Christus secundum quod homo, vidit in Verbo, et item per species concreatas, omnia quæ prædicavit. Et testimonium nostrum non accipitis, recte credendo atque humiliter meis sermonibus consentiendo. Quamvis enim quidam Judæorum crediderunt illi, tamen comparatione incredulorum fuerunt paucissimi. Unde per Osee Christus prædixit: Recesserunt a me; et ego erudivi eos, et in me cogitaverunt malitiam.
paras.en: Next the Saviour shows how certain His teaching is, for which reason it must be humbly believed. [[3:11|Amen, amen, I say to thee that|Amen, amen dico tibi, quia]] [[3:11|what we know|quod scimus]], We, the King Messiah, the only-begotten Son of God, the Lord of all things: what, I say, We know, that is, have known clearly from eternity as God (for the wisdom of the Father and of the Son is the same, and their intellect numerically one), [[3:11|we speak|loquimur]] now to you Jews, concerning the sacraments and teachings of the law of the Gospel. And [[3:11|what we have seen|quod vidimus]] with the eye of the mind, that is, know most certainly, [[3:11|we testify|testamur]], that is, firmly affirm, by preaching it to men. It can also be understood of Christ's created knowledge, by which from the instant of the incarnation He knew all the things that God knows by the knowledge of vision [that is, God's knowledge of all that actually was, is or will be, as distinct from His knowledge of what is merely possible]; and so Christ as man saw in the Word, and also through concreated species [that is, ideas infused into His human mind together with its creation], all the things that He preached. [[3:11|and you receive not our testimony|Et testimonium nostrum non accipitis]], by believing rightly and by humbly assenting to My words. For although some of the Jews believed in Him, yet compared with the unbelievers they were very few. Hence Christ foretold through Osee: [[Osee 7:13|they have departed from me|Recesserunt a me]]; [[Osee 7:15|And I have chastised them|et ego erudivi eos]] [Denis's Latin *erudivi* means rather "I have instructed"], [[Osee 7:15|and they have imagined evil against me|et in me cogitaverunt malitiam]].

paras.t: Si terrena dixi vobis, et non creditis: quomodo si dixero vobis cælestia, credetis? Quæ sunt ista terrena quæ Christus dixit Nicodemo atque Judæis? Secundum Augustinum et Bedam, ista terrena non sunt aliqua dicta in isto capitulo, sed quod supra in præcedenti capitulo fertur Christus dixisse Judæis: Solvite templum hoc, et in tribus diebus excitabo illud. Hoc enim disseruit de proprio corpore adhuc corruptibili, terreno ac mixto. Tanquam dicat: Si non creditis quod possim proprium corpus divina virtute suscitare a morte, quomodo credetis quod homines valeam ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto regenerare?
paras.en: [[3:12|If I have spoken to you earthly things, and you believe not: how will you believe, if I shall speak to you heavenly things?|Si terrena dixi vobis, et non creditis: quomodo, si dixero vobis cælestia, credetis?]] What are these earthly things that Christ spoke to Nicodemus and to the Jews? According to Augustine and Bede, these earthly things are not anything said in this chapter, but what Christ is related above, in the preceding chapter, to have said to the Jews: [[John 2:19|Destroy this temple; and in three days I will raise it up|Solvite templum hoc, et in tribus diebus excitabo illud]]. For this He spoke of His own body, still corruptible, earthly and compounded [that is, made of the mixed elements, as every earthly body is]. As if He said: If you do not believe that I can raise My own body from death by divine power, how will you believe that I am able to regenerate men of water and the Holy Ghost?

paras.t: Alii referunt ad Baptismum, qui dici potest terrenus, quoniam visibiliter exhibetur in terra, in aqua visibili, sub sensibili forma verborum. Est itaque sensus: Si terrena dixi, id est, de sensibilibus rebus locutus sum, vobis, videlicet de Baptismo et suscitatione corporis mei, et non creditis vera esse quæ dico, eo quod sint supra naturalem rationem. Quod ait, Et non creditis, non est referendum ad Nicodemum, sed ad Judæos incredulos, quos Christus sub persona Nicodemi affatur: de quibus paulo ante locutus est, Testimonium nostrum non accipitis. Quomodo si dixero vobis cælestia, loquendo de invisibilibus Dei, de unitate Trinitatis et trinitate unitatis, de emanatione divinarum Personarum ad intra, de immediata visione divinæ essentiæ, de hierarchiis aliisque secretis cælestibus, de quibus parum habetur in lege ac Prophetis, credetis? quasi dicat: Difficulter vel nequaquam crederetis, quum sint incomprehensibiliora et supernaturaliora prædictis terrenis. Necesse est ergo proprium intellectum auctoritati Christi subjicere, et his quæ rationem transcendunt, fidem præbere, præsertim quum Deus per sufficientissima argumenta ostenderit Jesum esse Christum Filium Dei. Propterea dicit Apostolus ad Corinthios: In captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi.
paras.en: Others refer it to Baptism, which can be called earthly because it is administered visibly on earth, in visible water, under a form of words perceived by the senses. So the sense is: [[3:12|If I have spoken to you earthly things|Si terrena dixi]], that is, if I have spoken to you of things perceived by the senses, namely of Baptism and of the raising of My body, [[3:12|and you believe not|et non creditis]] that what I say is true, because it is above natural reason. When He says, [[3:12|and you believe not|Et non creditis]], this is not to be referred to Nicodemus but to the unbelieving Jews, whom Christ addresses in the person of Nicodemus, and of whom He had said a little before, [[3:11|you receive not our testimony|Testimonium nostrum non accipitis]]. [[3:12|if I shall speak to you heavenly things|Quomodo si dixero vobis cælestia]], speaking of the invisible things of God, of the unity of the Trinity and the trinity of the unity, of the emanation of the divine Persons within [that is, the processions of the Son and the Holy Ghost within the Godhead itself, as distinct from God's works outside Himself], of the immediate vision of the divine essence, of the hierarchies [of angels] and the other heavenly secrets, of which little is found in the Law and the Prophets, [[3:12|how will you believe|credetis]]? As if He said: You would believe with difficulty, or not at all, since these things are more incomprehensible and more supernatural than the earthly things spoken of before. It is necessary, therefore, to subject one's own understanding to the authority of Christ, and to give faith to the things that transcend reason, especially since God has shown by the most sufficient arguments that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 10:5|bringing into captivity every understanding unto the obedience of Christ|In captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi]].

paras.t: Verumtamen, quoniam quædam secreta atque cælestia ad Christum pertinentia cunctis fidelibus sunt scienda, videlicet unitas personæ Dei et hominis in Christo, mysterium dominicæ passionis, et amor Dei ad genus humanum; idcirco Christus de talibus consequenter instruit Nicodemum. Et nemo ascendit in cælum empyreum, quod est locus et mansio Beatorum, sicut ecclesia fertur locus orantium. Nihilominus, sicut fideles orare possunt extra materialem ecclesiam, sic Beati Deum clare conspiciunt ubicumque exstiterint. Nisi qui descendit de cælo, humanam naturam assumendo, videlicet Filius hominis, qui est in cælo.
paras.en: Nevertheless, since certain secret and heavenly things belonging to Christ must be known by all the faithful, namely the unity of the person of God and man in Christ, the mystery of the Lord's Passion, and the love of God for the human race, Christ accordingly goes on to instruct Nicodemus about such things. [[3:13|And no man hath ascended into heaven|Et nemo ascendit in cælum]], the empyrean heaven [that is, the highest heaven, the heaven of fire and light], which is the place and dwelling of the Blessed, as a church is called the place of those who pray. Even so, just as the faithful can pray outside a material church, so the Blessed see God clearly wherever they may be. [[3:13|but he that descended from heaven|Nisi qui descendit de cælo]], by taking human nature, namely [[3:13|the Son of man who is in heaven|Filius hominis, qui est in cælo]].

paras.t: Verba hæc aquilina sicut in stilo simplicia atque facilia sunt, sic in profunditate sensus prorsus comprobantur altissima, difficillima, nimiumque divina. Quid enim est quod ait, Nemo ascendit in cælum, etc.? Nonne homines sancti a pœna et culpa purgati mox ascendunt in cælum, dicente Apostolo ad Corinthios, Scimus quoniam si terrestris domus nostra hujus habitationis dissolvatur, quod ædificationem habemus ex Deo, domum non manufactam, æternam in cælis? Certum est quod nunc quidam sanctorum hominum ascenderunt in cælum, non solum quantum ad animam, sed etiam quantum ad corpus, ut certum est de Virgine gloriosa; et de his qui cum Christo surrexerunt, apparueruntque in sancta civitate quamplurimis, pie creditur a quibusdam. Sed pensemus quando Christus verba hæc protulit: utique ante passionem, quando loquebatur in Jerusalem cum Nicodemo. Quod autem nullus electorum introierit regnum cælorum ante Christi passionem, cognoscimus. Itaque, quod ait, Nemo ascendit in cælum, verum est pro tempore illo, sumendo verbum, Ascendit, ut est præteriti temporis sive præsentis.
paras.en: These eagle-like words [the eagle is the emblem of St John], simple and easy as they are in style, are found in the depth of their meaning to be altogether most lofty, most difficult and exceedingly divine. For what does He mean by saying, [[3:13|no man hath ascended into heaven|Nemo ascendit in cælum]], etc.? Do not holy men, once cleansed of punishment and guilt, at once ascend into heaven, as the Apostle says to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 5:1|we know, if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, that we have a building of God, a house not made with hands, eternal in heaven|Scimus quoniam si terrestris domus nostra hujus habitationis dissolvatur, quod ædificationem habemus ex Deo, domum non manufactam, æternam in cælis?]]? It is certain that some holy men have now ascended into heaven, not only in soul but also in body: this is certain of the glorious Virgin; and of those who rose with Christ and appeared to very many in the holy city[[Matt 27:52||]][[Matt 27:53||]], it is piously believed by some. But let us consider when Christ uttered these words: before the Passion, of course, when He was speaking with Nicodemus in Jerusalem. And we know that none of the elect entered the kingdom of heaven before Christ's Passion. So what He says, [[3:13|no man hath ascended into heaven|Nemo ascendit in cælum]], is true for that time, taking the word *ascendit* as either past or present tense [in Latin the same form can mean "ascended" or "ascends"].

paras.t: Sed tunc quæstio oritur, quomodo verba sequentia verificentur. Subditur enim: Nisi Filius hominis. Ascendere quippe competit Christo ratione naturæ assumptæ, secundum quam pro tunc nondum ascendit. Non ergo excepisset se ipsum, si prædicto modo sumpsisset hoc verbum, Ascendit. Quæstio ista dupliciter solvitur: Primo, ut solus Filius hominis ascendisse dicatur, quoniam solus propria potestate, jure ac merito ascendebat; alii vero virtute et merito Christi, cujus passione fuerunt ab originalis peccati absoluti reatu. Secundo, ut nomine Christi intelligatur non solum Christi persona, sed et mysticum corpus ipsius, puta Ecclesia patrum quæ detinebatur in limbo, ceterique electi omnino mundati, de quibus specialiter ait: Veniam, et assumam vos ad me ipsum; et iterum: Pater, volo ut ubi ego sum, et illi sint mecum, ut videant claritatem meam. Juxta hunc sensum dicit Salvator: Ego sum ostium ovium; omnes quotquot venerunt, fures sunt et latrones. Sic igitur lucet quomodo nemo ascendit in cælum, nisi qui descendit de cælo. — Sed quomodo incircumscriptus et incommutabilis Filius Dei descendisse asseritur, qui locum non mutat secundum quod Deus? Responsio plana et facilis est. Quoniam sic descendit de cælo, quomodo venit in mundum, utpote non locum mutando, aut se ipsum movendo, sed nostram naturam induendo, ac visibiliter apparendo. Mansit ergo unde descendit.
paras.en: But then the question arises how the words that follow are to be verified [that is, shown to be true]. For it is added: [[3:13|but|Nisi]] [[3:13|the Son of man|Filius hominis]]. For ascending belongs to Christ by reason of the nature He assumed, according to which He had not yet ascended at that time. He would not, then, have excepted Himself, if He had taken the word *ascendit* in the way just described. This question is solved in two ways. First, that the Son of man alone is said to have ascended, because He alone ascended by His own power, right and merit, whereas the others ascended by the power and merit of Christ, by whose Passion they were absolved from the guilt of original sin. Secondly, that by the name of Christ is understood not only the person of Christ but also His mystical body, such as the Church of the fathers that was held in limbo, and the rest of the elect wholly cleansed, of whom He says in particular: [[John 14:3|I will come again and will take you to myself|Veniam, et assumam vos ad me ipsum]]; and again: [[John 17:24|Father, I will that where I am, they also|Pater, volo ut ubi ego sum, et illi]] [[John 17:24|may be with me: that they may see my glory|sint mecum, ut videant claritatem meam]]. In this sense the Saviour says: [[John 10:7|I am the door of the sheep|Ego sum ostium ovium]]; all, [[John 10:8|as many as have come, are thieves and robbers|quotquot venerunt, fures sunt et latrones]]. Thus it is clear how [[3:13|no man hath ascended into heaven, but he that descended from heaven|nemo ascendit in cælum, nisi qui descendit de cælo]]. But how is the Son of God, who is uncircumscribed and unchangeable, said to have descended, since as God He does not change place? The answer is plain and easy. He descended from heaven in the same way as He came into the world: not by changing place or moving Himself, but by putting on our nature and appearing visibly. So He remained where He descended from.

paras.t: Porro, quod subditur, Filius hominis, qui est in cælo, majorem habet difficultatem. Si enim Filius hominis descendit de cælo, videtur ante incarnationem fuisse in cælo. Sed Filius hominis est homo: ergo homo ante incarnationem fuisset in cælo. Item, si ita est, videtur quod Christus secum portavit corpus de cælo. Adhuc autem, quando Christus dixit verba hæc, erat cum Nicodemo in terra: quomodo ergo pro tunc fuit Filius hominis in cælo, ita ut diceret de se stante in terra, Filius hominis, qui est in cælo? Et respondendum, quod Christus hæc dixit ad insinuandum unitatem personæ utriusque naturæ in ipso. Tanta est enim unio divinæ naturæ seu Verbi atque humanæ in Christo, ut humana Deo, et divina homini vere conveniant. Sed pensandum quid propter quid dicatur. Dicendum ergo, quod Christus seu Filius hominis fuit ante incarnationem in cælo secundum naturam divinam; descenditque de cælo, non corpus cæleste secum ferendo, ut dixit Valentinus hæresiarcha, sed quia eadem est persona Dei et hominis in Christo. In talibus enim locutionibus, Jesus, seu Christus, vel Filius hominis, semper supponit personam divinam, increatam hypostasim, utpote Verbum æternum. Ideo istæ sunt veræ: Jesus est æternus, immensus, omnia implens; Christus est verus Deus, immortalis, omnipotens; Deus est passus, occisus, sepultus.
paras.en: Further, what follows, [[3:13|the Son of man who is in heaven|Filius hominis, qui est in cælo]], has greater difficulty. For if the Son of man descended from heaven, He seems to have been in heaven before the incarnation. But the Son of man is a man: therefore a man would have been in heaven before the incarnation. Again, if this is so, it seems that Christ brought a body with Him from heaven. Moreover, when Christ said these words He was on earth with Nicodemus: how then was the Son of man in heaven at that time, so that He could say of Himself while standing on earth, [[3:13|the Son of man who is in heaven|Filius hominis, qui est in cælo]]? The answer is that Christ said this to make known the unity of person of both natures in Him. For so great is the union of the divine nature, or the Word, and the human in Christ, that human things truly belong to God and divine things to man [the communication of idioms, by which what belongs to either nature is truly said of the one Person]. But we must weigh which is said on account of which. We must say, then, that Christ, or the Son of man, was in heaven before the incarnation according to the divine nature; and He descended from heaven, not by bringing a heavenly body with Him, as the heresiarch Valentinus said, but because the person of God and of man in Christ is the same.
