For in such expressions, Jesus, or Christ, or the Son of man, always supposits for [that is, stands for, as the subject of the statement] the divine person, the uncreated hypostasis [that is, the individual subsistent Person], namely the eternal Word. Therefore these statements are true: Jesus is eternal, immense, filling all things; Christ is true God, immortal, almighty; God suffered, was slain and was buried.

paras.t: Causa veritatis harum atque similium locutionum est unitas personalis præfata, et suppositio increatæ hypostasis. Idcirco de puero qui natus est nobis, et filio qui datus est nobis, Isaias prædixit, quod vocaretur Deus, Fortis, Pater futuri sæculi, etc. Unde de puero Jesu exsistente in utero, jacente in præsepio, pendente ad ubera, verum fuit dicere: Iste puer creavit cælum et terram, et ubique est per essentiam, præsentiam atque potentiam. Ad quod insinuandum dicit Apostolus: Jesus Christus heri et hodie, ipse et in sæcula. Judas quoque apostolus in sua epistola: Jesus, inquit, populum suum salvans de Ægypto, secundo eos qui non crediderunt, perdidit. Porro, de Christi ascensione Prophetæ sufficienter locuti sunt: ut est illud in Psalmo, Psallite Deo qui ascendit super cælum cæli ad orientem; et illud, Ascendit Deus in jubilo; itemque, Ascendisti in altum, cepisti captivitatem. — Prædictis consonat illud Apostoli: Qui descendit, ipse est et qui ascendit super omnes cælos.
paras.en: The cause of the truth of these and similar expressions is the personal unity already mentioned, and the supposition of the uncreated hypostasis [that is, that the subject of such statements always stands for the uncreated divine Person]. Therefore Isaias foretold of the child who is born to us, and the son who is given to us, that He would be called [[Is 9:6|God the Mighty, the Father of the world to come|Deus, Fortis, Pater futuri sæculi]], etc. Hence of the child Jesus, while He was in the womb, lying in the manger, hanging at the breast, it was true to say: This child created heaven and earth, and is everywhere by essence, presence and power. To make this known the Apostle says: [[Heb 13:8|Jesus Christ, yesterday, and today: and the same for ever.|Jesus Christus heri, et hodie: ipse et in sæcula.]] Jude the apostle too, in his epistle: [[Jude 1:5|Jesus|Jesus]], he says, [[Jude 1:5|having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, did afterwards destroy them that believed not|populum suum salvans de Ægypto, secundo eos qui non crediderunt, perdidit]][[Num 14:36||]][[Num 14:37||]]. Further, the Prophets have spoken sufficiently of Christ's ascension, as in that of the Psalm: [[Ps 67:33|Sing ye to God|Psallite Deo]], [[Ps 67:34|Who mounteth above the heaven of heavens, to the east|qui ascendit super cælum cæli ad orientem]]; and that: [[Ps 46:6|God is ascended with jubilee|Ascendit Deus in jubilo]]; and again: [[Ps 67:19|Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive|Ascendisti in altum, cepisti captivitatem]]. With these agrees that of the Apostle: [[Eph 4:10|He that descended is the same also that ascended above all the heavens|Qui descendit, ipse est et qui ascendit super omnes cælos]].

paras.t: Deinceps prædicit Salvator suam passionem, in lege per serpentem æneum præfiguratam. Et sicut Moyses exaltavit, id est, in loco alto erexit ac posuit, serpentem æneum, id est similitudinem serpentis factam de ære, in deserto Ægypti. Quomodo factum sit hoc, scriptum est in libro Numerorum. Quum enim tædere cœpisset populum Israel itineris ac laboris, murmurantesque contra Dominum ac Moysen dixissent, Anima nostra nauseat super cibo isto levissimo; misit Dominus in populum serpentes ignitos. A quibus quum multi occisi vel læsi fuissent, pœnituit populus; dixitque Dominus Moysi: Fac serpentem æneum, et pone eum pro signo; qui percussus adspexerit eum, vivet.
paras.en: Next the Saviour foretells His passion, prefigured in the Law by the brazen serpent. [[3:14|And as Moses lifted up|Et sicut Moyses exaltavit]], that is, set up and placed on a high spot, the brazen serpent, that is, the likeness of a serpent made of brass, [[3:14|in the desert|in deserto]] of Egypt. How this came about is written in the Book of Numbers. For when the people of Israel had begun to grow weary of the journey and the toil[[Num 21:4||]], and, murmuring against the Lord and Moses, had said, [[Num 21:5|our soul now loatheth this very light food|Anima nostra nauseat super cibo isto levissimo]], [[Num 21:6|the Lord sent among the people fiery serpents|misit Dominus in populum serpentes ignitos]]. And when many had been killed or wounded by them, the people repented[[Num 21:7||]]; and the Lord said to Moses: [[Num 21:8|Make a brazen serpent, and set it up for a sign: whosoever being struck shall look on it, shall live|Fac serpentem æneum, et pone eum pro signo; qui percussus adspexerit eum, vivet]].

paras.t: Ita exaltari, id est in cruce levari, oportet necessitate conditionata, non absoluta. Vel, Oportet, id est, decens et utile est. Christus enim oblatus est quia voluit, non quia necessitate fuit adstrictus. Oportuit tamen, quia præordinatum a Deo, et ut implerentur Scripturæ. Filium hominis. Sæpius nominat se Christus Filium hominis quam Filium Dei, ut humilitatis præstet exemplum.
paras.en: [[3:14|so must the Son of man be lifted up|Ita exaltari]], that is, be raised on the cross: it *must*, by a conditional necessity, not an absolute one [that is, a necessity that follows from something supposed, here God's decree and Christ's own will, not one that binds of itself]. Or, [[3:14|must|Oportet]], that is, it is fitting and profitable. For Christ [[Is 53:7|was offered because it was his own will|oblatus est quia voluit]], not because He was bound by necessity. Yet it had to be, because it was foreordained by God, and so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled. [[3:14|the Son of man|Filium hominis]]. Christ calls Himself the Son of man more often than the Son of God, to give an example of humility.

paras.t: Ratio quoque finalis exaltationis Christi in cruce, et fructus dominicæ passionis subjungitur. Ut omnis qui credit in eum fide formata ac operatoria, id est caritati unita et procedente in opus, dummodo operandi opportunitas adsit. Caritas namque est forma seu decor atque perfectio fidei: propter quod fides caritati conjuncta, vocatur formata. Non pereat, incurrendo mortem spiritualem, damnationemque perpetuam. Sed quia non sufficit liberari a malo, sed indigemus apprehendere bonum, subjungitur: sed habeat vitam æternam, id est, ad beatificam Dei visionem pertingat: quæ nunc habetur in spe, et post habetur in re, a puram mentem habentibus, ut apud Matthæum promittitur: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. De qua infra habetur: Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te verum Deum.
paras.en: Then is added the final cause [that is, the end or purpose for which a thing is done] of Christ's lifting up on the cross, and the fruit of the Lord's passion: [[3:15|That whosoever believeth in him|Ut omnis qui credit in eum]] with a formed and working faith, that is, one joined to charity and going forth into deeds, provided there is opportunity to act. For charity is the form, the beauty and the perfection of faith: for which reason faith joined to charity is called formed [*fides formata*: faith given its life and form by charity, as against "unformed" faith, which believes without charity]. [[3:15|may not perish|Non pereat]], by incurring spiritual death and everlasting damnation. But since it is not enough to be freed from evil, and we need also to lay hold of the good[[Ps 36:27||]], there is added: [[3:15|but may have life everlasting|sed habeat vitam æternam]], that is, may attain to the beatific vision of God: which is had now in hope, and hereafter in reality, by those who have a pure mind, as is promised in Matthew: [[Matt 5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart: they shall see God|Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt]]. Of this it is said further on: [[John 17:3|this is eternal life: That they may know thee|Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te]], the true God.

paras.t: Elucescit igitur quod serpens ille fuit figura Christi: et hoc, propter causas diversas. Primo, quoniam sicut serpens ille habuit figuram serpentis, et similitudinem venenati, non autem naturam serpentis, nec veritatem veneni: sic Christus habuit similitudinem carnis peccati, et inter peccatores communiter vixit; non tamen habuit culpam, nec communionem peccati cum impiis. Secundo, quoniam erectio illius serpentis, figuravit suspensionem Christi in ligno. Tertio, quia quemadmodum Judæi corporaliter læsi, intuendo illum serpentem sanabantur a morsu ignitorum serpentium: sic fideles fide intuendo Christi passionem seu Christum in cruce expansum, sanantur ab omni ardore incentivi peccati, ab omni tentatione diaboli, ab omni pigritia; animantur quoque ad fortiter præliandum, ad patientiam veram, ad omnem virtutem, optantes sequi vestigia Christi. Unde ad Hebræos monet Apostolus: Curramus ad propositum nobis certamen, adspicientes in auctorem fidei et consummatorem Jesum, qui proposito sibi gaudio sustinuit crucem, confusione contempta. Tanto præterea dignior fructuosiorque consistit erectio Christi in cruce quam serpentis illius, quanto melius est liberari a vulneribus animæ quam corporis, et adipisci vitam æternam quam temporalem.
paras.en: It is clear, then, that that serpent was a figure of Christ, and this for several reasons. First, because just as that serpent had the shape of a serpent and the likeness of a venomous one, but not the nature of a serpent nor the reality of venom, so Christ had [[Rom 8:3|the likeness of sinful flesh|similitudinem carnis peccati]], and lived among sinners in common with them[[Matt 9:10||]]; yet He had no guilt, nor any fellowship of sin with the wicked[[2 Cor 5:21||]]. Second, because the setting up of that serpent figured the hanging of Christ on the wood. Third, because just as the Jews who had been wounded in the body were healed of the bite of the fiery serpents by looking on that serpent, so the faithful, looking by faith on Christ's passion, or on Christ stretched out on the cross, are healed of all the burning of the incentive to sin [that is, the *fomes peccati*, the inclination to sin left in us by original sin], of every temptation of the devil, of all sloth; and they are also roused to fight bravely, to true patience, to every virtue, longing to follow in Christ's footsteps. Hence the Apostle exhorts the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:1|let us run|Curramus]] to [[Heb 12:1|the fight proposed to us|ad propositum nobis certamen]], [[Heb 12:2|Looking on Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, having joy set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame|adspicientes in auctorem fidei et consummatorem Jesum, qui proposito sibi gaudio sustinuit crucem, confusione contempta]]. Moreover, the lifting up of Christ on the cross is as much worthier and more fruitful than that of the serpent as it is better to be freed from the wounds of the soul than from those of the body, and to gain eternal life than temporal.

paras.t: Postremo passio Christi vocatur exaltatio: Primo, quia in aere elevatus est Christus in cruce. Secundo, quia per suam passionem maxime honoravit Deum Patrem, obediendo ei usque ad mortem. Propter quod ait: Ego non quæro gloriam meam, sed honorifico Patrem meum. Tertio, quia per suam passionem exaltavit genus humanum, reducendo illud ad regnum cœlorum. Quarto, quoniam sua passione meruit sibi ipsi accidentale præmium, omnis videlicet creaturæ prælationem, et corporis sui glorificationem, secundum quod dicit Apostolus ad Hebræos: Videmus Jesum propter passionem mortis gloria et honore coronatum; et alibi: Humiliavit semetipsum factus obediens usque ad mortem; propter quod et Deus exaltavit illum, et dedit ei nomen quod est super omne nomen.
paras.en: Lastly, Christ's passion is called a lifting up [*exaltatio*, which means both a raising up and an exalting]: first, because Christ was raised up into the air on the cross. Second, because by His passion He honoured God the Father supremely, obeying Him unto death[[Phil 2:8||]]. For which reason He says: [[John 8:50|I seek not my own glory|Ego non quæro gloriam meam]], [[John 8:49|but I honour my Father|sed honorifico Patrem meum]]. Third, because by His passion He exalted the human race, leading it back to the kingdom of heaven. Fourth, because by His passion He merited for Himself an accidental reward [that is, a reward added to the essential glory He had already, the vision of God], namely pre-eminence over every creature and the glorification of His body, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 2:9|we see Jesus|Videmus Jesum]] [[Heb 2:9|for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour|propter passionem mortis gloria et honore coronatum]]; and elsewhere: [[Phil 2:8|He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death|Humiliavit semetipsum factus obediens usque ad mortem]]; [[Phil 2:9|For which cause, God also hath exalted him and hath given him a name which is above all names|propter quod et Deus exaltavit illum, et dedit ei nomen quod est super omne nomen]].

paras.t: In libris Regum scriptum est, quod Ezechias fregit serpentem æneum quem fecit Moyses. Quod fecit Ezechias zelo divini honoris, ad vitandam omnem speciem idololatriæ, quia ut illic subjungitur, filii Israel usque ad illud tempus adolebant ei incensum.
paras.en: It is written in the Books of Kings that Ezechias [[4 Kings 18:4|broke the brazen serpent, which Moses had made|fregit serpentem æneum quem fecit Moyses]]. Ezechias did this out of zeal for God's honour, to avoid every appearance of idolatry, because, as is added there, [[4 Kings 18:4|till that time the children of Israel burnt incense to it|filii Israel usque ad illud tempus adolebant ei incensum]].

3.title: Prosecutio elucidationis præsentis capituli tertii, ab eo loco quo dicitur: Sic enim Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret.
3.title_en: Continuation of the explanation of the present third chapter, from the place where it is said: “For God so loved the world, as to give his only begotten Son.”

paras.t: Hucusque descripta sunt verba Christi ad Nicodemum. Sed an verba sequentia usque ad id, Post hæc venit Jesus et discipuli ejus in Judæam terram, sint verba Christi ad Nicodemum, vel potius verba Joannis evangelistæ, exponentis et declarantis præinducta eloquia Salvatoris, certum non habeo. Verumtamen, quomodocumque dicatur ad hoc, sensus est idem. Dixit quippe Salvator in verbis immediate præhabitis, atque in articulo præcedenti expositis, quod exaltari oportuerit Filium hominis, hoc est mori pro mundi salute; nunc ostendit causam beneficii tanti, quæ non est meritum nostrum, sed gratuita Dei dilectio.
paras.en: Thus far the words of Christ to Nicodemus have been set down. But whether the words that follow, up to the place [[3:22|After these things, Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea|Post hæc venit Jesus et discipuli ejus in Judæam terram]], are words of Christ to Nicodemus, or rather words of John the Evangelist, expounding and explaining the sayings of the Saviour just given, I do not know for certain. Yet however this is answered, the sense is the same. For in the words immediately preceding, which were expounded in the previous article, the Saviour said that the Son of man must be lifted up, that is, must die for the salvation of the world; now He shows the cause of so great a benefit, which is not our merit but the free love of God[[Eph 2:8||]][[2 Tim 1:9||]][[Tit 3:5||]] [the margin cites Eph. ii, 8–10, II Tim. i and Tit. iii, 5–7, partly unreadable in the scan].

paras.t: Sic enim Deus dilexit mundum, id est, tam ardenter Deus Pater dilexit genus humanum, præsertim homines prædestinatos, ut Filium suum unigenitum, non adoptivum, sed naturalem, consubstantialem, et unicum, daret hominibus, in Filii sui incarnatione ac passione. Dedit enim eum nobis, quemadmodum cecinit Isaias: Puer natus est nobis, filius datus est nobis. Et Apostolus: Proprio (inquit) Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro omnibus nobis tradidit illum.
paras.en: [[3:16|For God so loved the world|Sic enim Deus dilexit mundum]], that is, so ardently did God the Father love the human race, and especially men predestined, [[3:16|as to give his only begotten Son|ut Filium suum unigenitum]] (not an adopted Son, but His natural, consubstantial and only Son) to men, in the incarnation and passion of His Son. For He gave Him to us, as Isaias sang: [[Is 9:6|a CHILD IS BORN to us, and a son is given to us|Puer natus est nobis, filius datus est nobis]] [Denis gives the words as the Christmas Introit sings them, Puer, "a child", where the Vulgate has Parvulus]. And the Apostle: He [[Rom 8:32|spared not even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all|Proprio (inquit) Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro omnibus nobis tradidit illum]], he says.

paras.t: Dedit ergo eum nobis in incarnatione, faciens eum filium nostræ sororis, videlicet sacratissimæ Virginis, fratrem nostrum, mediatorem ac socium nostrum. Qui enim ante incarnationem erat Deus et Dominus noster, per incarnationem factus est frater et socius noster. Dedit quoque eum nobis in tota conversatione ejus in sæculo isto. Nam quidquid Christus fecit, prædicavit et pertulit, ordinavit Pater et etiam Filius, ad nostram salutem, et nobis meritorium fuit, non ipsi Christo, quantum ad præmium essentiale, quia hoc habuit anima Christi a primo suæ creationis instanti. Dedit etiam eum nobis in Sacramento altaris, quemadmodum infra testatur: Pater meus dat vobis panem verum. Postremo dedit eum nobis in passione, exponens Filium suum dilectum tantis tormentis pro nostra salute, quemadmodum Isaias prænuntiavit: Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum. Et Filius tempore passionis: Calicem, ait, quem dedit mihi Pater, non bibam illum? In passione enim Creator noster factus est salvator noster, judex noster factus est reconciliator noster, advocatus ac mediator. Sed quid retribuemus Deo Patri pro omnibus quæ retribuit nobis? Benedic, anima mea, Domino, et noli oblivisci omnes retributiones ejus. Quid enim, quale vel quantum bonum dedit nobis? Nonne Filium suum carissimum, sibi coæqualem et coimmensum, quem ex proprio corde æternaliter genuit, quem ex sua substantia peperit, quem non minus diligit quam se ipsum?
paras.en: So He gave Him to us in the incarnation, making Him the son of our sister, namely the most holy Virgin, and so our brother, our mediator and companion. For He who before the incarnation was our God and Lord, through the incarnation was made our brother and companion. He gave Him to us also in His whole way of life in this world. For whatever Christ did, preached and endured, the Father (and the Son also) ordained for our salvation, and it was meritorious for us, not for Christ Himself as regards the essential reward [the vision of God, as distinct from accidental rewards], since the soul of Christ had this from the first instant of its creation. He gave Him to us also in the Sacrament of the altar, as He testifies below: [[John 6:32|my Father giveth you the true bread|Pater meus dat vobis panem verum]]. Lastly He gave Him to us in the passion, exposing His beloved Son to such torments for our salvation, as Isaias foretold: [[Is 53:8|for the wickedness of my people have I struck him|Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum]]. And the Son says at the time of His passion: [[John 18:11|The chalice which my father hath given me, shall I not drink it?|Calicem, ait, quem dedit mihi Pater, non bibam illum?]] For in the passion our Creator was made our Saviour, our Judge was made our reconciler, advocate and mediator. But what shall we render to God the Father for all the things that He hath rendered to us?[[Ps 115:3||]] [Denis adapts the Psalm, "What shall I render to the Lord, for all the things that he hath rendered to me?"; the margin numbers it Ps. cxv, 12, as in the Hebrew count] [[Ps 102:2|Bless the Lord, O my soul, and never forget all he hath done for thee.|Benedic, anima mea, Domino, et noli oblivisci omnes retributiones ejus]] For what good, of what kind and how great, has He given us? Was it not His most dear Son, coequal and co-immense with Himself, whom He begot from His own heart from eternity, whom He brought forth from His own substance[[Ps 109:3||]], whom He loves no less than Himself?

paras.t: Porro, secundum Philosophum, diligere est alicui bonum velle. Vehementer ergo nos amat Pater, quibus dedit hoc bonum immensum. Quomodo etiam non omnia nobis cum illo donavit? Quid negabit petentibus, qui non petentibus dedit unigenitum Filium suum? Hinc ait Joannes in sua epistola: In hoc apparuit caritas Dei in nobis, quoniam Filium suum unigenitum misit in mundum, ut vivamus per eum. Et ne putemus nos propter merita nostra a Deo dilectos, adjecit: In hoc est caritas, non quasi nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos. Hinc et Paulus ipse ad Ephesios disseruit: Deus qui dives est in misericordia, propter nimiam caritatem suam qua dilexit nos, quum essemus mortui peccatis, convivificavit Christo, cujus gratia estis salvati.
paras.en: Moreover, according to the Philosopher, to love is to will good to someone [Aristotle, Rhetoric II, 4]. Vehemently, then, does the Father love us, to whom He has given this immense good. [[Rom 8:32|how hath he not also, with him, given us all things?|Quomodo etiam non omnia nobis cum illo donavit?]] What will He deny to those who ask, who gave His only begotten Son to those who did not ask? Hence John says in his epistle: [[1 John 4:9|By this hath the charity of God appeared towards us, because God hath sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we may live by him|In hoc apparuit caritas Dei in nobis, quoniam Filium suum unigenitum misit in mundum, ut vivamus per eum]]. And lest we think we are loved by God for our own merits, he added: [[1 John 4:10|In this is charity: not as though we had loved God, but because he hath first loved us|In hoc est caritas, non quasi nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos]]. Hence Paul too set it out to the Ephesians: [[Eph 2:4|God (who is rich in mercy) for his exceeding charity wherewith he loved us|Deus qui dives est in misericordia, propter nimiam caritatem suam qua dilexit nos]], [[Eph 2:5|when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together in Christ (by whose grace you are saved)|quum essemus mortui peccatis, convivificavit Christo, cujus gratia estis salvati]].

paras.t: Non ergo contemnamus neque negligamus nos ipsos, non vilificemus animas nostras summæ Trinitatis imagine insignitas, rebus terrenis, caducis aut carnalibus inhærendo: sed intentissima mente pensemus, quanti æstimati simus a Deo nostro, quanta pro nobis fecit et passus est Filius Dei, quanta nunc dedit, quanta se daturum nobis promisit; et dicamus Deo corde ferventi cum illustrissimo Isaia: Nomen tuum et memoriale tuum, Domine, in desiderio animæ; anima mea desideravit te in nocte, sed et spiritu meo in præcordiis meis, de mane vigilabo ad te. Et cum Psalmista: Diligam te, Domine, fortitudo mea. Ad hoc enim Deus suam nobis dilectionem manifestavit, ut eum redamaremus, ejusque amore succensi, ampliora beneficia perciperemus.
paras.en: Let us not, then, despise or neglect ourselves; let us not cheapen our souls, which bear the image of the most high Trinity, by clinging to earthly, perishable or carnal things: but let us weigh with the most intent mind how highly we are valued by our God, how much the Son of God did and suffered for us, how much He has given us now, how much He has promised to give us; and let us say to God with fervent heart, with the most illustrious Isaias: [[Is 26:8|thy name, and thy remembrance|Nomen tuum et memoriale tuum]], O Lord, [[Is 26:8|are the desire of the soul|in desiderio animæ]]; [[Is 26:9|My soul hath desired thee in the night: yea, and with my spirit within me in the morning early I will watch to thee|anima mea desideravit te in nocte, sed et spiritu meo in præcordiis meis, de mane vigilabo ad te]]. And with the Psalmist: [[Ps 17:2|I will love thee, O Lord, my strength|Diligam te, Domine, fortitudo mea]]. For God has shown His love to us to this end, that we might love Him in return and, set on fire with His love, receive still greater benefits.

paras.t: Quadruplex nobis causa est amandi Deum: prima, quoniam in se naturaliter bonus est; secunda, quoniam prior dilexit nos; tertia, quia jam multa nobis bona largitus est, videlicet bona naturæ et gratiæ; quarta, quia majora promisit, præparavit, et dare paratus est. Nobilis anima, quæ suum diligit Creatorem, et tanto nobilior, quanto in ejus amore ferventior. Illustrissima creatura, quæ igne divini amoris flammescens in dilectum super omnia, in Deum transformatur, et unus cum illo spiritus efficitur.
paras.en: We have a fourfold reason for loving God: first, because He is by nature good in Himself; second, because He first loved us[[1 John 4:10||]][[1 John 4:19||]]; third, because He has already bestowed many goods on us, namely the goods of nature and of grace; fourth, because He has promised, prepared and stands ready to give greater ones. Noble is the soul that loves its Creator, and the nobler, the more fervent it is in His love. Most illustrious is the creature which, blazing with the fire of divine love towards the One beloved above all things, is transformed into God and becomes one spirit with Him[[1 Cor 6:17||]].

paras.t: Convenientissime demum ait Evangelista, Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, ad insinuandum quod dilectio Dei est causa fontana omnium beneficiorum nobis divinitus præstitorum. Amor namque, secundum theologos, est primum donum, in quo omnia dona gratuita gratis donantur. Propter quod donum appropriatur Spiritui Sancto, qui est amor Patris et Filii.
paras.en: Most fittingly, finally, does the Evangelist say, [[3:16|God so loved the world, as to give his only begotten Son|Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret]], to suggest that the love of God is the fountain-cause of all the benefits divinely granted to us. For love, according to the theologians, is the first gift, in which all gifts of grace are freely given. Therefore the name Gift is appropriated to the Holy Ghost [that is, attributed to Him in particular, though the giving is common to the whole Trinity, because of His likeness to it as the Love proceeding], who is the love of the Father and the Son.

paras.t: Quæritur, si Deus Pater sic diligit mundum, cur scriptum est in Joanne: Nolite diligere mundum, neque ea quæ in mundo sunt; quia si quis diligit mundum, non est caritas Patris in eo. Et Jacobus in sua fatetur Canonica: Si quis voluerit amicus hujus mundi fieri, inimicus Dei constituetur.
paras.en: It is asked: if God the Father so loves the world, why is it written in John: [[1 John 2:15|Love not the world, nor the things which are in the world|Nolite diligere mundum, neque ea quæ in mundo sunt]]. [[1 John 2:15|If any man love the world, the charity of the Father is not in him|si quis diligit mundum, non est caritas Patris in eo]]. And James declares in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jas 4:4|Whosoever therefore will be a friend of this world becometh an enemy of God|Si quis voluerit amicus hujus mundi fieri, inimicus Dei constituetur]].

paras.t: Dicendum est, quod in Scripturis sacris mundus accipitur pro hominibus in terra degentibus. Et hoc tripliciter. Primo, pro mundanis et vitiosis hominibus: de quibus Paulus ad Galatas testatur, Si hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem. De hoc mundo scribit Joannes in sua Canonica, dicens: Ipsi de mundo sunt, et de mundo loquuntur, et mundus eos audit. Iste est mundus pertinens ad massam perditionis. Secundo, accipitur mundus pro hominibus prædestinatis in mundo isto sensibili peregrinantibus. Hujus mundi dicitur Christus esse salvator, quemadmodum loquitur Paulus ad Corinthios: Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi. De quo mundo promissum est Abrahæ: Benedicentur in te omnes tribus terræ. Unde secundum Apostolum ad Romanos, quarto capitulo, Abraham factus est hæres mundi.
paras.en: The answer is that in the sacred Scriptures "world" is taken for the men living on the earth, and this in three ways. First, for worldly and vicious men: of whom Paul testifies to the Galatians, [[Gal 1:10|If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ|Si hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem]]. Of this world John writes in his Canonical Epistle, saying: [[1 John 4:5|They are of the world|Ipsi de mundo sunt]], and [[1 John 4:5|of the world they speak: and the world heareth them|de mundo loquuntur, et mundus eos audit]]. This is the world that belongs to the mass of perdition [Augustine's name for fallen mankind as a whole, left to itself without grace]. Secondly, "world" is taken for the predestined, who are pilgrims in this world of the senses. Of this world Christ is said to be the Saviour, as Paul says to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 5:19|God indeed was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself|Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi]]. Of this world it was promised to Abraham: [[Gen 22:18|shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|Benedicentur in te omnes tribus terræ]] [the margin gives Gen. xxii, 18; Denis's wording, "in thee … all the tribes of the earth", is closer to Gen 12:3 and 28:14]. Hence, according to the Apostle to the Romans, in the fourth chapter, Abraham was made [[Rom 4:13|heir of the world|hæres mundi]].

paras.t: Tertio, sumitur mundus indifferenter pro quibuscumque hominibus in terra viventibus, electis et reprobis. Sic quoque accipi potest nunc; et in verbis immediate sequentibus dicitur: Non misit Deus Filium suum in mundum ut judicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum. Deus enim, ut dicitur Sapientiæ undecimo capitulo, diligit omnia quæ fecit: quanto magis rationalem creaturam? Vult enim omnes homines salvos fieri, voluntate antecedente: et secundum hoc, diligit omnes, et quantum in ipso est, neminem vult perire. Sicque pro universorum salute misit Pater Filium suum, ut omnes convertantur: et pro omnibus passus est Christus, quantum ad sufficientiam; sed quantum ad efficaciam, pro solis electis sustinuit omnia. Ideo Christus passione instante dixit ad Patrem: Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro his quos dedisti mihi de mundo, quia tui sunt. Hæc diversa acceptio mundi memoriter est tenenda, quoniam ad intelligentiam dicendorum necessaria est.
paras.en: Thirdly, "world" is taken without distinction for any men whatever living on the earth, elect and reprobate. So too it can be taken here; and in the words immediately following it is said: [[3:17|God sent not his Son into the world, to judge the world: but that the world may be saved by him|Non misit Deus Filium suum in mundum ut judicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum]]. For God, as is said in the eleventh chapter of Wisdom, loves all things that He has made[[Wis 11:25||]]: how much more the rational creature? For He [[1 Tim 2:4|will have all men to be saved|Vult enim omnes homines salvos fieri]], by His antecedent will [God's will considered in itself, before the circumstances of each person, such as his own refusal, are taken into account; contrasted with His consequent will]: and in this sense He loves all, and, as far as lies in Him, wills that none should perish. And so the Father sent His Son for the salvation of all, that all might be converted: and Christ suffered for all as regards sufficiency; but as regards efficacy He endured all things for the elect alone [His passion was enough to save every man, but it actually saves only those who receive its fruit]. Therefore Christ, as His passion drew near, said to the Father: [[John 17:9|I pray not for the world, but for them whom thou hast given me|Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro his quos dedisti mihi]] out of the world, [[John 17:9|because they are thine|quia tui sunt]]. These different senses of "world" must be kept in mind, since they are needed for understanding what is to be said.

paras.t: Denique ad hunc finem dedit Pater omnipotens Filium, ut omnis qui credit in eum, fide per dilectionem operante: nam fides sine operibus mortua est; non pereat, hoc est, non damnetur, sed habeat vitam æternam, quæ est visio summæ Trinitatis per speciem. Unde apud Marcum dicit Salvator: Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit. Et in Actibus Apostolorum Paulus ait Judæis: Per hunc vobis remissio peccatorum annuntiatur, et ab omnibus a quibus non potuistis in lege Moysis justificari. Hinc legitur Christus in Evangelio sæpe dixisse: Fides tua te salvum fecit. Per fidem enim primo conjungitur anima Christo, et ei incorporatur ad cognoscendum et recte sentiendum de ipso, ut sit particeps meriti et gratiæ Christi. Primo siquidem unitur homo Deo per intellectum illuminatum lumine fidei, deinde per voluntatem sive affectum divina caritate formatum. Propter quod Habacuc in secundo capitulo dicit: Qui incredulus est, non erit anima ejus recta in semetipso; justus autem in sua fide vivet. Credimus autem in Christum secundum quod Deus est, quia objectum fidei est veritas prima et increata.
paras.en: Lastly, the almighty Father gave His Son to this end, [[3:16|that whosoever believeth in him|ut omnis qui credit in eum]], with faith that worketh by charity[[Gal 5:6||]] (for [[Jas 2:26|faith without works is dead|fides sine operibus mortua est]][[Jas 2:17||]]), [[3:16|may not perish|non pereat]], that is, may not be damned, [[3:16|but may have life everlasting|sed habeat vitam æternam]], which is the vision of the most high Trinity by sight [that is, face to face, as opposed to by faith]. Hence in Mark the Saviour says: [[Mark 16:16|He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved|Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit]]. And in the Acts of the Apostles Paul says to the Jews: [[Acts 13:38|through him forgiveness of sins is preached to you: and from all the things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses|Per hunc vobis remissio peccatorum annuntiatur, et ab omnibus a quibus non potuistis in lege Moysis justificari]]. Hence we read in the Gospel that Christ often said: [[Mark 10:52|Thy faith hath made thee whole|Fides tua te salvum fecit]][[Matt 9:22||]][[Luke 7:50||]][[Luke 17:19||]] [the margin cites Matth. ix, 22, Marc. x, 52 and two further places, partly unreadable, most likely Luc. vii, 50 and xvii, 19]. For by faith the soul is first joined to Christ and incorporated into Him, so as to know Him and think rightly about Him, that it may share in the merit and grace of Christ. For man is first united to God through the intellect enlightened by the light of faith, and then through the will or affection formed by divine charity. Therefore Habacuc says in the second chapter: [[Hab 2:4|he that is unbelieving, his soul shall not be right in himself: but the just shall live in his faith|Qui incredulus est, non erit anima ejus recta in semetipso; justus autem in sua fide vivet]]. And we believe in Christ inasmuch as He is God, since the object of faith is the first and uncreated Truth.

paras.t: Consequenter declarat Evangelista, quod missio Filii Dei sit effectus paternæ atque divinæ dilectionis ad nos. Non enim misit per incarnationem Deus Pater Filium suum in mundum, hoc est in terram Judææ, seu inter homines. (Deus in hoc evangelio frequenter accipitur personaliter, scilicet pro certa Persona divina; quandoque vero essentialiter, ut quum dicitur: Spiritus est Deus. Nunc vero sumitur personaliter.) Ut Filius judicet mundum, hoc est homines, judicio condemnationis, justitiam exercendo et pœnam infligendo; sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum, videlicet merito conversationis et passionis Christi, cujus virtute et merito purgamur a culpa, et gratia adimplemur. Propter quod Petrus in Actibus Apostolorum ait: Non est aliud nomen datum hominibus, in quo oporteat eos salvos fieri. Præterea, quum Jacobus, et Joannes, cujus est hoc evangelium, zelantes pro Christo, contra quosdam qui eum non receperunt, dixissent: Vis dicimus ut descendat ignis de cœlo, et consumat eos? Christus respondit: Nescitis cujus spiritus estis; Filius enim hominis non venit animas perdere, sed salvare.
paras.en: Next the Evangelist declares that the sending of the Son of God is the effect of the fatherly and divine love towards us. [[3:17|For God sent not|Non enim misit]] (that is, God the Father, through the incarnation) [[3:17|his Son into the world|Filium suum in mundum]], that is, into the land of Judea, or among men. ("God" in this Gospel is often taken personally, that is, for a particular divine Person; but sometimes essentially [for the one divine nature common to the three Persons], as when it is said: [[John 4:24|God is a spirit|Spiritus est Deus]]. Here, however, it is taken personally.) That the Son should [[3:17|judge the world|judicet mundum]], that is, men, with the judgment of condemnation, exercising justice and inflicting punishment; [[3:17|but that the world may be saved by him|sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum]], namely by the merit of Christ's life and passion, by whose power and merit we are cleansed from guilt and filled with grace. Therefore Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: There is [[Acts 4:12|no other name under heaven given to men, whereby we must be saved|Non est aliud nomen datum hominibus, in quo oporteat eos salvos fieri]]. Moreover, when James and John (whose Gospel this is), zealous for Christ against certain men who did not receive Him[[Luke 9:53||]], had said: [[Luke 9:54|wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?|Vis dicimus ut descendat ignis de cœlo, et consumat eos?]] Christ answered: [[Luke 9:55|you know not of what spirit you are|Nescitis cujus spiritus estis]]; [[Luke 9:56|The Son of man came not to destroy souls, but to save|Filius enim hominis non venit animas perdere, sed salvare]].

paras.t: Videtur autem huic obviare, quod infra ait Salvator: Nunc judicium est mundi; et alibi, In judicium ego in hunc mundum veni. Isaias quoque ait: Non secundum visionem oculorum judicabit; sed judicabit in justitia pauperes, et arguet in æquitate pro mansuetis terræ. Et sicut alii Evangelistæ testantur, Christus in primo suo adventu dure et efficaciter redarguebat sacerdotes, Scribas ac Pharisæos. Talis autem redargutio non fit sine judicio, præsertim quum sæpe dixerit, Væ vobis; et denuo, Publicani et meretrices præcedent vos in regno cælorum.
paras.en: But this seems to be contradicted by what the Saviour says further on, [[John 12:31|Now is the judgment of the world|Nunc judicium est mundi]]; and elsewhere, [[John 9:39|For judgment I am come into this world|In judicium ego in hunc mundum veni]]. Isaias also says: [[Is 11:3|He shall not judge according to the sight of the eyes|Non secundum visionem oculorum judicabit]]; [[Is 11:4|But he shall judge the poor with justice, and shall reprove with equity the meek of the earth|sed judicabit in justitia pauperes, et arguet in æquitate pro mansuetis terræ]]. And, as the other Evangelists testify, Christ at His first coming rebuked the priests, Scribes and Pharisees harshly and to great effect. But such rebuke is not made without judgment, especially since He often said, [[Matt 23:13|Woe to you|Væ vobis]] [the margin prints Matth. xxi, probably for xxiii]; and again, [[Matt 21:31|the publicans and the harlots shall go into the kingdom of God before you|Publicani et meretrices præcedent vos in regno cælorum]] [Denis has "the kingdom of heaven"].

paras.t: Dicendum, quod duplex est Christi adventus, videlicet: Primus, quo venit occulte et in humilitate, ut judicaretur et liberaret. Secundus erit manifestus et in majestate, ut judicet atque remuneret. De quo fertur in Psalmo: Deus manifeste veniet, Deus noster, et non silebit; ignis in conspectu ejus exardescet. Judicium quoque est duplex. Est enim judicium discretionis, quo boni a malis secernuntur, malique vituperantur, et pretiosum a vili separatur voto aut merito. De quo Job ait: Numquid qui non amat judicium sanari potest? In hoc judicio impii non resurgunt, quia non surgunt a ruina peccati ad gratiam, judicando hoc modo se ipsos. Istud judicium fuit et fecit Christus in primo suo adventu. Multipliciter enim discrevit inter electos et reprobos, quosdam misericorditer vocando ad suum discipulatum et gratiam, quosdam juste deserendo, qui non erant ex ovibus suis: de quibus et dixit, Sinite illos, cæci sunt, et duces cæcorum. Aliud vero est judicium remunerationis et condemnationis per pœnæ illationem. Hoc Christus non fecit in primo suo adventu; sed in die judicii faciet id communiter, et in morte singulorum facit ipsum particulariter. Per has distinctiones faciliter concordantur auctoritates quæ repugnare videntur.
paras.en: The answer is that Christ's coming is twofold. The first, in which He came hidden and in humility, to be judged and to set free. The second will be manifest and in majesty, to judge and to reward. Of this it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 49:3|God shall come manifestly: our God shall come, and shall not keep silence. A fire shall burn before him|Deus manifeste veniet, Deus noster, et non silebit; ignis in conspectu ejus exardescet]]. Judgment, too, is twofold. There is the judgment of discernment, by which the good are set apart from the wicked, the wicked are reproved, and the precious is separated from the vile, in will or in merit. Of this Job says: [[Job 34:17|Can he be healed that loveth not judgment?|Numquid qui non amat judicium sanari potest]] In this judgment the wicked do not rise again[[Ps 1:5||]], because they do not rise from the ruin of sin to grace, and in this way they judge themselves. This judgment took place, and Christ made it, at His first coming. For He discerned in many ways between the elect and the reprobate, mercifully calling some to His discipleship and grace, and justly forsaking others, who were not of His sheep; of whom He also said, [[Matt 15:14|Let them alone: they are blind, and leaders of the blind|Sinite illos, cæci sunt, et duces cæcorum]]. The other is the judgment of reward and of condemnation by the infliction of punishment. This Christ did not do at His first coming; but on the day of judgment He will do it for all in common, and at the death of each He does it for each in particular. By these distinctions the authorities that seem to conflict are easily reconciled.

paras.t: Qui credit in eum perseveranter, usque ad finem fide et opere manens fidelis, non judicatur judicio reprobationis, sed approbationis, de quo dicit Apostolus: Qui judicat me, Dominus est. Unde in Apocalypsi legitur: Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, et dabo tibi coronam vitæ. Qui autem non credit, jam judicatus est, hoc est divinitus reprobatus. De quo reprobationis judicio Paulus testatur: Eos qui foris sunt Dominus judicabit.
paras.en: [[3:18|He that believeth in him|Qui credit in eum]] perseveringly, remaining faithful to the end in faith and in works, [[3:18|is not judged|non judicatur]] with the judgment of reprobation, but with that of approbation, of which the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 4:4|he that judgeth me is the Lord|Qui judicat me, Dominus est]]. Hence we read in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 2:10|Be thou faithful unto death: and I will give thee the crown of life|Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, et dabo tibi coronam vitæ]]. [[3:18|But he that doth not believe is already judged|Qui autem non credit, jam judicatus est]], that is, reprobated by God. Of this judgment of reprobation Paul testifies: [[1 Cor 5:13|them that are without, God will judge|Eos qui foris sunt Dominus judicabit]].

paras.t: Quæritur, quomodo infidelis jam judicatus dicatur, quum adhuc viator exsistat, necdumque oblatus sit tribunali judicis Christi. Et respondendum, quod dicitur jam judicatus tripliciter: Primo, quoniam pro judicato et reprobato habetur. Secundo, quoniam habet in se causam damnationis adeo evidentem, ut non sit dignum discussionem de ipso peragere. Quum enim careat fide, certum est quod nil meritorium habeat, sed mortali subjaceat culpæ, dummodo sit adultus, præsertim quum dicat Apostolus: Quidquid non est ex fide, peccatum est. Juxta hunc modum loquendi dicimus de homine agonizante vel veneno infecto, quod sit mortuus homo. Tertio, quia futura sunt Deo quasi præsentia, qui omnia conspicit atque præsentialiter cernit in ipso æternitatis momento. Verumtamen in hora mortis judicabitur quantum ad remunerationem seu pœnæ illationem, quantum ad animam, et in die novissimo, quantum ad corpus et animam, quando erit unus eorum quibus dicetur: Ite, maledicti, in ignem æternum. Judicantur insuper infideles post hanc vitam quoad hoc, quod non omnes æqualem sortiuntur miseriam, sed unusquisque juxta mensuram sui delicti, pœnis majoribus vel minoribus deputetur.
paras.en: It is asked how the unbeliever can be said to be already judged, since he is still a wayfarer [viator: one still on the road of this life, not yet at its end], and has not yet been brought before the tribunal of Christ the Judge. The answer is that he is said to be [[3:18|already judged|jam judicatus]] in three ways. First, because he is held as one judged and reprobate. Second, because he has in himself a cause of damnation so evident that it is not worth holding an inquiry about him. For since he lacks faith, it is certain that he has nothing meritorious, but lies under mortal guilt, provided he is an adult; especially since the Apostle says: [[Rom 14:23|all that is not of faith is sin|Quidquid non est ex fide, peccatum est]]. In this manner of speaking we say of a man in his death agony, or infected with poison, that he is a dead man. Third, because things to come are as present to God, who sees all things and beholds them as present in the very instant of eternity. Yet at the hour of death he will be judged as to reward, that is, the infliction of punishment, as regards the soul; and on the last day, as regards body and soul, when he will be one of those to whom it will be said: Go, [[Matt 25:41|you cursed, into everlasting fire|maledicti, in ignem æternum]]. Moreover, unbelievers are judged after this life in this respect, that they do not all receive equal misery, but each is allotted greater or lesser pains according to the measure of his fault.

paras.t: Causa autem cur judicatus jam sit infidelis, subjungitur: quia non credit in nomine unigeniti Filii Dei, hoc est in ipso Filio Dei naturali et unico: et per consequens mendacem facit Deum Patrem, secundum quod Joannes habet: Qui non credit in Filium, mendacem facit Deum, quia non credit in testimonium quod testificatus est Deus de Filio suo.
paras.en: The reason why the unbeliever is already judged is then added: [[3:18|because he believeth not in the name of the only begotten Son of God|quia non credit in nomine unigeniti Filii Dei]], that is, in the very Son of God, natural and only; and consequently he makes God the Father a liar, as John has it: [[1 John 5:10|He that believeth not the Son maketh him a liar: because he believeth not in the testimony which God hath testified of his Son|Qui non credit in Filium, mendacem facit Deum, quia non credit in testimonium quod testificatus est Deus de Filio suo]].

paras.t: Istud si universaliter atque simpliciter intelligatur, consequens esset quod nemo unquam salvatus est sine explicita fide Christi futuri, præsentis vel missi. Cujus contrarium tenent doctores, asserentes quod ante Christi adventum, simplicibus sufficiebat implicita fides de Christo, cum observantia legis naturalis quoad gentiles, vel scriptæ quoad Judæos, qui secundum quosdam, tenebantur ad explicitam fidem de Christo in generali: ita quod sufficiebat credere esse vitam post hanc vitam, et quod Deus haberet providentiam atque judicium actuum humanorum, et saluti hominum provideret secundum modum sibi placentem et ab ipso præordinatum. Unde Cornelius centurio tali fide placuit Deo. Erat enim vir religiosus et bonus, cujus orationes et eleemosynæ commemoratæ fuerunt coram Deo: et tamen nondum scivit determinate aliquid loqui de Christo. — Et respondendum, quod si verba Evangelistæ intelligantur de explicita fide Filii Dei, non erunt de omnibus hominibus intelligenda, sed de majoribus, puta Prophetis et Patriarchis, et eruditis ab illis, pro tempore legis scriptæ. Tempore autem evangelicæ legis omnes tenentur ad explicitam fidem de Christo et Trinitate. Idcirco jam nemo valet salvari nisi explicita fide de unigenito Filio Dei.
paras.en: If this were understood universally and without qualification, it would follow that no one has ever been saved without explicit faith in Christ, as to come, as present, or as sent. But the doctors hold the contrary, asserting that before Christ's coming an implicit faith in Christ [that is, faith contained within a more general belief, without distinct knowledge of Him] sufficed for the simple, together with the observance of the natural law in the case of the Gentiles, or of the written law in the case of the Jews, who, according to some, were bound to an explicit faith in Christ in general: so that it sufficed to believe that there is a life after this life, and that God has providence over human acts and judges them, and provides for the salvation of men in the way that pleases Him and that He has foreordained. Thus Cornelius the centurion pleased God by such a faith. For he was a religious and good man[[Acts 10:2||]], whose prayers and alms were remembered before God[[Acts 10:31||]][[Acts 10:4||]] [the margin's verse numbers are partly misread; Acts 10:2, 31 and 4 fit the words]; and yet he could not yet say anything definite about Christ. — The answer is that if the Evangelist's words are understood of explicit faith in the Son of God, they are not to be understood of all men, but of the greater ones, such as the Prophets and Patriarchs and those taught by them, for the time of the written law. But in the time of the law of the Gospel all are bound to explicit faith in Christ and in the Trinity. Therefore no one can now be saved except by explicit faith in the only-begotten Son of God.

paras.t: Hoc est autem judicium, hoc est, istud quod subditur, est causa meritoria judicii reprobationis infidelium omniumque perversorum: quia lux, hoc est Christus lux vera illuminans omnem hominem qui illuminatur. De quo dicit Michæas propheta: Quum sedero in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est. Et Apostolus dicit: Quum sit splendor gloriæ. Imo Pater, et Filius et Spiritus Sanctus, sunt una lux. Lux ergo, videlicet Verbum et Sapientia Patris, venit in mundum per incarnationis mysterium, et in terris visa, atque cum hominibus conversata est lux ista, assumpta humanitate velata. Christus quoque secundum naturam assumptam, est lux ineffabiliter clarior Apostolis, quibus dictum est: Vos estis lux mundi.
paras.en: [[3:19|And this is the judgment|Hoc est autem judicium]], that is, what follows is the meritorious cause [that is, the cause that merits it] of the judgment of reprobation of unbelievers and of all the perverse: [[3:19|Because the light|quia lux]], that is, Christ, [[John 1:9|the true light, which enlighteneth every man|lux vera illuminans omnem hominem]] that is enlightened; of whom the prophet Micheas says: [[Mich 7:8|when I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light|Quum sedero in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est]]. And the Apostle says: [[Heb 1:3|being the brightness of his glory|Quum sit splendor gloriæ]]. Indeed, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost are one light. [[3:19|The light|Lux]] therefore, namely the Word and Wisdom of the Father, [[3:19|is come into the world|venit in mundum]] through the mystery of the Incarnation; and this light, veiled in the humanity it assumed, was [[Bar 3:38|seen upon earth, and conversed with men|in terris visa, atque cum hominibus conversata est]]. Christ also, according to the nature He assumed, is a light[[John 9:5||]] ineffably brighter than the Apostles, to whom it was said: [[Matt 5:14|You are the light of the world|Vos estis lux mundi]].

paras.t: Et dilexerunt homines pro majori parte, non tamen omnes simpliciter, magis tenebras, hoc est passiones et vitia rationem obtenebrantia atque ad infernales tenebras perducentia, quam lucem, hoc est Christum, seu ejus doctrinam ac virtutum splendorem. De qualibus scriptum est in Job: Ipsi fuerunt rebelles lumini. Quicumque præfert concupiscentiam rationi, carnalem voluptatem spirituali consolationi, bonum creatum, caducum et variabile, bono divino, æterno et infinito: iste diligit tenebras magis quam lucem. Et qui peccata commissa potius vult occultare et prosequi quam humiliter confiteri, præfert absconsionem tenebrarum suarum manifestationi lucifluæ confessionis. Ideo Salomon in Proverbiis testatur: Qui abscondit scelera sua, non dirigetur; qui autem confessus fuerit et reliquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur. Et sanctus Job: Vias (inquit) meas in conspectu ejus arguam, et ipse erit salvator meus. Erant enim eorum mala opera, hoc est vitiosa: sicque ex electione mali et habitu vitioso peccabant, gloriantes in malis, suisque iniquitatibus firmiter adhærentes.
paras.en: [[3:19|And men loved|Et dilexerunt homines]], for the greater part, though not all without exception, [[3:19|darkness|magis tenebras]], that is, the passions and vices that darken the reason and lead to the darkness of hell, [[3:19|rather than the light|quam lucem]], that is, Christ, or His teaching and the splendour of the virtues. Of such it is written in Job: [[Job 24:13|They have been rebellious to the light|Ipsi fuerunt rebelles lumini]]. Whoever prefers concupiscence to reason, carnal pleasure to spiritual consolation, a created good, perishable and changeable, to the divine good, eternal and infinite, loves darkness rather than light. And he who would rather hide the sins he has committed and go on in them than humbly confess them, prefers the hiding of his darkness to the bright manifestation of confession. Therefore Solomon testifies in Proverbs: [[Prov 28:13|He that hideth his sins, shall not prosper: but he that shall confess, and forsake them, shall obtain mercy.|Qui abscondit scelera sua non dirigetur; qui autem confessus fuerit et reliquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur.]] And holy Job: [[Job 13:15|I will reprove my ways in his sight|Vias (inquit) meas in conspectu ejus arguam]], he says, [[Job 13:16|and he shall be my saviour|et ipse erit salvator meus]]. [[3:19|For their works were evil|Erant enim eorum mala opera]], that is, vicious: and so they sinned from choice of evil and from a vicious habit, glorying in evil things and clinging firmly to their iniquities.

paras.t: Sed quum dicat Dionysius, Nemo respiciens ad malum operatur, et nihil appetitur nisi bonum, quomodo potest quis plus diligere tenebras quam lucem, seu vitium quam virtutem? Et respondendum, quod nemo respiciens ad malum, operatur illud, hoc est, non perpetrat nec appetit malum, nisi sub ratione alicujus boni apparentis, utpote delectabilis, vel utilis. Propter quod Salomon ait: Via stulti recta in oculis ejus.
paras.en: But since Dionysius says, "No one acts with his eye on evil," and nothing is desired except the good, how can anyone love darkness more than light, or vice more than virtue? The answer is that no one does evil with his eye on evil, that is, no one commits or desires evil except under the aspect [sub ratione: as having the character] of some apparent good, as pleasant or useful. That is why Solomon says: [[Prov 12:15|The way of a fool is right in his own eyes|Via stulti recta in oculis ejus]].

paras.t: Omnis enim qui male agit, non solum ex infirmitate, vel ignorantia, sed ex certa malitia, seu habitu pravo, odit lucem, id est justitiam veramque doctrinam, et etiam Christum aliquando, quem vellet non esse, ut possit pœnas futuras evadere, et non venit ad lucem, hoc est ad peccatorum suorum salutarem ac lucidam confessionem; vel, non venit in publicum, ex verecundia aut timore pœnarum; ut non arguantur, id est, reprehendantur seu corrigantur a prælatis et justis hominibus, opera ejus tenebrosa.
paras.en: [[3:20|For every one that doth evil|Omnis enim qui male agit]], not only from weakness or ignorance but from certain malice [ex certa malitia: sin committed knowingly and by deliberate choice], or from a depraved habit, [[3:20|hateth the light|odit lucem]], that is, justice and true teaching, and sometimes even Christ, whom he would wish not to exist, so that he might escape the punishments to come; [[3:20|and cometh not to the light|et non venit ad lucem]], that is, to the saving and lucid confession of his sins; or, he does not come out into the open, from shame or fear of punishment; [[3:20|that his works may not be reproved|ut non arguantur opera ejus]], that is, that his dark works may not be rebuked or corrected by prelates and just men.

paras.t: Sed his contrariari videtur, quod asserit Isaias: Peccatum suum quasi Sodoma prædicaverunt, nec absconderunt. Et obstinato populo loquitur Jeremias: Frons mulieris meretricis facta est tibi, noluisti erubescere. Tales utique, testante Salomone, Lætantur quum malefecerint, et sine ullo timore perpetrant mala. Veniunt ergo ad publicum, et in præsentia hominum peccare non erubescunt. — Et respondendum, quod verba præinducta universaliter vera sunt, sed de diversis generibus male agentium diversimode verificantur. Aliqui enim adeo mali sunt, ut respuant increpari, juxta illud Amos: Odio habuerunt corripientem. Isti publice peccant, et sæpe peccasse se jactant. Alii sunt hypocritæ, simulatores et callidi, humana vituperia magis quam divinum judicium formidantes. Isti peccant in abditis, dicente Apostolo: Quæ in occulto fiunt ab ipsis, turpe est dicere. Alii sunt famuli Dei, sed imperfecti, non ambulantes timorate et satis sollicite coram Deo, sed cum observantia debitorum seu præceptorum contenti. Isti multa venialia faciunt in secreto, quæ nequaquam facerent præsentibus aliis; et interdum non veniunt ad lucem ex verecundia, ne confundantur. Unde quicumque peccat, aliquo modo odit lucem et refugit eam, loquendo de peccatis a quibus homo merito denominatur peccator. Nihilominus sunt aliqui viri virtuosi tam ferventes et humiles, quod semper parati sunt increpari, et cupiunt sua peccata manifestare, correctionemque pati pronissimi sunt.
paras.en: But this seems to be contradicted by what Isaias asserts: [[Is 3:9|they have proclaimed abroad their sin as Sodom, and they have not hid it|peccatum suum quasi Sodoma prædicaverunt, nec absconderunt]]. And Jeremias says to an obstinate people: [[Jer 3:3|thou hadst a harlot's forehead, thou wouldst not blush|Frons mulieris meretricis facta est tibi, noluisti erubescere]]. Such men indeed, as Solomon testifies, [[Prov 2:14|are glad when they have done evil|Lætantur quum malefecerint]], and [[Eccles 8:11|commit evils without any fear|sine ullo timore perpetrant mala]]. They come out, then, into the open, and are not ashamed to sin in the presence of men. — The answer is that the words cited above are universally true, but they are verified in different ways of the different kinds of evildoers. For some are so wicked that they spurn being rebuked, according to that saying of Amos: [[Amos 5:10|They have hated him that rebuketh|Odio habuerunt corripientem]]. These sin publicly, and often boast of having sinned. Others are hypocrites, dissemblers and crafty men, who fear human reproach more than the judgment of God. These sin in hidden places, as the Apostle says: [[Eph 5:12|the things that are done by them in secret, it is a shame even to speak of|Quæ in occulto fiunt ab ipsis, turpe est dicere]]. Others are servants of God, but imperfect ones, who do not walk fearfully and carefully enough before God, but are content with keeping what is owed, that is, the commandments. These commit many venial sins in secret which they would never commit in the presence of others; and at times they do not come to the light out of shame, lest they be put to confusion. Hence whoever sins in some way hates the light and flees from it, speaking of those sins on account of which a man is rightly called a sinner. Nevertheless there are some virtuous men so fervent and humble that they are always ready to be rebuked, and desire to make their sins known, and are most willing to undergo correction.

paras.t: Qui autem facit veritatem doctrinæ et vitæ atque justitiæ, hoc est, qui vera loquitur, et eadem operatur, justitiamque sectatur. Triplex enim est veritas, scilicet doctrinæ, vitæ, et justitiæ; et quælibet harum est suo modo facienda. Venit ad lucem, hoc est, apparere non erubescit, lucem sapientiæ sequitur, et coram aliis exemplarem se exhibet, ut manifestentur opera ejus ad gloriam Dei ædificationemque proximi, quia in Deo sunt facta, id est secundum voluntatem Dei, quæ nobis in Scripturis declaratur. Istud præcipue verum est de operibus bonis ad quæ aliquis obligatur, quæ nullam singularitatem prætendunt, et sine nota vanitatis possunt manifestari. De his enim ait Salvator: Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant opera vestra bona, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cælis est.
paras.en: [[3:21|But he that doth truth|qui autem facit veritatem]] of doctrine and of life and of justice, that is, he who speaks true things, and does the same, and pursues justice. For truth is threefold: namely, of doctrine, of life and of justice; and each of these is to be done in its own way. [[3:21|cometh to the light|venit ad lucem]], that is, he is not ashamed to appear, he follows the light of wisdom, and shows himself an example before others, [[3:21|that his works may be made manifest|ut manifestentur opera ejus]] to the glory of God and the edification of his neighbour, [[3:21|because they are done in God|quia in Deo sunt facta]], that is, according to the will of God, which is declared to us in the Scriptures. This is true above all of the good works to which one is bound, which make no show of singularity and can be made known without any taint of vanity. For of these the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:16|So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven|Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant opera vestra bona, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cælis est]].

paras.t: Sed si omnis qui facit veritatem venit ad lucem ut manifestentur opera ejus, quid est quod aliqui de bonis actibus verecundantur? Sunt enim nonnulli, qui si a suis consortibus inveniantur orare, confiteri, vel aliquid devotionis peragere, erubescunt, cupientes latere, non tam ex humilitate, quam ex humano rubore. Denique sunt aliqui solitarii et inclusi, optimæ vitæ, qui nunquam in publicum veniunt. Et multi ex vera humilitate abscondunt bona quæ operantur. Unde et Christus jubet in cubiculo, id est in loco absconso, orare. Et rursus: Videte, ait, ne justitiam vestram faciatis coram hominibus, ut videamini ab illis.
paras.en: But if everyone [[3:21|that doth truth cometh to the light, that his works may be made manifest|qui facit veritatem venit ad lucem ut manifestentur opera ejus]], how is it that some are ashamed of good acts? For there are some who, if they are found by their companions praying, confessing, or doing some act of devotion, blush and wish to be hidden, not so much out of humility as out of human shame. Then there are some solitaries and recluses, of the best life, who never come out into the open. And many out of true humility hide the good they do. Hence Christ too bids us pray in the chamber, that is, in a hidden place[[Matt 6:6||]]. And again He says: [[Matt 6:1|Take heed that you do not your justice before men, to be seen by them|Videte, ait, ne justitiam vestram faciatis coram hominibus, ut videamini ab illis]].

paras.t: Dicendum, quod verba hæc evangelica verissima sunt atque pulcherrima, sed de diversis justorum generibus verificantur variis modis. Primo enim universaliter verum est, quod quicumque facit veritatem, id est, meritorie operatur, venit ad lucem, quæ Christus est, ut manifestentur a Christo opera ejus in die judicii, quando laus erit unicuique a Deo, et ut Christus confiteatur eum coram Patre suo cælesti. Rursus, quicumque sic agit, venit ad lucem, id est ad rectæ rationis judicium, ut manifestentur opera ejus pro loco, causa et tempore, scilicet quando ratio dictat, et caritas exigit. Qui vero de actibus bonis non excedentibus communem devotionem verecundantur, sunt homines pusilli et imperfecti, qui apprehendunt bonum honestum sub ratione rei turpis, in quantum formidant propter bona opera derideri. Solitarii autem veniunt ad lucem interiorem, quamvis non veniunt ad humanos adspectus. Porro verba Salvatoris intelligenda sunt quantum ad intentionem, videlicet, ut non oremus nec bona agamus ad hunc finem, quatenus videamur et commendemur a proximis, sed ad gloriam Dei, propriamque salutem, et proximorum ædificationem.
paras.en: The answer is that these words of the Gospel are most true and most beautiful, but they are verified in various ways of the different kinds of the just. For first, it is universally true that whoever [[3:21|doth truth|facit veritatem]], that is, works meritoriously, [[3:21|cometh to the light|venit ad lucem]], which is Christ[[John 9:5||]], [[3:21|that his works may be made manifest|ut manifestentur opera ejus]] by Christ on the day of judgment, when [[1 Cor 4:5|then shall every man have praise from God|laus erit unicuique a Deo]], and that Christ may confess him before His heavenly Father[[Matt 10:32||]]. Again, whoever acts in this way comes to the light, that is, to the judgment of right reason, so that his works are made manifest according to place, cause and time, namely when reason dictates and charity requires. But those who are ashamed of good acts that do not go beyond common devotion are small-souled and imperfect men, who take what is good and honourable [bonum honestum: the good that is worthy for its own sake, as distinct from the useful or the pleasant] under the aspect of something shameful, in so far as they fear being mocked for their good works. The solitaries, for their part, come to the inner light, though they do not come before the eyes of men. Further, the Saviour's words are to be understood with regard to the intention: namely, that we should not pray or do good for this end, that we may be seen and praised by our neighbours, but for the glory of God, our own salvation, and the edification of our neighbours.

paras.t: Elucescit ex his, quod justitia est res audax, secura, fiducialis, jucunda et victoriosa. Injustitia vero contrario modo se habet. Propter quod scriptum est: Quum sit timida nequitia, dat testimonium condemnata; semper enim præsumit sæva, perturbata conscientia. Hinc etiam Job ait: Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii; et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur. Nec dissonat quod Salomon Proverbiorum vicesimo octavo adstruit: Fugit impius nemine persequente; justus autem quasi leo confidens absque terrore erit. Ideo dicit Apostolus: Vis non timere potestatem? fac bene, et habebis laudem ex ea. Propterea quoque ait Philosophus, quod qui bene se habent in divinis, sunt melioris fiduciæ. Audiamus vocem justi venientis ad lucem, et sciemus quanta sit securæ mentis fiducia. Ecce apud Isaiam ait vir justus: Juxta est qui justificat me, quis contradicit mihi? Stemus simul, quis est adversarius meus? accedat ad me. Ecce Dominus Deus auxiliator meus, quis est qui condemnet me? Tales fuerunt martyres sancti, qui facientes veritatem legis et fidei christianæ, venerunt ad lucem, quoniam non erubuerunt Christum ejusque sermones, sed confessi sunt eum coram hominibus: ideo Christus confitetur eos coram Patre suo, sicque manifestat eorum opera bona.
paras.en: It is clear from this that justice is a bold thing, secure, confident, joyful and victorious. Injustice behaves in the contrary way. Wherefore it is written: [[Wis 17:10|For whereas wickedness is fearful, it beareth witness of its condemnation: for a troubled conscience always forecasteth grievous things|Quum sit timida nequitia, dat testimonium condemnata; semper enim præsumit sæva, perturbata conscientia]]. Hence also Job says: [[Job 15:21|The sound of dread is always in his ears: and when there is peace, he always suspecteth treason|Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii; et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur]]. Nor does what Solomon lays down in the twenty-eighth chapter of Proverbs disagree: [[Prov 28:1|The wicked man fleeth, when no man pursueth: but the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread|Fugit impius nemine persequente; justus autem quasi leo confidens absque terrore erit]]. Therefore the Apostle says: [[Rom 13:3|Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? Do that which is good: and thou shalt have praise from the same|Vis non timere potestatem? fac bene, et habebis laudem ex ea]]. For this reason too the Philosopher says that those who stand well in divine things are of greater confidence. Let us hear the voice of the just man coming to the light, and we shall know how great is the confidence of a secure mind. Behold, in Isaias the just man says: [[Is 50:8|He is near that justifieth me, who will contend with me? let us stand together, who is my adversary? let him come near to me|Juxta est qui justificat me, quis contradicit mihi? Stemus simul, quis est adversarius meus? accedat ad me]]. [[Is 50:9|Behold the Lord God is my helper: who is he that shall condemn me|Ecce Dominus Deus auxiliator meus, quis est qui condemnet me]]? Such were the holy martyrs, who, doing the truth of the law and of the Christian faith, came to the light, since they were not ashamed of Christ and His words, but confessed Him before men: therefore Christ confesses them before His Father[[Matt 10:32||]] [the margin reads Matt. x, 33; the words answer to v. 32], and so makes their good works manifest.

3.title: Explanatio residuæ partis hujus capituli tertii, ab eo loco quo dicitur: Post hæc venit Jesus et discipuli ejus in terram Judæam.
3.title_en: Explanation of the remaining part of this third chapter, from the place where it is said: “After these things Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea.”

paras.t: Descripto sermone quem habuit Christus cum Nicodemo, aliquibus forsitan verbis ab Evangelista adjectis, nunc consequenter ostenditur exordium usus Baptismatis evangelicæ legis; et quid Joannes Baptista de Christo perhibuit, plenius edocetur. Post hæc, videlicet consummato sermone præscripto quem habuit ad Nicodemum Salvator, venit Jesus et discipuli ejus in terram Judæam, hoc est ad alia loca Judææ. Postquam enim fuit in civitate Judæorum metropoli, puta Jerusalem, ubi Nicodemum instruxit, processit ad alia loca ejusdem provinciæ, ut ibi prædicaret. Sed quum Jerusalem sit principalis urbs Judææ, quidam dixerunt quod Christus venit post prædicta in Judæam, non statim et immediate, sed postquam Galilæam intravit. Et illic demorabatur cum eis in domibus alienis, tanquam pauper et hospes, quia non habuit ubi caput reclinaret.
paras.en: The discourse that Christ held with Nicodemus having been described, some words perhaps being added by the Evangelist, there is now shown in consequence the beginning of the use of the Baptism of the Gospel law; and what John the Baptist bore witness to concerning Christ is more fully taught. [[3:22|After these things|Post hæc]], that is, once the discourse set down above which the Saviour held with Nicodemus was finished, [[3:22|Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea|venit Jesus et discipuli ejus in terram Judæam]], that is, to other places of Judea. For after He had been in the chief city of the Jews, namely Jerusalem, where He instructed Nicodemus, He went on to other places of the same province, to preach there. But since Jerusalem is the principal city of Judea, some have said that Christ came into Judea after the things related above, not straightway and immediately, but after He had entered Galilee. [[3:22|and there he abode with them|Et illic demorabatur cum eis]], in other men's houses, as a poor man and a guest, because He had not [[Matt 8:20|where to lay his head|ubi caput reclinaret]].

paras.t: Et baptizabat. Secundum Chrysostomum, Christus in propria persona non baptizavit, quia sequenti capitulo scribitur: Quanquam Jesus non baptizaret, sed discipuli ejus. Dicitur tamen baptizasse quia discipulis suis officium baptizandi commisit: quemadmodum rex facere dicitur quod facit per suos ministros. Dicit quoque Chrysostomus, quod discipuli baptizabant, non Baptismate Christi, sed Joannis, quia secundum positionem hanc, Baptisma Christi nondum fuerat institutum. Habet enim efficaciam a merito passionis dominicæ, quæ tunc nondum erat peracta. Et Apostolis dixit Christus post resurrectionem, quando ascendit: Joannes baptizavit aqua, vos autem baptizabimini Spiritu Sancto. Si autem Christus propriis manibus non baptizavit Apostolos, ergo nec aliquem alium.
paras.en: [[3:22|and baptized|Et baptizabat]]. According to Chrysostom, Christ did not baptize in His own person, because it is written in the following chapter: [[John 4:2|Though Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples|Quanquam Jesus non baptizaret, sed discipuli ejus]]. Yet He is said to have baptized because He committed the office of baptizing to His disciples, just as a king is said to do what he does through his ministers. Chrysostom says also that the disciples baptized, not with the Baptism of Christ, but with that of John, because, according to this position, the Baptism of Christ had not yet been instituted. For it has its efficacy from the merit of the Lord's passion, which had not yet then been accomplished. And Christ said to the Apostles after the resurrection, when He ascended: [[Acts 1:5|John indeed baptized with water: but you shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost|Joannes baptizavit aqua, vos autem baptizabimini Spiritu Sancto]]. But if Christ did not baptize the Apostles with His own hands, then neither did He baptize anyone else.

paras.t: Sed melius videtur ut cum Augustino dicamus, quod Christus primo per se ipsum baptizavit, præsertim Apostolos aliosque discipulos suos. Nec dubium quin proprio Baptismate gratiam conferente baptizaverit. Instituit enim sacramenta novæ legis per se ipsum, et exercuit ea, saltem quædam eorum. Postmodum vero commisit Apostolis Baptismatis sui exercitium, et ipse altioribus intendebat, videlicet doctrinæ et prædicationis officio. Quod et Apostoli post resurrectionem sæpe fecisse leguntur, quando multos converterunt, ne per baptizandi officium, quod ab inferioribus atque indoctioribus fieri potuit, a verbo prædicationis impedirentur. Unde ad Corinthios Paulus testatur: Neminem vestrum baptizavi, nisi Crispum et Caium, et Stephanæ domum; non enim misit me Christus baptizare, sed evangelizare. Nec obstat quod ait Salvator Apostolis: Docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti. Hoc quippe intelligendum est, quod baptizarent eas per se, vel per suos adjutores atque discipulos. — Postremo, quod objicitur, de facili solvitur. Passio enim Christi hoc contulit futura, quod præstat jam facta. Tota enim efficacia ac idoneitas meriti Christi, fuit a persona Verbi præsentialiter, quæ æterna est, et unius potestatis ante passionem et postea. Quod vero Apostolis dictum est, Vos autem baptizabimini Spiritu Sancto, intelligitur de interiori perfusione gratiæ Spiritus Sancti sub signo visibili.
paras.en: But it seems better to say with Augustine that Christ at first baptized by Himself, especially the Apostles and His other disciples. Nor is there any doubt that He baptized with His own Baptism, which confers grace. For He instituted the sacraments of the new law by Himself, and exercised them, at least some of them. Afterwards, however, He committed the exercise of His Baptism to the Apostles, and Himself gave His attention to higher things, namely to the office of teaching and preaching. And the Apostles too are read to have often done this after the resurrection, when they converted many, lest they should be hindered from the word of preaching by the office of baptizing, which could be done by lesser and less learned men. Hence Paul testifies to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 1:14|I baptized none of you but Crispus and Caius|Neminem vestrum baptizavi, nisi Crispum et Caium]], and [[1 Cor 1:16|the household of Stephanus|Stephanæ domum]]; [[1 Cor 1:17|For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel|non enim misit me Christus baptizare, sed evangelizare]]. Nor does it stand in the way that the Saviour says to the Apostles: [[Matt 28:19|teach ye all nations: baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost|Docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti]]. For this is to be understood to mean that they should baptize them by themselves, or through their helpers and disciples. — Lastly, the objection is easily answered. For the passion of Christ, while yet to come, conferred the same thing that it bestows once accomplished. For the whole efficacy and fitness of Christ's merit came from the Person of the Word, as already present [præsentialiter: that is, the merit drew its power from the Person, who is always present, and not only from the passion once it had taken place], which is eternal and of one and the same power before the passion and after it. And what was said to the Apostles, [[Acts 1:5|you shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost|Vos autem baptizabimini Spiritu Sancto]], is understood of the inward outpouring of the grace of the Holy Ghost under a visible sign [that is, at Pentecost].

paras.t: Erat autem et Joannes baptizans in Ænnon, id est loco sic dicto, juxta Salim, urbem sitam prope Jordanem, quia aquæ multæ erant illic, videlicet juxta Salim. Erat enim ibi lacus, secundum Bedam, et ideo fuit locus ad baptizandum conveniens. Et veniebant Judæi ad Joannem, et baptizabantur ab eo. Nondum enim missus fuerat Joannes in carcerem ab Herode tetrarcha, qui ad Herodiadis suggestionem incarceravit Joannem, ut Marcus refert. Per hoc innuit Evangelista, quod omnia a se hucusque descripta de actibus Christi, sunt ab aliis Evangelistis omissa, qui sic loquuntur de Christo ac si post incarcerationem Joannis incepisset prædicare et signa peragere.
paras.en: [[3:23|And John also was baptizing in Ennon|Erat autem et Joannes baptizans in Ænnon]], that is, in a place so called, [[3:23|near Salim|juxta Salim]], a city situated near the Jordan, [[3:23|because there was much water there|quia aquæ multæ erant illic]], namely near Salim. For there was a lake there, according to Bede, and therefore it was a place suitable for baptizing. [[3:23|And they came|Et veniebant]] (the Jews to John) [[3:23|and were baptized|et baptizabantur]] by him. [[3:24|For John was not yet cast into prison|Nondum enim missus fuerat Joannes in carcerem]] by Herod the tetrarch, who imprisoned John at the prompting of Herodias, as Mark relates[[Mark 6:17||]]. By this the Evangelist intimates that all the things he has described so far of the deeds of Christ were left out by the other Evangelists, who speak of Christ as though He had begun to preach and to work signs after the imprisonment of John.

paras.t: Facta est ergo quæstio, hoc est, ex quo Christus baptizabat per se et per suos Apostolos, idcirco mota est quæstio contentiosa ex indiscreto zelo procedens, ex discipulis, id est ab aliquibus de numero discipulorum, Joannis Baptistæ, cum Judæis qui baptizabantur a Christo, de purificatione, hoc est de baptismo, qui est lotio purgans. Baptismus autem Christi vere intus purificat: unde activa purificatio appellatur. Ista quæstio fuit, cujus baptismus esset præstantior, Christi vel Joannis. Joannis namque discipuli volentes magistrum suum præferre, dixerunt quod ejus baptismus dignior esset.
