Judæi autem baptizati a Christo, dixerunt oppositum: scientes quale testimonium perhibuisset Joannes Christo, dicens, Ego baptizo vos aqua, ille baptizabit vos Spiritu Sancto; et etiam quia Joannes venientes ad se misit ad Jesum, ut baptizarentur ab eo, non autem misit Christus venientes ad se ad Joannem.
paras.en: [[3:25|And there arose a question|Facta est ergo quæstio]], that is, since Christ was baptizing by Himself and by His Apostles, there was therefore stirred up a contentious question, proceeding from an indiscreet zeal, [[3:25|of John's disciples|ex discipulis]], that is, by some of the number of the disciples of John the Baptist, [[3:25|and the Jews|cum Judæis]] who were being baptized by Christ, [[3:25|concerning purification|de purificatione]], that is, concerning baptism, which is a cleansing washing. Now the baptism of Christ truly purifies within: hence it is called an active purification [that is, one that itself cleanses, and does not merely signify cleansing]. The question was this: whose baptism was the more excellent, Christ's or John's. For John's disciples, wishing to prefer their master, said that his baptism was the worthier. But the Jews baptized by Christ said the opposite, knowing what testimony John had borne to Christ, saying, [[Mark 1:8|I have baptized you with water: but he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost|Ego baptizo vos aqua, ille baptizabit vos Spiritu Sancto]]; and also because John sent those who came to him to Jesus, to be baptized by Him, whereas Christ did not send those who came to Him to John.

paras.t: Et venerunt discipuli Joannis ad Joannem, ut quæstionem hanc solveret, propriique baptismi honorem defenderet; et dixerunt ei, dolentes et querulantes quod honor magistri sui, et per consequens honor eorum, minueretur: Rabbi, qui erat tecum trans Jordanem (sicut superius dictum est), cui tu testimonium perhibuisti, dicendo, Ecce Agnus Dei; ecce hic baptizat, per se et suos discipulos, et omnes veniunt ad eum, hoc est tam multi, ut pene nulli videantur qui te accedunt, quia et tu ipse mittis tuos ad eum. Quasi dicant: Ibi frequentia, hic paucitas; illi honor impenditur, tu incipis parvi pendi: et tu ipse es in causa, quia sic illum verbis tuis magnificasti. Isti discipuli Joannis nondum perfecti fuerunt, sed aliquid invidentiæ inerat eis, ægre ferentibus quod Christus et ejus discipuli Joanni et ejus discipulis præferebantur. Unde sæpe conjunxerunt se Pharisæis, quos noverant æmulos Christi, contra Jesum, sicut Matthæus habet: Accesserunt ad Jesum discipuli Joannis, dicentes: Quare nos et Pharisæi jejunamus frequenter, tui autem discipuli non jejunant?
paras.en: [[3:26|And they came|Et venerunt]] (the disciples of John) [[3:26|to John|ad Joannem]], that he might settle this question and defend the honour of his own baptism; [[3:26|and said to him|et dixerunt ei]], grieving and complaining that the honour of their master, and in consequence their own honour, was being lessened: [[3:26|Rabbi, he that was with thee beyond the Jordan|Rabbi, qui erat tecum trans Jordanem]] (as was said above), [[3:26|to whom thou gavest testimony|cui tu testimonium perhibuisti]], by saying, [[John 1:29|Behold the Lamb of God|Ecce Agnus Dei]][[John 1:36||]]; [[3:26|behold, he baptizeth|ecce hic baptizat]], by Himself and His disciples, [[3:26|and all men come to him|et omnes veniunt ad eum]], that is, so many that hardly any seem to be left who come to thee, because thou thyself also sendest thine own to Him. As if they said: There, a throng; here, a few; honour is paid to Him, thou beginnest to be thought little of: and thou thyself art the cause of it, because thou hast so magnified Him by thy words. These disciples of John were not yet perfect, but there was some envy in them, who took it ill that Christ and His disciples were preferred to John and his disciples. Hence they often joined themselves with the Pharisees, whom they knew to be Christ's rivals, against Jesus, as Matthew has it: [[Matt 9:14|Then came to him the disciples of John, saying: Why do we and the Pharisees, fast often, but thy disciples do not fast?|Accesserunt ad Jesum discipuli Joannis, dicentes: Quare nos et Pharisæi jejunamus frequenter, tui autem discipuli non jejunant?]]

paras.t: Deinceps Joannes Baptista benigne docet et corrigit suos discipulos. Respondit Joannes, et dixit: Non potest homo accipere quidquam, hoc est, nihil boni habere vel accipere potest, nisi fuerit ei datum de cælo, hoc est a Deo concessum, mediate vel immediate. Omnia etenim bona, cuncta dona naturæ, universa munera gratiæ, a Deo sublimi et benedicto fontaliter profluunt. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Quid habes quod non accepisti? Et: Non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis; sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est. Et apud Osee loquitur Deus: Perditio tua ex te, in me tantummodo auxilium tuum. Quamvis homo universaliter ita sit, tamen Joannes id dicit de semetipso, tanquam dicat: Ego quum homo sim, potestatem baptizandi non habeo nisi ex Deo; ille quum Deus sit, propria auctoritate baptizat: ideo mihi non derogatur, dum ille præ me honoratur; nec debetis hoc impatienter accipere.
paras.en: Next, John the Baptist gently teaches and corrects his disciples. [[3:27|John answered and said|Respondit Joannes, et dixit]]: [[3:27|A man cannot receive any thing|Non potest homo accipere quidquam]], that is, he can have or receive nothing good, [[3:27|unless it be given him from heaven|nisi fuerit ei datum de cælo]], that is, granted by God, mediately or immediately. For all good things, all the gifts of nature, all the bestowals of grace, flow from God most high and blessed as from their fountainhead. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 4:7|what hast thou that thou hast not received|Quid habes quod non accepisti?]]? And: [[2 Cor 3:5|Not that we are sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves: but our sufficiency is from God|Non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis; sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est]]. And in Osee God says: [[Osee 13:9|Destruction is thy own|Perditio tua]]: [[Osee 13:9|thy help is only in me|tantummodo auxilium tuum]] [the margin prints Osee xi, 9; the words are those of Osee 13:9]. Although this holds of man universally, John nevertheless says it of himself, as if to say: Since I am a man, I have the power of baptizing only from God; He, since He is God, baptizes by His own authority. So nothing is taken from me while He is honoured above me; nor ought you to take this impatiently.

paras.t: Ipsi vos mihi testimonium perhibetis, qui verba mea de Christo dicta audistis, quod dixerim, audientibus vobis, coram turba: Non sum ego Christus, id est: non sum filius naturalis et unicus, magnum mihi est esse filium adoptivum; non sum finis, sed via et medium ad finem deducens; non sum Salvator, sed servus, gratia ejus indigens, cui et dixi: Ego a te debeo baptizari, et tu venis ad me? Sed quoniam missus sum ante ipsum tanquam præcursor et præco, ut prædicando ac baptizando disponerem homines ad doctrinam gratiamque illius. De hoc superius multa jam dicta sunt.
paras.en: [[3:28|You yourselves do bear me witness|Ipsi vos mihi testimonium perhibetis]], you who heard the words I spoke about Christ, [[3:28|that I said|quod dixerim]], in your hearing, before the crowd: [[3:28|I am not Christ|Non sum ego Christus]]; that is, I am not the natural and only Son: it is a great thing for me to be an adopted son. I am not the end, but the way and the means that leads to the end; I am not the Saviour, but a servant, in need of His grace, to whom I also said: [[Matt 3:14|I ought to be baptized by thee, and comest thou to me?|Ego a te debeo baptizari, et tu venis ad me?]]? [[3:28|but that I am sent before him|Sed quoniam missus sum ante ipsum]] as forerunner and herald, so that by preaching and baptizing I might dispose men for His teaching and His grace. Much has already been said of this above [the margin refers to Art. VI, passim].

paras.t: Insuper ponit Joannes Baptista copiosam differentiam grandemque distantiam inter Christum et se: et quia discipuli sui minus sublimiter senserunt de Jesu, ideo Joannes ejus magnificentiam fidelissime atque clarissime pandit, non brevi versiculo, sed longo sermone. Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est. Amicus autem sponsi qui stat et audit eum, gaudio gaudet, id est, intime cordialiterque exsultat, propter vocem sponsi cui congratulatur. Hoc ad litteram in hominibus ita est; spiritualiter quoque sic fuit inter Christum et ejus præcursorem. Per sponsum ergo Joannes intelligit Christum, cujus sponsa est Ecclesia, quam sibi in incarnatione, Baptismo et passione desponsavit, eam sibi incorporando, per gratiam fecundando, spirituales filios ex ea generando. Quum enim sponsus ex sponsa generet prolem, convenit Christo procreare in Baptismo filios spirituales per Ecclesiam, quasi per matrem fidelium, quæ virtute et gratia sui sponsi regenerat. Joanni ergo non conveniebat spiritualiter regenerare, sed ad regenerationem disponere. De hoc sponso et sponsa ait Apostolus ad Ephesios: Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, et tradidit semetipsum pro ea, ut illam sanctificaret. Et ideo Joannes in Apocalypsi: Venerunt (inquit) nuptiæ Agni, et uxor ejus præparavit se; et rursus, Vidi Jerusalem, id est Ecclesiam, a Deo paratam quasi sponsam ornatam viro suo. De hoc sponso ac sponsa cantatur Canticum canticorum.
paras.en: Further, John the Baptist sets out the great difference and the wide distance between Christ and himself; and because his disciples thought less loftily of Jesus than they should, John unfolds His greatness most faithfully and most clearly, not in a short verse but in a long discourse. [[3:29|He that hath the bride is the bridegroom|Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est]]. [[3:29|but the friend of the bridegroom, who standeth and heareth Him, rejoiceth with joy|Amicus autem sponsi qui stat et audit eum, gaudio gaudet]], that is, exults inwardly and from the heart, [[3:29|because of the bridegroom's voice|propter vocem sponsi]], with whom he rejoices. Literally, this is so among men; and spiritually it was so between Christ and His forerunner. By the bridegroom, then, John understands Christ, whose bride is the Church, which He espoused to Himself in the Incarnation, in Baptism and in the Passion: incorporating her into Himself, making her fruitful by grace, and begetting spiritual children of her. For since the bridegroom begets offspring of the bride, it belongs to Christ to beget spiritual children in Baptism through the Church, as through the mother of the faithful, who regenerates by the power and grace of her Bridegroom. It did not belong to John, then, to regenerate spiritually, but to dispose men for regeneration. Of this Bridegroom and bride the Apostle says to the Ephesians: [[Eph 5:25|Christ also loved the church and delivered himself up for it|Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, et tradidit semetipsum pro ea]], [[Eph 5:26|That he might sanctify it|ut illam sanctificaret]]. And so John in the Apocalypse says: [[Apoc 19:7|the marriage of the Lamb is come: and his wife hath prepared herself|nuptiæ Agni, et uxor ejus præparavit se]]; and again: I saw Jerusalem, that is, the Church, [[Apoc 21:2|from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband|a Deo paratam quasi sponsam ornatam viro suo]]. Of this Bridegroom and bride the Canticle of Canticles sings.

paras.t: Habet autem Christus triplicem sponsam: [universalem, quæ est Ec]clesia omnium electorum, quam sibi ab origine mundi desponsare exorsus est per fidem et caritatem; sponsam particularem, quæ est anima sancta, quam sibi quotidie desponsat, quosdam ad se convertendo per gratiam; sponsam singularem, quæ est Virgo beatissima, quam sibi desponsavit in utero suæ Matris. Verum hæ duæ sponsæ continentur in prima, ut pars in toto. Propter quod dici potest, quod Christus non habet nisi unam sponsam in terra, sicut et unam dumtaxat Ecclesiam habere asseritur, quamvis sint multæ particulares Ecclesiæ non discordantes ab Ecclesia universali. Quum itaque sit Filius Dei sponsus noster seu animarum nostrarum, constat quod fornicatur adulteriumque committit, qui magis adhæret rebus terrenis, variabilibus et caducis, quam sibi. Hoc est spirituale adulterium, de quo Psalmista loquitur Deo: Ecce qui elongant se a te peribunt; perdidisti omnes qui fornicantur abs te. De quo scriptum est apud Osee: Noli lætari, Israel, quia fornicatus es a Deo tuo.
paras.en: Now Christ has a threefold bride: a universal one, which is the Church [one line is unreadable in the OCR here; "a universal one, which is the" is supplied from the sense] of all the elect, which He began to espouse to Himself from the beginning of the world through faith and charity; a particular bride, which is the holy soul, which He espouses to Himself daily, converting some to Himself by grace; and a singular bride, which is the most blessed Virgin, whom He espoused to Himself in His Mother's womb. But these two brides are contained in the first, as a part in the whole. Hence it can be said that Christ has only one bride on earth, just as He is said to have only one Church, although there are many particular Churches not at variance with the universal Church. Since, therefore, the Son of God is our Bridegroom, or the Bridegroom of our souls, it is plain that whoever clings more to earthly, changeable and perishable things than to Him commits fornication and adultery. This is the spiritual adultery of which the Psalmist says to God: [[Ps 72:27|behold they that go far from thee shall perish: thou hast destroyed all them that are disloyal to thee|Ecce qui elongant se a te peribunt; perdidisti omnes qui fornicantur abs te]] [the Latin is *fornicantur*, "commit fornication", which the Douay-Rheims renders "are disloyal"]. Of it it is written in Osee: [[Osee 9:1|Rejoice not, O Israel|Noli lætari, Israel]], [[Osee 9:1|for thou hast committed fornication against thy God|quia fornicatus es a Deo tuo]].

paras.t: Magna plane nobilitas atque ineffabilis dignitas animæ, imo totius Ecclesiæ, esse sponsam sui Creatoris, cujus semine impregnatur, videlicet lumine gratiæ cœliformis, ut sit fecunda in fructibus Spiritus Sancti, de quibus ad Galatas dicit Apostolus: Fructus Spiritus est caritas, gaudium, pax, patientia, longanimitas, bonitas, fides, modestia.
paras.en: Great indeed is the nobility, and unspeakable the dignity, of the soul, nay, of the whole Church, to be the bride of her Creator, by whose seed she is made fruitful, namely by the light of grace that shapes her to the likeness of heaven, so that she may be fruitful in the fruits of the Holy Ghost, of which the Apostle says to the Galatians: [[Gal 5:22|the fruit of the Spirit is, charity, joy, peace, patience|Fructus Spiritus est caritas, gaudium, pax, patientia]], longanimity, goodness, [[Gal 5:23|faith, modesty|fides, modestia]].

paras.t: Denique, per amicum sponsi intelligit Joannes se ipsum, quem certum est in Christi amore ardentissimum exstitisse. Qui stetit corporaliter juxta Jesum circa Jordanem; spiritualiter quoque stetit, tanquam in omni virtute erectus, in Christi caritate perfectus, nec ad dexteram nec ad sinistram deflectens animæ gressus, quia non erat arundo vento agitata. Audivitque verba Sponsi cœlestis, quæ non sunt in toto descripta: nec dubium quin in verbis Christi cordialissime delectabatur. Ideo subditur: Hoc ergo gaudium meum impletum est, id est, de adsistentia et audientia qua Sponso Ecclesiæ adstiti ejusque vocem audivi, jam vehementer lætatus sum, excellentiæ Christi mentaliter congaudendo. Fuit autem Joannes non solum Sponsi hujus amicus, sed etiam paranymphus, quoniam inter Christum et homines fecit copulam spiritualem, Sponsam Sponso conjungens.
paras.en: Lastly, by the friend of the bridegroom John means himself, who, it is certain, was most ardent in the love of Christ. He stood bodily beside Jesus by the Jordan; and he stood spiritually as well, upright, as it were, in every virtue, perfect in the charity of Christ, turning the steps of his soul neither to the right hand nor to the left, for he was not a reed shaken by the wind[[Luke 7:24||]]. And he heard the words of the heavenly Bridegroom, which are not all written down; and there is no doubt that he took the most heartfelt delight in the words of Christ. Therefore it is added: [[3:29|This my joy therefore is fulfilled|Hoc ergo gaudium meum impletum est]]; that is, at standing by the Bridegroom of the Church and hearing His voice I have now rejoiced exceedingly, sharing in mind the joy of Christ's excellence. And John was not only the friend of this Bridegroom but also His paranymph [that is, the groomsman who brings the bride to the bridegroom], since he made a spiritual union between Christ and men, joining the Bride to the Bridegroom.

paras.t: Sed si Joannes ita dilexerat Christum, nonne mirum est quod nunquam corporaliter secutus est eum sicut discipuli, præsertim quum, teste divino Dionysio, amor sit virtus unitiva? Imo istud in tantum displicuit Manichæis, ut dicerent Joannem esse damnatum. Et respondendum, quod amor Joannis fuit veraciter spiritualis, idcirco in spirituali conjunctione quievit contentusque fuit. Per quod docemur de corporali conjunctione seu præsentia non debere curare, nisi ad spiritualem profectum fuerit opportunum. Caro nempe, ut ait Salvator, non prodest, sed spiritus est qui vivificat. Unde Apostolis in corporali præsentia Christi minus ordinate delectationem habentibus, professus est Christus: Expedit vobis ut ego vadam: si enim non abiero, Paracletus non veniet ad vos; si autem abiero, mittam eum ad vos. Spiritualiter ergo amandus et contrectandus est, non solum Christus, sed et quilibet proximus. Idcirco enim dicit Apostolus: Et si novimus secundum carnem Christum, tamen jam nunc non novimus; itemque, Itaque nos jam neminem secundum carnem novimus. Deificata namque et spiritualizata erat affectio sancti Apostoli: cujus sectemur vestigia.
paras.en: But if John loved Christ so, is it not strange that he never followed Him bodily as the disciples did, especially since, on the witness of the divine Dionysius, love is a unitive power? Indeed this so offended the Manichees that they said John was damned. The answer is that John's love was truly spiritual, and therefore it rested in a spiritual union and was content with it. By this we are taught not to care for bodily union or presence except where it serves spiritual progress. For [[John 6:64|the flesh|Caro]], as the Saviour says, [[John 6:64|profiteth nothing|non prodest]], but [[John 6:64|It is the spirit that quickeneth|spiritus est qui vivificat]]. So when the Apostles took a delight not rightly ordered in the bodily presence of Christ, Christ declared: [[John 16:7|it is expedient to you that I go. For if I go not, the Paraclete will not come to you: but if I go, I will send him to you|Expedit vobis ut ego vadam: si enim non abiero, Paracletus non veniet ad vos; si autem abiero, mittam eum ad vos]]. Not only Christ, then, but every neighbour is to be loved and embraced spiritually. For this reason the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 5:16|And if we have known Christ according to the flesh: but now we know him so no longer|Et si novimus secundum carnem Christum, tamen jam nunc non novimus]]; and again: [[2 Cor 5:16|we know no man according to the flesh|Itaque nos jam neminem secundum carnem novimus]]. For the affection of the holy Apostle had been made godlike and spiritual: let us follow in his footsteps.

paras.t: Quæritur, cur et quomodo Joannes, qui superius dixit se esse indignum solvere calceamenta Christi, nunc appellat se ejus amicum. Dicendum, quod ibi loquebatur turbæ, quæ Christi majestatem non noverit: idcirco se ibi maxime humiliavit, et Christum exaltavit. Nunc vero loquitur suis discipulis invidia tactis, et inter Jesum ac Joannem aversionem quamdam facere cupientibus: hinc Joannes dicit se amicum illius, ut et discipulos suos ad Christi provocet caritatem. Sic et nos facere par est, dum sentimus seminatorem discordiæ nos affari, dicendo verba invidiæ provocativa. Tunc ergo caritative loquamur de eo inter quem et nos nititur seminare discordiam. Uterque autem sermo Joannis est verus: quia Joannes quantum ad id quod fuit per naturam et propriam fragilitatem, dignus non fuit solvere calceamenta Christi; quantum vero ad id quod fuit per caritatem et gratiam Salvatoris, erat præcipuus ejus amicus, non minor quam evangelista Joannes.
paras.en: It is asked why and how John, who said above that he was unworthy to loose Christ's shoes[[John 1:27||]], now calls himself His friend. The answer is that there he was speaking to the crowd, which did not know Christ's majesty; therefore he humbled himself there as low as he could and exalted Christ. But now he is speaking to his own disciples, who were touched with envy and wished to set up some estrangement between Jesus and John; hence John calls himself His friend, so as to stir his disciples too to the love of Christ. So it is right for us to do as well, when we perceive that a sower of discord is addressing us, speaking words meant to provoke envy: then let us speak charitably of the one between whom and ourselves he is trying to sow discord. Both of John's sayings are true: for as to what John was by nature and by his own frailty, he was not worthy to loose Christ's shoes; but as to what he was by charity and by the Saviour's grace, he was His chief friend, no less than John the Evangelist.

paras.t: Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui. Quando Joannes hoc dixit, fuit Christus perfectæ quantitatis in corpore, et perfectæ sanctitatis, sapientiæ et gratiæ in anima; secundum divinitatem vero, in se ipso omnino incommutabilis permanet. Quod ergo ait Joannes, Illum, videlicet Christum, oportet crescere, sic intelligendum est quomodo Deus dicitur magnificari et exaltari a nobis: non quod in se ipso major fiat vel altior; sed quod ejus magnitudinem et sublimitatem agnoscimus, profitemur, laudamus. Sic Christus crevit quantum ad magnitudinem famæ et hominum æstimationem. Joannes vero minoratus est hoc modo. Populus enim putavit Joannem esse Christum, et Jesum esse prophetam, non Messiam; sed tempore procedente, radiantibus signis documentisque Jesu, et testimonio Joannis cooperante, cœpit populus Jesum tenere pro Christo rege Messia, Joannem vero pro vate, præcursore ac nuntio Jesu Christi. Augustinus tangit alium sensum, referendo verba Joannis ad passionem utriusque, ut Christus dicatur crevisse, quia distentus in cruce; Joannes vero minutus, quoniam decollatus. Sed quia discipuli Joannis conquerebantur de hoc quod multi accesserunt Jesum, et pauci Joannem, potest ita intelligi: Illum oportet crescere, acquirendo plures discipulos spiritualesque filios in Baptismo; me autem minui, quantum ad numerum discipulorum: quia nonnulli ex discipulis Joannis adhæserunt Christo.
paras.en: [[3:30|He must increase: but I must decrease|Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui]]. When John said this, Christ was of perfect stature in body, and of perfect holiness, wisdom and grace in soul; while according to His divinity He remains in Himself wholly unchangeable. What John says, then, [[3:30|He must increase|Illum oportet crescere]] (He, that is, Christ), is to be understood in the way God is said to be magnified and exalted by us: not that He becomes greater or higher in Himself, but that we acknowledge, profess and praise His greatness and sublimity. So Christ increased as to the greatness of His fame and the esteem of men. And John was made less in this way. For the people thought that John was the Christ, and that Jesus was a prophet, not the Messias; but as time went on, through the shining signs and teachings of Jesus, and with John's testimony working together with them, the people began to hold Jesus for the Christ, the King Messias, and John for a prophet, the forerunner and herald of Jesus Christ. Augustine touches on another sense, referring John's words to the passion of each: so that Christ is said to have increased because He was stretched out on the cross, and John to have been diminished because he was beheaded. But since John's disciples were complaining that many went to Jesus and few to John, it can be understood thus: [[3:30|He must increase|Illum oportet crescere]], by gaining more disciples and spiritual sons in Baptism; [[3:30|but I must decrease|me autem minui]], as to the number of disciples, because some of John's disciples went over to Christ.

paras.t: Hujus incrementi et decrementi ponit Joannes Baptista aliquas rationes. Primam tangit, dicendo: Qui desursum venit, id est Christus Unigenitus Dei, cujus a summo cælo fuit egressio, quantum ad divinitatem, quoniam natus a Patre æterno, et quantum ad humanitatem, quoniam supernaturaliter conceptus et natus ex Virgine, Spiritu Sancto corpus ejus formante; super omnes est, id est, omnibus creaturis sublimior est, quantum ad utramque suam naturam. Nam quoad divinam, cunctis præstantior est in infinitum. Hæc ergo ratio excellentiæ Christi, sumpta est ex parte suæ originis.
paras.en: Of this increase and decrease John the Baptist gives several reasons. The first he touches on in saying: [[3:31|He that cometh from above|Qui desursum venit]], that is, Christ, the Only-begotten of God, whose [[Ps 18:7|going out is from the end of heaven|a summo cælo fuit egressio]] [Latin *a summo cælo*, 'from the highest heaven'], as to His divinity, since He was born of the eternal Father; and as to His humanity, since He was conceived and born of the Virgin supernaturally, the Holy Ghost forming His body[[Luke 1:35||]]; [[3:31|is above all|super omnes est]], that is, He is higher than all creatures, as to each of His natures. For as to the divine nature He surpasses all things infinitely. This reason for Christ's excellence, then, is taken from His origin.

paras.t: Secunda vero accipitur ex qualitate suæ sapientiæ et doctrinæ. Unde subjungitur: Qui est de terra, id est, ex humanis parentibus viro et femina natus est, de terra est, quantum ad generationis originem, et de terra loquitur, id est, de inferioribus et terrenis tractat, quantum est ex parte suæ terrenæ originis. Nihilo minus loquitur de divinis atque cœlestibus, sive per naturalem rationem, sicut philosophi, sive per gratiæ infusionem et supernaturalem illuminationem, quemadmodum Prophetæ et Apostoli, ipse quoque B. Joannes Baptista, quem certum est hoc loco de cœlestibus fari, imo de supercœlestibus eloqui, scilicet de Patre et Filio. Qui de cælo venit, humanam naturam assumendo, et visibiliter apparendo supernaturalique modo nascendo, super omnes est, perfectione naturæ quoad suam divinitatem, et excellentia gratiæ quoad humanitatem assumptam.
paras.en: The second is taken from the quality of His wisdom and teaching. Hence it is added: [[3:31|He that is of the earth|Qui est de terra]], that is, is born of human parents, a man and a woman, [[3:31|of the earth he is|de terra est]], as to the origin of his generation, [[3:31|and of the earth he speaketh|et de terra loquitur]], that is, treats of lower and earthly things, so far as lies with his earthly origin. Nevertheless he does speak of divine and heavenly things, either through natural reason, as the philosophers do, or through the infusion of grace and supernatural enlightenment, as the Prophets and Apostles do, and blessed John the Baptist himself, who certainly speaks here of heavenly things, nay, discourses of things above the heavens, namely of the Father and the Son. [[3:31|He that cometh from heaven|Qui de cælo venit]], by taking human nature, appearing visibly and being born in a supernatural way, [[3:31|is above all|super omnes est]], by the perfection of His nature as to His divinity, and by the excellence of grace as to the humanity He assumed.

paras.t: Et quod vidit et audivit, hoc testatur, et testimonium ejus nemo accipit. Hoc verbum Præcursoris alludit ei quod supra Christus dixit ad Nicodemum: Amen dico tibi, quia quod scimus loquimur, et quod vidimus testamur; et testimonium nostrum non accipitis. Quod quomodo intelligendum sit, paulo ante expositum est. Ea enim quæ Christus docuit, vidit oculo intellectuali secundum utramque naturam, cognoscendo videlicet omnia per scientiam increatam, ut Deus, et per scientiam infusam, ut homo. Denique ut homo, audivit auribus cordis a Deo Trinitate in primo instanti incarnationis, quidquid Deus sibi revelavit. Sed quomodo secundum naturam divinam audit aliquid a Patre, quum ipse sit sermo Patris? Dicendum, quod Filio Dei idem est generari a Patre, et audire a Patre. Nascendo quippe a Patre, recipit plenitudinem deitatis, et per consequens sapientiam omnemque perfectionem, a Patre. Idcirco dicitur audire a Patre, non quasi primo subsistens, et postea audiens, vel a Patre distans, sed eamdem sapientiam atque essentiam recipiendo a Patre, quam habet Pater. Audit ergo, id est, intellectualiter percipit, a Patre, quidquid intelligit Pater.
paras.en: [[3:32|And what he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth|Et quod vidit et audivit, hoc testatur]], [[3:32|and no man receiveth his testimony|et testimonium ejus nemo accipit]]. This saying of the Forerunner alludes to what Christ said above to Nicodemus: Amen, [[3:11|I say to thee that we speak what we know and we testify what we have seen: and you receive not our testimony|dico tibi, quia quod scimus loquimur, et quod vidimus testamur; et testimonium nostrum non accipitis]]. How this is to be understood was explained a little before. For the things that Christ taught He saw with the eye of the intellect according to each nature, knowing all things, that is, by uncreated knowledge as God, and by infused knowledge as man. And further, as man He heard with the ears of the heart from God the Trinity, in the first instant of the Incarnation, whatever God revealed to Him. But how, according to the divine nature, does He hear anything from the Father, since He is Himself the Word of the Father? The answer is that for the Son of God to be begotten of the Father and to hear from the Father are one and the same. For in being born of the Father He receives from the Father the fullness of the Godhead, and consequently wisdom and every perfection. Therefore He is said to hear from the Father, not as though He first subsisted and afterwards heard, or as though He were distant from the Father, but because He receives from the Father the same wisdom and essence that the Father has. He hears, then, that is, He perceives intellectually, from the Father whatever the Father understands.

paras.t: Sed quomodo dicit Præcursor de Christo, Testimonium ejus nemo accipit? quum in Daniele scriptum sit, Omnes populi, tribus et linguæ servient ei; itemque in Psalmo, Reminiscentur et convertentur ad Dominum universæ familiæ gentium. Sed et quando Joannes hæc dixit, habuit Christus nonnullos discipulos; et ipse quoque Baptista utique testimonium Christi accepit. Et respondendum, quod Joannes hoc asserit ad insinuandum paucitatem Judæorum in Christum credentium. Juxta quem modum dicit Apostolus: Omnes quæ sua sunt quærunt, non quæ Jesu Christi. Sic etiam Michæas dicit: Periit sanctus de terra, et rectus in hominibus non est.
paras.en: But how does the Forerunner say of Christ, [[3:32|no man receiveth his testimony|Testimonium ejus nemo accipit]], when it is written in Daniel: [[Dan 7:14|all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him|Omnes populi, tribus et linguæ servient ei]]; and likewise in the Psalm: [[Ps 21:28|shall remember, and shall be converted to the Lord|Reminiscentur et convertentur ad Dominum]], [[Ps 21:28|all the kindreds of the Gentiles|universæ familiæ gentium]]? Moreover, when John said this, Christ had a number of disciples; and the Baptist himself certainly received Christ's testimony. The answer is that John says this to point to how few of the Jews believed in Christ. In the same way the Apostle says: [[Phil 2:21|all seek the things that are their own not the things that are Jesus Christ's|Omnes quæ sua sunt quærunt, non quæ Jesu Christi]]. So too Micheas says: [[Mich 7:2|The holy man is perished out of the earth, and there is none upright among men|Periit sanctus de terra, et rectus in hominibus non est]].

paras.t: Qui autem acceperit ejus testimonium, verbis Christi credendo, signavit, id est, consideravit et suo actu monstravit ac indicavit, quia Deus Pater seu Trinitas verax est in se ipso, in verbis suis atque operibus, qui per diversa argumenta probavit quod Jesus sit Christus Filius Dei, videlicet: in baptismo, per descensum Spiritus Sancti in forma columbæ, et per vocem qua dixit Pater, Hic est Filius meus dilectus; per miracula quoque in Jerusalem facta, de quibus confessus est Nicodemus, Nemo potest hæc signa facere, nisi fuerit Deus cum eo. Verus etiam ostenditur Deus, quia in Jesu implevit quæcumque per Prophetas prænuntiavit de Christo.
paras.en: [[3:33|He that hath received his testimony|Qui autem acceperit ejus testimonium]], by believing Christ's words, [[3:33|hath set to his seal|signavit]] [*signavit*, 'has sealed': has put his seal to it, as a witness does to a document], that is, has considered, and has shown and declared by his own act, [[3:33|that God is true|quia Deus verax est]] (God the Father, or the Trinity), true in Himself, in His words and in His works; who proved by various arguments that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God: namely in the baptism, by the descent of the Holy Ghost in the form of a dove[[Matt 3:16||]], and by the voice in which the Father said: [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]]; and also by the miracles done in Jerusalem[[John 2:23||]], of which Nicodemus confessed: [[3:2|no man can do these signs|Nemo potest hæc signa facere]], [[3:2|unless God be with him|nisi fuerit Deus cum eo]]. God is shown to be true also in that He fulfilled in Jesus whatever He had foretold of Christ through the Prophets.

paras.t: Quem enim misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur. Quamvis hoc verum sit de ipso Baptista (de quo dictum est supra, Fuit homo missus a Deo), atque Apostolis, imo universis prædicatoribus sanctis, qui sunt missi a Deo, et verba Dei hominibus prædicant; hoc tamen de Christo antonomastice dicitur, quum ipse sit omnium missorum atque divina loquentium summus.
paras.en: [[3:34|For he whom God hath sent speaketh the words of God|Quem enim misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur]]. Although this is true of the Baptist himself (of whom it was said above: [[John 1:6|There was a man sent from God|Fuit homo missus a Deo]]), and of the Apostles, nay, of all holy preachers, who are sent by God and preach the words of God to men, yet it is said of Christ by antonomasia [that is, as of the one to whom the description belongs pre-eminently], since He is the highest of all who are sent and who speak divine things.

paras.t: Præterea ostendit Baptista excellentiam Christi ex parte gratiæ sibi concessæ. Non enim ad mensuram, id est secundum determinatum gradum et particularem perfectionem, dat Deus Spiritum Sanctum, id est gratiam ejus: supplendum est, Christo homini, de quo Joannes nunc loquitur. Ex his autem quæ dicta sunt in expositione primi capituli, super illud, Plenum gratiæ et veritatis, patet quomodo gratia Christi sit perfecta, summa et multiplex; nec jam resumenda sunt illa. Sed quia Præcursor jam adstruit quod sine mensura Deus præstitit gratiam Christo, oportet fateri quod gratia Christi sit aliquo modo infinita. Gratia autem Christi habitualis non est secundum essentiam infinita, quum sit pura creatura, quæ non potest simpliciter esse infinita, sed necessario est determinatæ perfectionis et limitatæ capacitatis. Gratia vero unionis in Christo est simpliciter infinita, quum non sit quid creatum, sed ipsum Verbum humanæ naturæ gratis unitum.
paras.en: Further, the Baptist shows Christ's excellence on the side of the grace granted Him: [[3:34|for God doth not give the Spirit by measure|non enim ad mensuram dat Deus spiritum]]: not by measure, that is, not according to a fixed degree and a particular perfection, does God give the Holy Ghost, that is, His grace; we must supply 'to Christ as man', of whom John is now speaking. From what was said in the exposition of the first chapter, on the words [[John 1:14|full of grace and truth|Plenum gratiæ et veritatis]], it is plain how the grace of Christ is perfect, supreme and manifold; and those things need not be gone over again now. But since the Forerunner here maintains that God bestowed grace on Christ without measure, we must confess that the grace of Christ is in some way infinite. Now Christ's habitual grace [the grace that abides in the soul as a lasting quality, as distinct from the grace of union] is not infinite in its essence, since it is a mere creature, which cannot be infinite absolutely, but is necessarily of a determinate perfection and a limited capacity. The grace of union in Christ, on the other hand, is infinite absolutely, since it is not something created, but the very Word, united freely [*gratis*: whence it is called grace] to human nature.

paras.t: Nihilo minus gratia habitualis in Christo est quodammodo infinita: primo, quia idonea est ad omnes gratiarum effectus; secundo, quoniam major gratia nulli communicari potest; tertio, quia tota capacitas animæ Christi repleta est gratia; quarto, quoniam plena atque sufficiens est aliis influere incessanter. Aliis vero datur gratia secundum aliquem gradum et determinatam perfectionem, prout Apostolus dicit: Unicuique nostrum data est gratia secundum mensuram donationis Christi. Infinita est ergo gratia Christi, quoniam Verbum tantam gratiam influxit animæ Christi, quantam capere potuit, eratque paratum plus dare, si illa potuisset plus capere. Unio enim Verbi cum humana natura, non est facta per gratiam habitualem intermediam; sed gratia ista consecuta est hypostaticam unionem, tanquam effectus ipsius. Et quoniam unio hypostatica seu personalis, est summa ac propinquissima, ideo ex ea derivata est tanta gratia ad animam Christi, quod tota ejus capacitas fuit repleta.
paras.en: Nevertheless the habitual grace in Christ is in a certain way infinite: first, because it is fit for all the effects of graces; second, because no greater grace can be communicated to anyone; third, because the whole capacity of Christ's soul is filled with grace; fourth, because it is full and sufficient to flow ceaselessly into others. To others, however, grace is given according to some degree and a determinate perfection, as the Apostle says: [[Eph 4:7|to every one of us is given grace, according to the measure of the giving of Christ|Unicuique nostrum data est gratia secundum mensuram donationis Christi]]. The grace of Christ is therefore infinite, since the Word poured as much grace into the soul of Christ as it could receive, and was ready to give more, had that soul been able to receive more. For the union of the Word with human nature was not made by means of habitual grace coming between; rather, that grace followed upon the hypostatic union, as its effect. And since the hypostatic, or personal, union is the highest and closest of unions, there flowed from it so much grace into the soul of Christ that its whole capacity was filled.

paras.t: Pater enim diligit Filium amore immenso, omni creaturæ inexperto, superæstuanti ac superdulcissimo, quantum ad Filii divinitatem. Propter quod dicit Apostolus ad Colossenses: Gratias agimus Deo et Patri, qui nos transtulit in regnum Filii dilectionis suæ. Quum autem dicit, Pater diligit Filium, non est simpliciter accipiendum, quum Deus diligat cuncta quæ fecit; sed innuitur quod incomparabilis sit dilectio Patris ad Filium, secundum quod apud Marcum ait Pater: Hic est Filius meus carissimus. Diligit quoque Pater Filium secundum naturam assumptam, amore finito, sed singulari, et ampliori quam totum universum, quoniam majus bonum dedit ei soli quam omnibus simul, videlicet personalem unionem cum Verbo.
paras.en: For [[3:35|the Father loveth the Son|Pater enim diligit Filium]] with a love immeasurable, never experienced by any creature, overflowing and sweet beyond all sweetness, as to the Son's divinity. Therefore the Apostle says to the Colossians: [[Col 1:3|We give thanks to God and the Father|Gratias agimus Deo et Patri]][[Col 1:12||]], who [[Col 1:13|hath translated us into the kingdom of the Son of his love|transtulit in regnum Filii dilectionis suæ]]. But when he says, [[3:35|The Father loveth the Son|Pater diligit Filium]], it is not to be taken simply, since God loves all the things that He has made[[Wis 11:25||]]; rather it is implied that the Father's love for the Son is beyond compare, according to what the Father says in Mark: [[Mark 9:6|This is my most beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus carissimus]]. The Father loves the Son also according to the nature assumed, with a love that is finite but singular, and greater than for the whole universe, since He gave to Him alone a greater good than to all things together, namely personal union with the Word.

paras.t: Et omnia dedit in manu ejus, id est in potestate Filii, secundum utramque ejus naturam. Pater enim dedit omnia in potestate Filii secundum naturam ejus divinam, in quantum dedit eamdem ei essentiam atque potentiam quam habet Pater. Dando equidem ipsi potentiam istam, dedit ei omnium potestatem, ita quod Filius est universorum Dominus per auctoritatem, potens creare, annihilare, et quidquid voluerit facere. Denique, secundum assumptam humanitatem dedit omnia in manu ejus, quoniam omni creaturæ præposuit Christum, prout in Matthæo ait: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo et in terra. Ut enim Damascenus testatur, dato Christo homini quod majus est, etiam datum est ei quod minus est. Quoniam ergo datum est ei personale esse Verbi, ut sit Filius naturalis, quia humanitas Christi subsistit in increato personalique esse Verbi, imo ipsum Verbum est persona seu personalis subsistentia naturæ assumptæ; ideo datum est ei omnibus creaturis præsidere ac dominari. — Sed contra hoc videtur esse illud Apostoli ad Hebræos: Nondum videmus omnia ei subjecta. Dicendum, quod nondum sunt omnia Christo homini subjecta, quantum ad suæ potestatis plenariam exsecutionem et universalem manifestationem; sed hoc fiet in die judicii, quando ad eum venient et confundentur omnes qui repugnant ei, ut Isaias dicit.
paras.en: [[3:35|And he hath given all things into his hand|Et omnia dedit in manu ejus]], that is, into the power of the Son, according to each of His natures. For the Father gave all things into the Son's power according to His divine nature, inasmuch as He gave Him the same essence and power that the Father has. For in giving Him that power, He gave Him power over all things, so that the Son is Lord of all things by authority, able to create, to annihilate, and to do whatever He will. Then, according to the humanity assumed, He gave all things into His hand, since He set Christ over every creature, as He says in Matthew: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo et in terra]]. For, as Damascene testifies, when what is greater has been given to Christ as man, what is less has been given him too. Since, then, the personal being of the Word was given to Him, so that He is the natural Son (because the humanity of Christ subsists in the uncreated and personal being of the Word; nay, the Word Himself is the person, or the personal subsistence, of the nature assumed), therefore it was given Him to preside over and rule all creatures. — But against this seems to be that saying of the Apostle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 2:8|we see not as yet all things subject to him|Nondum videmus omnia ei subjecta]]. The answer is that not all things are yet subject to Christ as man as regards the full exercise and the universal manifestation of His power; but this will come about on the day of judgement, when [[Is 45:25|they shall come to him, and all that resist him shall be confounded|ad eum venient et confundentur omnes qui repugnant ei]], as Isaias says.

paras.t: Per hoc itaque Pater dedit omnia in manu Filii secundum suam divinitatem, quod genuit Filium sibi æqualem, Omnipotens omnipotentem, ut qualis et quantus est Pater, talis ac tantus sit Filius, ita quod dare, aliud non fuit quam generare.
paras.en: In this way, therefore, the Father gave all things into the Son's hand according to His divinity: in that He begot the Son equal to Himself, the Almighty an almighty Son, so that such and so great as the Father is, such and so great is the Son; so that to give was nothing other than to beget.

paras.t: Qui credit in Filium, fide formata perseveranti et operatoria, habet vitam æternam, id est beatitudinem sempiternam, nunc in spe, in merito et in radice. Non enim inaniter eam præstolatur; sed habet causam adipiscendi eam, quæ est actio bona ex caritate procedens, in adultis. In infantibus vero sufficit fides formata sine opere proprio, cum merito Christi.
paras.en: [[3:36|He that believeth in the Son|Qui credit in Filium]], with formed faith [faith given its form, that is, its life, by charity], persevering and working, [[3:36|hath life everlasting|habet vitam æternam]], that is, everlasting beatitude: now in hope, in merit and in its root. For he does not wait for it in vain, but has the cause of obtaining it, which, in adults, is good action proceeding from charity. In infants, formed faith without any work of their own suffices, together with the merit of Christ.

paras.t: Qui autem incredulus est Filio Dei, non videbit vitam æternam, id est, divina visione privabitur quantum ad pœnam damni, quemadmodum scriptum est: Tollatur impius, ne videat gloriam Dei. Unde et in Isaia habetur: Qui incredulus est, infideliter agit. Sed quum vita æterna sit visio Dei, quomodo infidelis dicitur non visurus vitam æternam, quasi fideles sint eam visuri? Et respondendum, quod intellectus reflectitur super proprium actum: ideo Sancti in patria suam beatificam visionem vident, hoc est, cognoscunt. Potest quoque per vitam æternam intelligi beatitudo objectalis, quæ est Deus, quem increduli non videbunt per speciem. Sed ira Dei, id est justa vindicta, manet super eum, id est, æternam damnationem incurret quantum ad pœnam damni. Omnes quidem, teste Apostolo, nascimur filii iræ. Sed ira Dei non manet super electos atque fideles. Super infideles vero in sua perfidia persistentes, sine fine manebit. Unde in Apocalypsi inducitur: Timidis autem, et incredulis, et exsecratis, pars illorum erit in stagno ardenti igne et sulfure.
paras.en: [[3:36|But he that believeth not the Son|qui autem incredulus est Filio]] of God [[3:36|shall not see life|non videbit vitam]] everlasting, that is, he will be deprived of the divine vision as to the pain of loss [the punishment of being deprived of God, as distinct from the 'pain of sense'], as it is written: 'Let the wicked be taken away, that he may not see the glory of God'[[Is 26:10||]] [Is 26:10 as the Septuagint reads it, as the margin notes; the Vulgate has 'he shall not see the glory of the Lord']. And so in Isaias we have: [[Is 21:2|he that is unfaithful dealeth unfaithfully|Qui incredulus est, infideliter agit]] [*incredulus*, the word the Gospel uses here for 'he that believeth not']. But since everlasting life is the vision of God, how is the unbeliever said not to be going to see everlasting life, as though the faithful were going to see it? The answer is that the intellect reflects upon its own act: hence the Saints in the heavenly country see, that is, know, their own beatific vision. By everlasting life may also be understood objective beatitude [beatitude taken as its object, God Himself, as distinct from the act of seeing Him], which is God, whom unbelievers will not see face to face [literally 'by sight', as opposed to faith]. [[3:36|But the wrath of God|Sed ira Dei]], that is, just vengeance, [[3:36|abideth on him|manet super eum]], that is, he will incur eternal damnation as to the pain of loss. All of us indeed, as the Apostle testifies, are born [[Eph 2:3|children of wrath|filii iræ]]. But the wrath of God does not abide on the elect and the faithful; on unbelievers who persist in their unbelief, however, it will abide without end. Hence it is set down in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:8|But the fearful and unbelieving and the abominable|Timidis autem, et incredulis, et exsecratis]], [[Apoc 21:8|they shall have their portion in the pool burning with fire and brimstone|pars illorum erit in stagno ardenti igne et sulfure]].

paras.t: Ex præinductis verbis et factis Joannis moraliter edocemur, ne indigne feramus dum alii nobis præferuntur, quibus majores æstimabamur; nec aliquid boni propriis viribus adscribamus, quia non potest homo habere vel accipere quidquam, nisi fuerit ei datum de cælo. Patet quoque ex his quanta sit certitudo fidei christianæ, quæ data est ab unigenito Filio Dei, qui non alia nobis narravit quam quæ vidit in Patre et audivit ab eo. Propterea multo damnabilius est non recipere legem evangelicam, quam fuit non credere legi Mosaicæ, prout ad Hebræos plenius docet Apostolus.
paras.en: From the foregoing words and deeds of John we are taught, in the moral sense, not to take it ill when others are preferred to us, though we were thought greater than they; and not to ascribe any good to our own powers, since [[3:27|a man cannot receive any thing, unless it be given him from heaven|non potest homo habere vel accipere quidquam, nisi fuerit ei datum de cælo]][[John 19:11||]] [Denis has 'cannot have or receive'; the margin gives John xix, 11, 'Thou shouldst not have any power … unless it were given thee from above', which he seems to blend with v. 27]. It is plain too from this how great is the certainty of the Christian faith, which was given by the only-begotten Son of God, who told us nothing other than what He saw in the Father and heard from Him. Therefore it is far more damnable not to receive the law of the Gospel than it was not to believe the law of Moses, as the Apostle teaches more fully to the Hebrews[[Heb 2:2||]] [the margin reference is only partly readable (Hebr. ii?); see Heb 2:2–3, and also Heb 10:28–29].

20.title: PROSECUTIO EXPOSITIONIS PRÆSENTIS VICESIMI CAPITULI : QUUM SERO ESSET DIE ILLA, UNA SABBATORUM.
20.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this twentieth chapter: When it was late that same day, the first of the week

paras.t: HOC loco describit Evangelista quintam Christi apparitionem, factam in die Paschæ, et etiam sextam, quæ facta est præsente Thoma, in octava Paschæ. Quinquies enim apparuit Christus in die Paschæ : Primo, Magdalenæ, quemadmodum in Marco legitur : Surgens Jesus mane prima sabbati, apparuit primo Mariæ Magdalene. Secundo, mulieribus redeuntibus a sepulcro, juxta illud Matthæi : Ecce Jesus occurrit illis, dicens, Avete. Tertio, Petro, quamvis locus ignoretur; creditur tamen quod redeunti a monumento. Quarto, duobus discipulis euntibus in Emmaus, secundum quod recitat Lucas. Quinto, undecim Apostolis in conclavi, sicut nunc contestatur Joannes.
paras.en: In this place the Evangelist describes the fifth appearance of Christ, made on the day of the Pasch, and also the sixth, which was made with Thomas present, on the octave of the Pasch. For Christ appeared five times on the day of the Pasch. First, to Magdalen, as is read in Mark: [[Mark 16:9|But he rising early the first day of the week, appeared first to Mary Magdalen|Surgens Jesus mane prima sabbati, apparuit primo Mariæ Magdalene]]. Second, to the women returning from the sepulchre, according to that of Matthew: [[Matt 28:9|behold, Jesus met them, saying: All hail|Ecce Jesus occurrit illis, dicens, Avete]]. Third, to Peter[[Luke 24:34||]][[1 Cor 15:5||]], though the place is unknown; yet it is believed that it was as he returned from the tomb. Fourth, to the two disciples going to Emmaus, as Luke recounts[[Luke 24:13||]]. Fifth, to the eleven Apostles in the closed room, as John now bears witness.

paras.t: Quum sero esset, hoc est hora vespertina, et nocte incipiente, die illa, in qua apparuit Magdalenæ, una sabbatorum, id est, quæ dies fuit una dierum illius hebdomadæ, qui omnes dicebantur sabbata, quia festivi, et fores, id est januæ, essent clausæ, ubi erant discipuli, hoc est Apostoli, et etiam alii, secundum Lucam, congregati propter metum Judæorum : in quo patet eorum infirmitas, qui timebant eos qui corpus potuerunt occidere. Dicunt quidam, quod Apostoli erant dispersi in die propter metum Judæorum, sed de sero conveniebant ad locum unum. Evangelista vero nunc dicit, quod erant congregati propter metum prædictum. Lucas quoque habet, quod mulieres regressæ a monumento, nuntiaverunt quæ audierunt illis undecim : quod fuit clara die, quia post hoc Petrus et Joannes cucurrerunt ad monumentum. Ex quibus patet, quod discipuli etiam in die sederunt collecti januis clausis, propter metum Judæorum : imo minus audebant exire diebus quam noctibus.
paras.en: [[20:19|Now when it was late|Cum ergo sero esset]], that is, at the evening hour, as night was beginning, [[20:19|the same day|die illo]], on which He appeared to Magdalen, [[20:19|the first of the week|una sabbatorum]], that is, the day which was one of the days of that week, all of which were called sabbaths because they were festal, [[20:19|and the doors were shut, where the disciples were|et fores essent clausæ, ubi erant discipuli]], that is, the Apostles, and others too, according to Luke[[Luke 24:33||]], [[20:19|gathered together, for fear of the Jews|congregati propter metum Judæorum]]: in which their weakness is plain, who feared those who could kill the body[[Matt 10:28||]]. Some say that the Apostles were scattered by day for fear of the Jews, but in the evening came together to one place. But the Evangelist now says that they were gathered together for the said fear. Luke also has it that the women, returning from the tomb, told what they had heard to the eleven[[Luke 24:9||]]: which was in broad day, since after this Peter and John ran to the tomb[[Luke 24:12||]]. From which it is plain that the disciples sat gathered with the doors shut even by day, for fear of the Jews: indeed they dared go out less by day than by night.

paras.t: Venit Jesus ostio clauso, per penetrationem dimensionum. Corpora enim glorificata omnia penetrant per dotem subtilitatis, secundum quosdam : non tamen sine grandi miraculo, prout Thomas super quartum Sententiarum satis demonstrat. Quemadmodum igitur Jesus exivit uterum Matris, ea integra remanente, sic intravit et exiit domum non apertam, divina omnipotente virtute. Et stetit in medio discipulorum. Ipse namque est mediator, doctor reconciliatorque noster, ideo competebat ei esse in medio, sicut et ante passionem locutus est : Ego in medio vestrum sum. Magister quippe virtutum, medium semper elegit, quia in medio virtus consistit. Quomodo autem factum sit quod nunc refert Joannes, Lucas plenius edocet : quo legitur, quod quum Jesus cognitus fuisset a duobus discipulis in fractione panis, et disparuisset, illi surgentes regressi sunt in Jerusalem eadem hora, inveneruntque undecim congregatos, et eos qui cum illis erant, quibus dixerunt quomodo Jesus apparuisset eis in via, et qualiter eum cognoverunt : quibus ista narrantibus, venit Jesus, et stetit in medio discipulorum.
paras.en: [[20:19|Jesus came|venit Jesus]] with the door shut, by penetration of dimensions [[that is, two bodies occupying the same place]]. For glorified bodies penetrate all things by the endowment of subtlety, according to some: yet not without a great miracle, as Thomas amply shows on the fourth book of the Sentences. As therefore Jesus came forth from His Mother's womb while she remained intact, so He entered and left the unopened house by the almighty power of God. [[20:19|And stood in the midst|et stetit in medio]] of the disciples. For He is our mediator, teacher and reconciler, and so it befitted Him to be in the midst, as He also said before the passion: [[Luke 22:27|I am in the midst of you|Ego in medio vestrum sum]]. For the Master of the virtues always chose the mean, since virtue consists in the mean. How what John now relates came about, Luke teaches more fully: where it is read that when Jesus had been known by the two disciples in the breaking of bread and had vanished[[Luke 24:30||]], they rose up and returned to Jerusalem the same hour, and found the eleven gathered together, [[Luke 24:33|and those that were with them|et eos qui cum illis erant]], to whom they told how Jesus had appeared to them on the way and how they knew Him[[Luke 24:35||]]: and as they were telling these things, Jesus came and stood in the midst of the disciples[[Luke 24:36||]].

paras.t: Et dixit eis : Pax vobis. Quod docuit Christus, hoc fecit. Præcepit autem discipulis : In quamcumque domum intraveritis, primum dicite : Pax huic domui. Hinc ipse domum ingrediens in qua erant carissimi sui electissimique discipuli, ait : Pax vobis. Rursus, sic eos salutavit, quoniam paulo ante, in qua nocte tradebatur, disseruit : Pacem relinquo vobis. Quod igitur tunc reliquit, nunc attulit, dedit et auxit. Discipuli quoque pace maxime indigebant, quoniam multipliciter conturbati erant, ac territi, videlicet propter præteritam Christi passionem, propter Judæorum crudelitatem, et proprii cordis quamdam hæsitationem de Christi resurrectione, de cujus veritate nondum fuerant roborati. Insuper sic salutavit discipulos, quoniam pax est maximum bonum, omnique Christiano præcipue appetendum : per quam homines fiunt filii Dei, quemadmodum scriptum est : Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur. Propter quod ait Dionysius, quod omnia appetunt pacem, et propter hanc agunt omne quod agunt. Ex quo concluditur, quod pax est vel ipsa beatitudo, vel proxima ad beatitudinem dispositio.
paras.en: [[20:19|and said to them: Peace be to you|et dixit eis: Pax vobis]]. What Christ taught, that He did. For He commanded the disciples: [[Luke 10:5|Into whatever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house|In quamcumque domum intraveritis, primum dicite : Pax huic domui]]. Hence He Himself, entering the house in which were His dearest and most chosen disciples, says: Peace be to you. Again, He so greeted them because a little before, on the night He was betrayed, He had said: [[John 14:27|Peace I leave with you|Pacem relinquo vobis]]. What He left then, therefore, He now brought, gave and increased. The disciples too were in the greatest need of peace, since they were troubled and frightened in many ways: by the passion of Christ now past, by the cruelty of the Jews, and by a certain hesitation of their own hearts about Christ's resurrection, of whose truth they had not yet been made firm. Moreover, He so greeted the disciples because peace is the greatest good, to be sought above all by every Christian: through which men become sons of God, as it is written: [[Matt 5:9|Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.|Beati pacifici: quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur.]]. Wherefore Dionysius says that all things seek peace, and for its sake do all that they do. From which it is concluded that peace is either beatitude itself, or the disposition nearest to beatitude.

paras.t: Christus autem præsertim nunc loquitur de pace interna, quæ est tranquillitas animi, utpote quies a motibus propriis inordinatis, videlicet a timore immoderato, a tristitia sæculi, quæ secundum Apostolum, mortem operatur, a dolore rationem impediente. Non enim optavit discipulis quietem ab exterioribus persecutionibus ad tempus, quos in medio luporum erat missurus, sed ut in omni turbatione extrinseca conservarent pacem internam. Propterea ad Hebræos monet Apostolus : Pacem sequimini et sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo Deum videbit.
paras.en: But Christ is here speaking chiefly of inward peace, which is tranquillity of mind, namely rest from one's own disordered motions: from immoderate fear, from the sorrow of the world, which, according to the Apostle, worketh death[[2 Cor 7:10||]], from grief that hinders reason. For He did not wish His disciples rest from outward persecutions for the time, since He was about to send them into the midst of wolves[[Matt 10:16||]], but that amid every outward disturbance they might keep inward peace. Hence the Apostle admonishes the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:14|Follow peace with all men and holiness: without which no man shall see God|Pacem sequimini et sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo Deum videbit]].

paras.t: Et quum hoc dixisset, ostendit eis manus et latus, forte et pedes : imo et pedes, ut infra ex verbis Lucæ evangelistæ patebit. In his quinque vulnerum remanserunt cicatrices, in testimonium identitatis corporis passi, resuscitati, et glorificati, itemque in signum victoriæ Salvatoris. Ostendit ergo discipulis manus perfossas, et latus lancea perforatum, ut scirent quod ipse esset qui paulo ante pendebat in ligno, et quod idem numero corpus resumpsisset. — Multa hoc loco omittit Joannes, quæ recitat Lucas; ea quoque quæ Lucas omisit, supplevit Joannes. Itaque Luca testante, Christus discipulis dixit : Videte manus meas et pedes meos; palpate et videte, quoniam spiritus carnem et ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere. Et alia multa in hac apparitione dicta et facta recitat Lucas.
paras.en: [[20:20|And when he had said this, he shewed them his hands and his side|Et cum hoc dixisset, ostendit eis manus et latus]], perhaps the feet too: indeed the feet too, as will appear below from the words of Luke the Evangelist. In these the scars of the five wounds remained, in witness of the identity of the body that suffered, was raised and was glorified, and also as a sign of the Saviour's victory. He showed the disciples, then, the pierced hands and the side opened by the lance, that they might know that He was the one who a little before hung on the wood, and that He had taken again the body numerically the same. — Many things John omits in this place which Luke recounts; and what Luke omitted, John supplied. So, by Luke's witness, Christ said to the disciples: [[Luke 24:39|See my hands and feet, that it is I myself. Handle, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as you see me to have|Videte manus meas et pedes meos; palpate et videte, quoniam spiritus carnem et ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere]]. And Luke recounts many other things said and done in this appearance[[Luke 24:36||]].

paras.t: Gavisi sunt ergo discipuli, viso Domino dominorum, qui in femore suo scriptum habet : Rex regum et Dominus dominantium. Gaudium nempe est diffusio animi in conceptione boni, oriturque ex unione potentiæ cum bono convenienti. Quoniam ergo discipuli viderunt Jesum, summum et convenientissimum bonum, quem maxime diligebant, de cujus passione vehementer dolebant, cujus beatitudini cordialiter congratulabantur : ideo viso eo, ultra quam æstimari posset aut exprimi, lætabantur. Gavisi sunt autem propter Jesum, et propter se ipsos : quia magistro suo intime congaudebant ; et de suo profectu exhilarati sunt, videntes se non esse deceptos sequendo Jesum, propter quem omnia sua reliquerunt, et multa perpessi fuerunt ac patiebantur.
paras.en: [[20:20|The disciples therefore were glad, when they saw the Lord|Gavisi sunt ergo discipuli, viso Domino]] of lords, who hath on His thigh written: [[Apoc 19:16|KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS|Rex regum et Dominus dominantium]]. For joy is the expansion of the mind in the conceiving of a good, and arises from the union of a power with a fitting good. Since, then, the disciples saw Jesus, the highest and most fitting good, whom they loved most, for whose passion they grieved vehemently, in whose beatitude they heartily rejoiced with Him: therefore, seeing Him, they were glad beyond what could be reckoned or expressed. They rejoiced for Jesus' sake and for their own: because they rejoiced inwardly with their Master; and they were cheered at their own advancement, seeing that they had not been deceived in following Jesus, for whom they had left all they had[[Matt 19:27||]], and had suffered and were suffering much.

paras.t: Dixit ergo eis iterum : Pax vobis. Siquidem viso Domino Jesu, conturbati fuerunt atque conterriti, juxta Lucam : ideo repetit, Pax vobis. Quæ etiam repetitio, confirmationis indicium est, dilectionisque signum, et admonitio discipulorum ut pacem jugiter appetant, præcipueque exquirant. Vel, ideo bis ait, Pax vobis, quia optavit eis pacem gratiæ in præsenti, et pacem gloriæ in futuro. Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos : id est, quemadmodum Pater misit me ex vera caritate et pietate, ad prædicandum Evangelium vitæ Judæis, a quibus multas persecutiones, et tandem amarissimam perpessus sum mortem, quorum tamen hominum nonnullos converti; sic ego nunc mittam vos ad prædicandum evangelicam legem Judæis ac gentibus, ex caritate et pietate ad vos, et item ad illos, a quibus multa adversa et mortem sustinebitis, quosdam vero eorum convertetis.
paras.en: [[20:21|He said therefore to them again: Peace be to you|Dixit ergo eis iterum: Pax vobis]]. For on seeing the Lord Jesus they were troubled and terrified, according to Luke[[Luke 24:37||]]: therefore He repeats, Peace be to you. This repetition too is a token of confirmation and a sign of love, and an admonition to the disciples to seek peace constantly and to pursue it above all. Or, He says Peace be to you twice because He wished them the peace of grace in the present and the peace of glory in the future. [[20:21|As the Father hath sent me, I also send you|Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos]]: that is, as the Father sent Me out of true charity and loving-kindness to preach the Gospel of life to the Jews, from whom I suffered many persecutions and at last a most bitter death, and yet some of whom I converted; so I now will send you to preach the law of the Gospel to Jews and Gentiles, out of charity and loving-kindness towards you and likewise towards them, from whom you will endure many adversities and death, but some of whom you will convert.

paras.t: Hæc quum dixisset, insufflavit, et dixit eis : Accipite Spiritum Sanctum. Postquam Salvator dixit discipulis, Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos, infudit discipulis Spiritum Sanctum, quia officium prædicationis quod eis commisit, sine speciali gratia Spiritus Sancti expleri non valuit. Oportet enim ut prædicator verbi cœlestis, in se ipso abundet caritatis fervore, et sapientia divinorum, quatenus ignita proferat verba, motiva et penetrativa, sitque sententiosus, discretus et instructivus in sermonibus suis. Denique, per corporalem illam insufflationem et inspirationem, evidenter signavit superintellectualem atque æternam processionem seu spirationem qua Spiritus Sanctus ab ipso procedit, prout plenius probat Anselmus in libro de Processione Spiritus Sancti. Rursus, dicendo, Accipite Spiritum Sanctum, insinuavit se per auctoritatem dare Spiritum Sanctum : quod nequaquam sic esset, nisi Spiritus Sanctus ab ipso procederet. Sed nonne Apostoli ante hanc horam habuerunt Spiritum Sanctum? Habuerunt utique, non autem tam copiose et efficaciter, seu ad tot tantosque effectus, ut ex hac hora, quia et nunc data est omnibus eis potestas ligandi atque solvendi, sicut mox introducetur.
paras.en: [[20:22|When he had said this, he breathed on them; and he said to them: Receive ye the Holy Ghost|Hæc cum dixisset, insufflavit, et dixit eis: Accipite Spiritum Sanctum]]. After the Saviour had said to the disciples, As the Father hath sent me, I also send you, He poured the Holy Ghost into them, because the office of preaching which He committed to them could not be fulfilled without a special grace of the Holy Ghost. For the preacher of the heavenly word must abound in himself with the fervour of charity and with wisdom in divine things, so that he may utter fiery words, moving and piercing, and be weighty, discerning and instructive in his sermons. Further, by that bodily breathing and inbreathing He plainly signified the supra-intellectual and eternal procession or spiration by which the Holy Ghost proceeds from Him, as Anselm proves more fully in his book On the Procession of the Holy Ghost. Again, by saying, Receive ye the Holy Ghost, He intimated that He gives the Holy Ghost by authority: which would by no means be so unless the Holy Ghost proceeded from Him. But did not the Apostles have the Holy Ghost before this hour? They did indeed, but not so abundantly and effectively, or for so many and such great effects, as from this hour, since now too the power of binding and loosing was given to them all, as will shortly be brought in.

paras.t: Augustinus facit hic grandem quæstionem, cujus se solutionem nescire fatetur. Quærit ergo, cur Christus bis dedit Spiritum Sanctum, semel in terra ante ascensionem, et semel de cœlo post ascensionem. Tangit autem Augustinus quamdam solutionem sub dubio, puta quod ideo, quoniam duo sunt præcepta caritatis. Quam rationem Gregorius et Beda affirmant esse hujus rei causam, videlicet, quod in terra dedit, ut diligatur proximus, deinde de cœlo, ut diligatur Deus. Sed quia per eamdem gratiam utrumque præceptum impletur, nec unum sine alio valet impleri, imo et unus est habitus caritatis qua Deus proximusque diligitur, ideo potest alia ratio assignari. Ut enim Dionysius docet, Natura non procedit a distanti in distans, nisi per medium. Quem processum auctor naturæ Deus sublimis et benedictus, observat frequenter, præsertim quum teste Apostolo, Quæ a Deo sunt, ordinata sunt. Unde et admonet : Omnia decenter et secundum ordinem fiant in vobis. Hinc ergo Christus sapientia Patris, disponens universa suaviter, suos discipulos paulatim ad sublimiora attollens, ac pedetentim ad perfectionem perducens, primo dedit eis Spiritum Sanctum in terra per insufflationem, non in tanta plenitudine, nec in signo tam evidenti ut postea, quatenus per istam ad illam exuberantissimam Spiritus Sancti susceptionem quæ facta est in die sancto Pentecostes, disponerentur.
paras.en: Augustine here raises a great question, the solution of which he confesses he does not know. He asks, then, why Christ gave the Holy Ghost twice, once on earth before the ascension and once from heaven after the ascension. Augustine touches, though doubtfully, on one solution: namely that it was because there are two precepts of charity. This reason Gregory and Bede affirm to be the cause of the matter: that He gave the Spirit on earth that our neighbour may be loved, and then from heaven that God may be loved. But since both precepts are fulfilled by the same grace, and one cannot be fulfilled without the other, and indeed there is one habit of charity by which God and neighbour are loved, another reason can be assigned. For as Dionysius teaches, nature does not proceed from one extreme to another except through a mean. This procedure God, the sublime and blessed author of nature, frequently observes, especially since, as the Apostle witnesses, [[Rom 13:1|those that are ordained of God|Quæ a Deo sunt, ordinata sunt]]. Whence he also admonishes: [[1 Cor 14:40|let all things be done decently and according to order|Omnia decenter et secundum ordinem]] among you. Hence Christ, the wisdom of the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]], ordering all things sweetly[[Wis 8:1||]], raising His disciples little by little to higher things and leading them step by step to perfection, first gave them the Holy Ghost on earth by breathing, not in such fullness nor with so evident a sign as afterwards, so that by this they might be disposed for that most overflowing reception of the Holy Ghost which took place on the holy day of Pentecost.

paras.t: Quorum remiseritis peccata, eos legitime absolvendo, et divinæ virtuti, quæ sola dimittit peccata ut causa principalis, instrumentaliter vi clavium cooperando, remittuntur eis a Deo, saltem quoad culpam, non tamen semper aut totaliter quantum ad pœnam. Tamen, per orationem sacerdotis virtutemque clavium, et per pudorem ac contritionem confitentis, aliquid pœnæ dimittitur, tanto utique amplius, quanto pudor et contritio fuerint fortiores. Possent enim esse tam magni, quod tota pœna dimitteretur. Et quorum peccata retinueritis, id est, non dimiseritis, sed retinenda judicaveritis, eo quod non vere pœniteant, nec dignos se præbeant ad indulgentiam obtinendam, retenta sunt, id est, Deus illa imputabit hominibus talibus. Oportet itaque ut judicium Ecclesiæ conformetur divino judicio, servando videlicet rectum processum, et debitum clavium usum. Unde ultimo Ecclesiasticæ hierarchiæ capitulo, ait Theologus : Sacerdotes hierarchicis sibi collatis virtutibus uti oportet, prout Deitas moverit eos. Agens enim instrumentale non sortitur efficaciam, nisi secundum quod a principali causa movetur. Propter quod profitetur Apostolus : Secundum potestatem quæ data est mihi in ædificationem, et non in destructionem.
paras.en: [[20:23|Whose sins you shall forgive|Quorum remiseritis peccata]], by lawfully absolving them, and cooperating instrumentally by the power of the keys with the divine power, which alone forgives sins as principal cause, [[20:23|they are forgiven them|remittuntur eis]] by God, at least as to the guilt, though not always or wholly as to the punishment. Yet by the prayer of the priest and the power of the keys, and by the shame and contrition of the penitent, something of the punishment is remitted, and the more so the stronger the shame and contrition are. For they could be so great that the whole punishment would be remitted. [[20:23|And whose sins you shall retain|Et quorum retinueritis]], that is, do not forgive, but judge must be retained, because they do not truly repent nor show themselves worthy to obtain pardon, [[20:23|they are retained|retenta sunt]], that is, God will impute them to such men. The judgement of the Church, therefore, must be conformed to the divine judgement, by keeping a right procedure and the due use of the keys. Whence in the last chapter of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy the Theologian [[that is, Dionysius]] says: Priests must use the hierarchical powers conferred on them as the Godhead moves them. For an instrumental agent has no efficacy except as it is moved by the principal cause. Wherefore the Apostle professes: [[2 Cor 13:10|according to the power which the Lord hath given me unto edification and not unto destruction|Secundum potestatem quæ data est mihi in ædificationem, et non in destructionem]].

paras.t: Itaque Christus nunc ait et confert universis Apostolis, quod ante passionem Petro singulariter dixit : Quodcumque, inquiens, ligaveris super terram, erit ligatum et in cœlis ; et quodcumque solveris super terram, erit solutum et in cœlis. Ideo autem Petro tanquam principaliori inter Apostolos et capiti universalis Ecclesiæ, hoc dictum est singulariter, ut quum sit ordo in Ecclesia, hæc potestas credatur primo ac principaliter residere in summo Pontifice, S. Petri vicario, atque ab ipso derivari in archiepiscopos et episcopos, et ab ipsis tanquam a mediis, in simplices sacerdotes. Verumtamen, quamvis omnis sacerdos in sua ordinatione ligandi ac solvendi potestatem recipiat, quum secundum Thomam, realiter idem sint character sacerdotalis, et potestas prædicta, quæ etiam clavis vocatur; non tamen habet hujus potestatis exsecutionem, nisi ei subjiciatur materia, scilicet homines super quos sibi jurisdictio detur, seu cura animarum committatur a superiore, qui sicut dat eam inferiori, sic potest eam ei auferre in toto vel parte, legitima causa occurrente.
paras.en: So Christ now says to, and confers on, all the Apostles what before the passion He said to Peter singly: [[Matt 16:19|whatsoever thou shalt bind upon earth, it shall be bound also in heaven|Quodcumque … ligaveris … et in cœlis]]. It was said to Peter singly, as the chief among the Apostles and head of the universal Church, so that, there being order in the Church, this power may be believed to reside first and principally in the supreme Pontiff, the vicar of St Peter, and to be derived from him to archbishops and bishops, and from them, as intermediaries, to simple priests. Nevertheless, although every priest receives in his ordination the power of binding and loosing, since according to Thomas the priestly character and the said power, which is also called the key, are really the same, yet he does not have the exercise of this power unless matter is subjected to him, namely men over whom jurisdiction is given him, or the care of souls is committed to him by a superior; who, as he gives it to the inferior, so can take it from him in whole or in part, when a lawful cause arises.

paras.t: Præterea, Christus dicendo discipulis, Quorum remiseritis peccata, etc., manifeste ostendit se esse verum Deum, qui solus potest tantam conferre potestatem hominibus, quæ nec angelis data est. Decuit autem ut postquam Deus assumpsit humanam naturam, homines ab illo acciperent divinam virtutem, et supernaturalem quamdam deificationem : quod maxime datum est sacerdotibus, per hoc quod sunt dispensatores sacramentorum novæ legis, in quibus gratia continetur et datur. Omnibus quoque fidelibus datur deificatio talis, per diversa dona et gratiam Spiritus Sancti, secundum quod in epistola canonica Petri inducitur : Maxima et pretiosa nobis promissa donavit, ut per hæc efficiamini divinæ consortes naturæ. — Postremo, de hac materia, et quid sit clavis, et quomodo sacerdos evangelicæ legis dicatur peccata dimittere, an scilicet aliquid cooperando, vel dumtaxat ostendendo, de verbis quoque Hieronymi circa hoc, plurima dixi super Matthæum : quæ non sunt hoc loco repetenda, quamvis ista sine illis plene intelligi nequeant.
paras.en: Further, Christ, by saying to the disciples, Whose sins you shall forgive, etc., plainly showed Himself to be true God, who alone can confer on men so great a power, one not given even to the angels. And it was fitting that, after God had assumed human nature, men should receive from Him a divine power and a certain supernatural deification: which is given above all to priests, in that they are dispensers of the sacraments of the new law, in which grace is contained and given. Such deification is also given to all the faithful, through the divers gifts and grace of the Holy Ghost, as is set down in the canonical epistle of Peter: [[2 Pet 1:4|he hath given us most great and precious promises: that by these you may be made partakers of the divine nature|Maxima et pretiosa nobis promissa donavit, ut per hæc efficiamini divinæ consortes naturæ]]. — Lastly, on this matter, what the key is, how the priest of the Gospel law is said to forgive sins, whether by cooperating in some way or only by declaring, and on Jerome's words about it, I said a great deal on Matthew[[Matt 16:19||]]: which is not to be repeated here, though these things cannot be fully understood without it.

paras.t: Dedit itaque Christus Apostolis eorumque successoribus divinam et admirabilem potestatem, qua alios possunt solvere et ligare, a regno excludere, et in illud inducere. Sed videant ministri Ecclesiæ ut tanta virtute digne utantur, exsistendo in gratia, causasque confitentium sapienter pensando ac discernendo, et privatum amorem ac odium, ceterasque inordinatas affectiones penitus repellendo : quoniam si indignos absolvant, vel dignos ligent, dicetur de eis illud Ezechielis : Interfecerunt animas quæ non moriuntur, et vivificabant animas quæ non vivunt.
paras.en: So Christ gave the Apostles and their successors a divine and wonderful power, by which they can loose and bind others, shut them out of the kingdom and bring them into it.
